title: CK3 Elder Traits Explained: What Replaced the Infirm Trait
metaDescription: CK3 retired the old Infirm trait for a new tiered Elder Traits system. Here's how Faltering Heart, Fragile Bones, Clouded Eyes, and Withering Mind actually work.
keywords: ck3 elder traits, ck3 infirm trait, ck3 aging system, ck3 faltering heart, ck3 domain limit stewardship
content:
If you have played Crusader Kings 3 for long, you have met the Infirm trait. It arrived slowly, dragged down a ruler's stats, and then usually killed them. For years it was the game's one-size-fits-all marker of old age, the same generic debuff slapped on every aging character regardless of how they had lived. In the Realm Maintenance update, whose open beta began March 30 2026, Paradox retired that single catch-all and replaced it with something far more interesting: a tiered Elder Traits system built from specific, named afflictions.

This is live, current content, not a preview. The system was already in open beta when this went to print, so everything here is the real mechanic rather than a promise about a future patch. The change matters because aging in CK3 is no longer one flat tax on your ruler. It has become four separate stories, each with its own name, its own mechanical penalty, and its own way of getting worse.

## Why the Infirm trait retired

The Infirm trait was simple and, after a few hundred hours of play, dull. A character became Infirm, their abilities dropped, and everyone moved on. The new system replaces that with Elder Traits: specific, named afflictions that reflect genuine medieval-style ailments rather than one generic debuff.

Faltering Heart, Fragile Bones, Clouded Eyes, and Withering Mind are the four confirmed traits. Each carries its own unique mechanical penalty, which matters far more than it sounds. A ruler losing their eyesight is not having the same problem as a ruler whose mind is going, and the game now treats those as meaningfully different situations rather than funneling everyone through the same Infirm-shaped hole.

For anyone who worries this is just cosmetic wrapping on the old system, the rest of the design pushes back: these traits start mild and get worse over time. Aging is a progression now, not an instant debuff. Your middle-aged ruler might develop a mild health issue that stays a background nuisance, or it might grow into something that genuinely changes how you play them.

## The four Elder Traits

What determines how a trait manifests and how quickly it progresses? The confirmed framing is threefold: the character's lifestyle, their genetic factors, and an element of luck. How your ruler has lived their life feeds directly into what kind of old age they end up with. A warrior who spent decades at war is building toward a different set of elder problems than a scholar who rarely left the court.

Maintaining health and managing stress are described as crucial to coping with, or slowing, these traits. This is a nice piece of design in practice: old age stops being something that simply happens to you and becomes something you can partially steer. Keep your ruler's health up, keep their stress down, and the odds tilt in your favor. Let stress spiral and health slide, and the afflictions are more likely to bite harder and arrive faster.

The new events triggered by Elder Traits are not just ruler problems. The traits of family members or loved ones become relevant too. A wife with Clouded Eyes, an heir with Withering Mind, a beloved uncle slowly losing his strength to Fragile Bones: these are now gameplay moments rather than background flavor. The strategy layer around your court has to account for what is happening to the people around you, not just the person you control.

## Domain limit and the Story Tracker

The Realm Maintenance update bundled several other changes alongside the aging rework, and two are worth knowing about even though they fall outside the Elder Traits system itself.

First, the domain limit rework. Stewardship no longer affects a ruler's domain limit. The developers' own community has described this as the most controversial change in the update, and it is easy to see why: high-stewardship characters previously stacked a much larger domain than intended, turning stewardship into the game's most reliable expansion stat. The exact new formula was not detailed, so treat the change directionally: stewardship is now about income and efficiency rather than raw territory count, and a sprawling personal domain takes a different kind of ruler.

Second, the Story Tracker. This new feature surfaces and tracks the game's existing story cycle content, the recurring narrative event chains that have been in CK3 for a long time. The developers say this content had previously been hidden away and hard for players to actually notice or follow. The Story Tracker pulls those chains into view so you can see what narrative threads your characters are actually living through.

The update as a whole bundled more than 1,500 bug fixes, adjustments, and changes, which in CK3 terms is a genuinely enormous patch. The aging rework is the headline, but it arrived inside one of the biggest single updates the game has seen.

## The opt-out rules

If the new system is not for you, the game rules are the answer. A setting lets you revert to the old Infirm-only system, giving you the familiar single trait back instead of the tiered afflictions. A separate option can disable all aging consequences entirely, which is the nuclear choice for anyone who simply does not want their ruler to grow old.

That second option comes with a real cost: choosing it disables achievements. Your save will still work and your dynasty will still rule, but the achievement track is turned off for that campaign. It is a clean tradeoff, and it means the Elder Traits system is opt-in by design rather than forced on every player.

My genuine opinion: the tiered system is the better game. The old Infirm trait was a clock ticking toward death with no texture. These four traits, with their mild-to-severe progression and their entanglement with lifestyle and stress, turn your ruler's final decades into something you actively manage. And the fact that your family's elder traits matter too makes the dynastic fantasy stronger, not weaker. Old age was always coming in CK3. Now it actually has something to say before it arrives.

title: CK3 Silk and Silver: How the Merchant Playstyle Actually Works
metaDescription: A deep dive into CK3 Silk and Silver's Merchant playstyle: Trade Routes, Commission Routes, the Silk Road bonus group, and how loans and Usury work.
keywords: ck3 silk and silver merchants, ck3 merchant playstyle, ck3 trade routes, ck3 commission routes, ck3 loans usury
content:
If you have read the site's [Silk and Silver overview](/blog/ck3-silk-and-silver-preview/), you already know the shape of the expansion: a new trade system, roughly 900 duchy markets, playable Republics, and Merchants as the landless side of the commercial coin. This guide goes one level deeper, into the Merchant playstyle specifically. It is built from the two dev diaries that have focused on merchants, Dev Diary #3, Profit Above All: Merchants Vision, and the direct follow-up that iterated on it, and everything here is confirmed design rather than live content. Silk and Silver still has no release date, and it remains deep in development, so treat each detail below as the current confirmed picture rather than locked-in final mechanics.

One clarification so nothing gets tangled: this is not By God Alone. That expansion is the religion overhaul. Silk and Silver is the trade one, and everything in this guide belongs to the trade side of the Chapter V equation.

## The confirmed Merchant systems

Merchants come with a bundle of named systems that the developers established in the first merchant diary and reference directly in the follow-up: Merchant Monopolies, Trade Expertise, Trade Contracts, Company Domicile, and the Merchant's relationship to their Patron. Those are all confirmed real parts of the playstyle, and the honest state of the research is that beyond the names, no further mechanical detail has been shared publicly yet. A preview article can get a lot of words out of guessing what these systems do, and this one will not do that. What the developers have confirmed is written below, nothing more.

## Trade routes, commission routes, and rival families

Merchants make their living on trade routes. Their own regular trade routes are profit-motivated, the merchant's core business of moving goods between markets. Sitting alongside them are Commission Routes: offers that landed rulers regularly send to merchants in order to meet trade needs between markets. The merchant takes the job, and the ruler pays for it.

The rivalries are just as important as the routes. The follow-up dev diary dives specifically into the interplay between competing Merchant Families, confirming that rival merchant dynasties are a designed source of tension rather than background flavor. Two merchant houses serving the same cities are not simply coexisting, they are competing for the same contracts, the same routes, and the same favor. For the full mechanics of routes and their costs, the site's [Silk and Silver overview](/blog/ck3-silk-and-silver-preview/) covers them in detail; this guide focuses on the systems the overview deliberately left shallow.

## The Silk Road Participant Group

Merchants operating within the Silk Road region belong to a new Participant Group. The group grants bonuses to three things: the maximum Route Length a merchant can run, Route Capacity, and Expertise decay, which is how quickly a merchant's trade expertise erodes over time. How large those bonuses are depends on the active Phase in the merchant's geographical sub-region. No specific figures for these bonuses were given in the dev diary, and this guide will not invent any. The confirmed shape is that the Silk Road is not a flat bonus field: it is a set of sub-regions, each in its own phase that changes how much the group helps a merchant there.

There is an important ownership clarification here, because this is the detail most likely to confuse a player who does not own the other expansion. The Silk Road Participant Group works for anyone who owns Silk and Silver. It does not require the separate All Under Heaven DLC to function at all. What is gated behind owning both expansions is only the group's interaction with the Dynastic Cycle mechanic, since Dynastic Cycle is a system that belongs to All Under Heaven, not to Silk and Silver. Own only Silk and Silver and the group works and its bonuses apply. Own both, and the Dynastic Cycle interaction comes into play on top of them.

## Usury, loans, and the Creditor focus

Lending is where the merchant playstyle gets openly flavorful. A new Usury Doctrine has been added, which gives each faith its own distinct stance on lending money and profiting from it. Some faiths will treat moneylending as everyday commerce, and others as a sin, and the doctrine shapes how the realm around you reacts to the practice.

The crucial mechanical line is that any Merchant can Loan Gold, regardless of their doctrine. Doctrine changes the moral and social framing, not the availability. A merchant who wants to make lending their whole identity can take the Creditor focus, which turns moneylending from an occasional side activity into the character's primary business.

When a merchant loans gold, the offer is not pocket change. It is a substantial sum scaled to the landed ruler's income, because the whole point is leverage. In exchange for the gold, the merchant receives a Strong Hook over the ruler, and that relationship lasts for exactly as long as the debt remains outstanding. Picture the gameplay and the design intent is obvious: a merchant can put a kingdom into debt and hold a firm lever of influence over its throne until that debt is paid. Players coming from EU4 will recognize the strategic theme, and the site's [EU4 trade power, merchants, and steering guide](/blog/eu4-trade-power-merchants-steering/) covers the same commercial-leverage ideas in EU4's own mechanics.

## What to watch next

Two specific things are worth tracking in the next Silk and Silver dev diaries. First, how the Silk Road Participant Group's Phases are determined: by geography, trade flows, era, or something else entirely. That single decision decides how central the region is to the merchant experience. Second, how the Usury Doctrine plays out across faiths with different stances, since a merchant operating in a realm whose faith condemns lending is a very different strategic animal from one working where lending is blessed.

The follow-up dev diary is clear that the developers are still iterating on all of this, so this guide, like the overview, is a living document that will be refreshed as new diaries publish. The shape already on the table is concrete enough to plan around, though. The Silk Road group decides how much geography matters, the Usury doctrine decides how much faith matters, and the Strong Hook decides how much debt matters. That is a merchant playstyle with real texture, and it will only get sharper as the developers finish iterating on it.

title: CK3 Silk and Silver: Everything Confirmed About the New Trade and Republics Expansion
metaDescription: Crusader Kings III's Silk and Silver expansion reworks trade and adds playable Republics and Merchants. Here's everything confirmed so far.
keywords: ck3 silk and silver, ck3 republics, ck3 trade rework, ck3 merchant government, crusader kings 3 silk and silver
content:
Silk and Silver is the other half of Crusader Kings III's Chapter V line-up. Where By God Alone is the religion overhaul, Silk and Silver is the economic one: a new expansion that promises to rework the economy of the entire game. It was announced as part of the Chapter V reveal in April 2026, and it is still in active development. As of this guide, the developers have published six dev diaries on it, and the most recent one, from September 15 2026, confirms they are deep in the iteration phase, still refining systems based on feedback. There is no confirmed exact release date yet, with the expansion expected by late 2026.

One quick clarification before we start: this is not By God Alone. The two are separate, unrelated expansions in the same content pass, and it is worth keeping them distinct. By God Alone is about the Church and religious systems. Silk and Silver is about trade, cities, and the power of money. If you are here for the trade rework, you are in the right place.

The material below comes from the official developer diary series, read directly, cross-corroborated against independent press coverage. Because the project is explicitly still iterating, treat everything here as a strong picture of the design rather than locked-in final mechanics.

## Merchants and Republics: the two new government types

The heart of Silk and Silver is a pair of brand-new government types: Merchants and Republics. They sit at opposite ends of the same commercial idea.

Merchants are landless. They live on trade, moving goods and money between markets rather than ruling territory. Republics are the landed version: small, tightly-packed city-states inspired by, but not limited to, historical Venice, Florence, and the free cities of the Holy Roman Empire. Paradox frames them as a playstyle for people who do not want to go wide and build a massive realm, and who would rather focus on internal politicking, scheming, changing laws, and trade. Every republic has a ruler plus patricians who trade in some fashion to fund their political endeavors.

Republics feature a unique assembly voting mechanic. Players have to navigate internal politics and buy influence to stay in power, because big decisions are made in the assembly rather than by royal decree. Noble families within a republic have their own ambitions and can influence laws through parliament, pursuing their own political influence. The court of public opinion weighs more heavily here than under a monarchy: being a very unpopular ruler in a republic can have real consequences.

Republics also grow differently from normal realms. Instead of seizing territory, a republic develops its capital and gradually raises its level, expanding inward rather than outward. Merchants can travel to and from a Republic and retain their accumulated improvements when they do, which makes the two government types natural partners.

There is a real historical thread underneath all of it. Many famous historical republics began as communal city-states before growing semi-tyrannical under the grip of a single family, and the developers are explicitly drawing on that arc. They wanted families to matter, and to both squabble and plot together, which is why the patrician dynasties sit at the center of the experience.

The most recent dev diary digs deeper into the merchant side and introduces the pieces that make a merchant company tick: Merchant Monopolies, Trade Expertise, Trade Contracts, a Company Domicile, and the merchant's relationship with their Patron. Competing merchant families are a focus too, with the developers showing how they push up against each other. None of this should be read as final, since this part of the system is exactly what the iteration phase is reshaping. The merchant side of the expansion now has its own [dedicated deep-dive](/blog/ck3-silk-and-silver-merchants/).

## Trade, routes, and commercial rivalry

The trade system is the other half of the expansion, and it is built around roughly 900 distinct duchy markets. Merchant governments move goods across the map, with silk and silver as the named examples, to meet specific building requirements. The result is realm prosperity tied to real supply lines rather than passive gold generation.

Merchants get two types of trade routes. Regular trade routes are their own business, built for profit. Commission routes are created specifically by order of a ruler, who hires a merchant to move goods between markets. A merchant can hold up to four commission routes at once, depending on their company size level. The merchant receives an upfront lump sum for starting one, but acts only as a middleman: they cannot assign traders, make changes to the route, or earn Trade Expertise or monthly income while it is active. Commission routes last ten years, and a merchant can cancel one early if a better offer comes around, refunding some of the money and picking up a secret tied to a new fame trait called the Dealbreaker.

Routes are managed by a dedicated trader role, which can increase a route's profitability, capacity, or trading expertise. The better your trader, the more value you extract from each line.

Competition is a contact sport. Rivals can be lured away, sabotaged, stripped of trading privileges, or absorbed entirely through mergers or hostile takeovers. If you have played the trade side of EU4, the strategic shape here will feel familiar, and the site's [EU4 trade power, merchants, and steering guide](/blog/eu4-trade-power-merchants-steering/) and [EU4 trade companies guide](/blog/eu4-trade-companies-explained/) cover the equivalent systems in depth.

Loans are a separate system that sits on top of all this. Merchants can issue gold to a ruler at interest, gaining leverage and expecting repayment over time. Money in Silk and Silver is a political weapon as much as a commercial one.

## Trade posts and trade leagues: the Hanseatic hook

Trade Posts are a new kind of district that a republic can establish in someone else's territory. Every county in the world can have one, though your patricians are limited in how many they can hold at any one time. Posts serve as forward bases for commerce: they can negotiate culturally exclusive mercenaries, or improve goods prices via specific buildings, pulling foreign territory into your commercial web whether its ruler welcomes it or not.

Trade leagues are the collective version of that ambition. Explicitly inspired by the historical Hanseatic League, they let multiple republics pool their resources and dominate markets together. The developers position a successful league at the top of the game's hierarchy, with members able to overpower less well-connected rivals through sheer combined influence.

## Buying victories is about to get much harder

One of the quietest but most significant changes is a hard limit on mercenary usage. The developers are introducing a cap specifically to stop players from simply buying military victory, something they note was always curious: anyone with a lot of money could in theory throw enough gold at a war to win it.

Republics start with a slightly higher mercenary limit than other government types, to compensate for their generally lower inherent military strength. The goal is to reward players who are actually good at war, not just rich.

And a final reminder on where this all stands. Silk and Silver is still deep in the iteration phase, with systems being tuned against community feedback, so none of what is described here is locked-in final design. This guide is a living document and will be updated as new dev diary entries publish. The broad shape is clear, though: trade becomes a battleground between merchant dynasties, and the economy of the entire game is about to change.

title: EU4 Estates, Crownland, Privileges, and the Disaster Nobody Warns You About
metaDescription: EU4 estates and crownland explained: the 100-influence disaster trigger, how Seize Land and conquest really work, and the loyalty catch players keep missing.
content:
Every EU4 estate has a disaster the game never really warns you about until it is already ticking. Let any single estate's influence hit 100, and its disaster begins ticking toward firing. Let it keep ticking, and it fires: the Nobility's Aristocratic Coup, the Ghilmans' Ghilman Independence, the Janissaries' Janissary Independence, the Eunuchs' Domination of the Eunuchs. Different names, different governments, exactly the same trigger. And when it fires, it is not a flavor event. It is a persistent national penalty that outlasts the dramatic screen: a -40% modifier in most cases, and -20% for a Nobility takeover. That single threshold quietly causes more campaign-ending surprises than any other estate mechanic, and it is confirmed identically across the wiki's individual estate pages.

The reason this needs its own article instead of a wiki page link is that players have been tripping over this system's quieter edges for years. A 2021 forum thread shows a player genuinely baffled by the core tradeoff: privileges that grant bonuses but cost crownland, plus a mysterious event that gives crownland back while piling on autonomy they did not understand. A 2022 thread shows someone convinced Seize Land is broken because it suddenly returned nothing, when the real cause was a specific privilege quietly protecting an estate from losing land. These are not isolated cases. The wiki explains the pieces accurately. Nobody had assembled the whole picture into one place. Now there is one place

## The 100 influence disaster, and why it is universal

The influence figure is not a soft suggestion. At 100 influence, an estate's disaster starts ticking toward triggering, and the only way to stop it is to push that estate's influence back under the line. The wiki confirms the same structural rule across the Nobility, the Ghilmans, the Janissaries, and the Eunuchs, which are about as different a set of estates as this game has, belonging to completely different governments, cultures, and regions. If the trigger repeated for only one estate, you could call it flavor. It repeating across all of them is the tell that it is a deliberate, universal design rule rather than an accident any single nation introduced. That is genuinely good design in a genre where disaster conditions often feel bolted on per-nation. Here, the game is telling any government, anywhere on the map, to treat estate influence as a hard ceiling instead of a soft preference.

The lasting penalty matters because it changes how you should read a lost disaster. This is not a burst of rebels you deal with and move on from. When an estate seizes control of the nation, the country carries the aftermath: -40% for most estate takeovers, and -20% specifically for a Nobility coup. Losing is survivable, and it is also a real, compounding setback you will feel in your numbers for years afterward. That is exactly why keeping every estate under 100 influence should sit near the top of your estate routine, not in the emergency drawer.

## What crownland actually is

Crownland is the share of your realm's land that the crown controls directly, rather than the share divided among the estates. It is not a set of specific provinces highlighted on the map. It is an abstract percentage representing the balance of power between you and your estates. Most nations start a campaign at a base 30% crownland. The Papal States are a notable exception, starting at 50%, which is part of why they feel unusually strong and stable in the early game.

Why bother raising it? A higher crownland share unlocks better bonuses as your realm becomes more centralized. This is the entire reason the privileges-versus-crownland tradeoff exists. Privileges buy you useful effects today, at the cost of the long-term centralization you could otherwise earn. Every privilege you hand out is a small, quiet bet that the short-term bonus is worth more than the permanent drift toward centralization. Sometimes it is. Sometimes you are just pushing an estate closer to the 100 influence line without meaning to

## Seize Land, and the privilege that makes it look broken

The Seize Land interaction is the crown's main proactive tool for taking back unused power from the estates. It can be used once every five years, and it provides an instant 5% boost to crownland. That is not a wiki approximation, it matches the actual experience of real players precisely. The cost is a real loyalty hit to the estates you seize from, and the exact number varies between circumstances and sources, so treat it as a real loyalty cost rather than a single fixed figure you can plan around to the decimal.

The part that trips up veterans and new players alike is this: certain privileges explicitly protect specific estates from losing land when you use Seize Land. If you have handed out land-protecting privileges to every estate, Seize Land returns nothing, because every estate is protected. Players have reported this as a bug for years, convinced the interaction is broken. It is not broken. It is working exactly as the protecting privileges requested. The wiki describes the protections correctly, but until you know they exist, they read as a silent bug rather than a cause. This is the kind of self-inflicted confusion that clears up the instant you know the pieces, which is the whole point of this guide.

One more honest note before we move on: privilege availability is not uniform across installs. Some privileges are gated behind expansions, with the Emperor DLC being a well-known example. If you are missing a privilege someone on a forum insists you take, the short answer is often that they own a DLC you do not. Which expansions are actually worth owning is its own question, and the site's [best EU4 DLC guide](/blog/best-eu4-dlc/) answers it without bloat.

## The quieter crownland levers

Seize Land is the obvious crownland lever. It is not the only one, and two others are easy to miss entirely.

Developing a province adds 0.2 crownland each time you develop it. It is a small number, but it is real, and it escalates: every development click is a tiny step toward centralization on top of whatever province improvement you wanted anyway. Players who develop aggressively end up with noticeably higher crownland than players who ignore development, and the wiki's crownland thresholds reflect exactly that pattern.

Conquest works differently than most players assume. Taking new territory does not simply add crownland in a flat lump. Instead, your crownland percentage shifts toward a midpoint that is influenced by estate power and your absolutism level. In practice this means that very low crownland recovers a meaningful share on conquest, because the shift pulls you upward, while very high crownland can actually nudge slightly down on new conquest, which surprises players expecting a flat addition. It is a balancing system, not a reward bank. Absolutism is one of the pieces that feeds into that equilibrium, and it is part of the larger government reform system covered on this site in the [Government Reforms guide](/blog/eu4-government-reforms/)

## The privilege tradeoff, framed properly

If there is a single mental model that makes the whole estates system click, it is this: estates trade you power for linear bonuses, and the bill always comes due somewhere. A privilege gives you a bonus you can feel today, costs you crownland you will want tomorrow, and pushes the estate holding it closer to the 100 influence disaster line. All three of those effects are happening at once, which is why the system feels opaque. Players usually notice the bonus immediately, forget the crownland until they wonder why their realm stopped centralizing, and then meet the disaster cold when influence finally peaks.

The fix is not to avoid privileges entirely. The fix is to treat them like a portfolio: check influence before every grant, keep Seize Land on its five-year clock so you are clawing crownland back steadily rather than in a panic, and never let any single estate accumulate enough power to matter more than your crown does. New players lose more campaigns to this system than to most battles, which is exactly why it is a recurring entry in the site's [list of common EU4 beginner mistakes](/blog/eu4-beginner-mistakes/).

## Crownland is a balance sheet, and the disaster is the audit

Every five years, the crown gets to rebalance the sheet. Every privilege writes a new line item on it. And every estate influence bar is a countdown that only runs one direction. The game does not make a big deal out of the 100 influence threshold when you start a campaign, and it will not remind you as an estate approaches it, which is precisely why the disaster keeps surprising people who have played for hundreds of hours. Check the influence tab with the same loyalty you give your borders. Keep every estate under the line. And when Seize Land suddenly stops returning crownland, check the privileges before you blame the code. The system works the way it is designed to work. It just was never all written down in one place, until now.

title: EU5 1.4 Combat Changes: Cavalry Nerfed, Sieges Reworked
metaDescription: EU5's update 1.4 lowers cavalry combat power, cuts flanking bonuses, and changes how forts surrender. Here's every confirmed combat and siege change so far.
keywords: eu5 1.4 combat changes, eu5 cavalry nerf, eu5 siege changes, eu5 flanking bonus, eu5 napoleonic warfare
content:
If you fight wars in Europa Universalis V, update 1.4 touches you. It does not touch some niche single-country system or a corner of the map most players ignore. It rebalances cavalry, the punchiest unit class in open battle, and it changes how every siege resolves. Both are core to nearly every campaign, which is exactly why these changes deserve their own guide rather than living only inside the general [1.4 hub article](/blog/eu5-update-1-4-rio-salado/).

One important framing note up front. Everything here comes from Tinto Talks 118, posted July 29 2026, and it is all preview content for update 1.4. None of these values are live in the current build, and update 1.4 is not in open beta yet. Treat these as confirmed developer-diary numbers, not something you can test right now. The current versions of these mechanics are covered in the site's [EU5 combat guide](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) and [EU5 sieges guide](/blog/eu5-sieges-explained/), and this piece is specifically about what changes in 1.4.

## The cavalry rebalance

Cavalry gets hit in three separate places, and together they add up to a genuine repositioning of the unit class.

Combat power drops from 4 to 3.25. That alone is roughly a 19% reduction in raw punch, and it matters for every cavalry stack on the field regardless of what bonuses you have layered on top.

Then the flanking bonus gets flattened hard. Previously, light cavalry flanked at +110% and heavy cavalry at +100%. In 1.4 both drop to a flat +60%. This is the most strategically significant cut in the update. Flanking is the mechanic that lets cavalry swing around and punish the edges of an enemy line, and the biggest single reduction falls on light cavalry, which loses more than half of its flanking bonus. Heavy cavalry also starts the update lower than it was, but proportionally it is the safer of the two.

The Napoleonic Warfare advance gets reworked too. It previously let cavalry ignore zones of control, which made it excellent at slipping behind enemy lines to cut supply lines and pounce on reinforcements. In 1.4 it instead grants +5% discipline. Discipline is a strong stat, and the advance is still worth taking on that basis alone, but the tactical job it does changes completely: you lose the behind-the-lines mobility trick and gain a flat combat quality boost instead.

For a fuller picture of how these numbers fit into the wider system, the site's [EU5 combat guide](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) walks through the current mechanics in depth.

## The siege changes: a stepping stone, not the end

Sieges get two changes, and both nudge them toward faster resolutions.

Artillery now needs only 2 regiments per bonus point against forts, down from 3. Practically, this means a besieging army reaches its artillery bonus with a smaller train, or pushes more bonus points with the same guns. Sieges should resolve somewhat faster and cost somewhat less in heavy-unit upkeep.

The surrender threshold also changes in kind, not just in number. Forts previously surrendered below 10 defenders, a flat count. In 1.4 the threshold becomes percentage-based: a fort auto-surrender below 5% of its garrison strength. That is a real difference in how the rule works, because a large, well-provisioned garrison now capitulates at a far higher absolute number of troops than a small one. Whatever the raw defender count, the fort gives up once it is reduced to a twentieth of its strength.

Here is the honest bit worth remembering. The developers explicitly describe these siege changes as a small stepping stone ahead of a larger, more comprehensive siege rework planned for a future update, 1.5. The changes above are the first touch, not the final word. If you go looking for the end state of EU5 sieges, the short answer is that it has not been designed yet.

For the current mechanic in full, the site's [EU5 sieges guide](/blog/eu5-sieges-explained/) covers how forts and garrisons work today.

## What it means for your next campaign

The practical takeaway is pretty direct. If your current strategy leans on a heavy cavalry flanking wing, 1.4 is going to make that noticeably weaker, and light cavalry flanking pays for most of the update's bill. It is not a death sentence for the class, cavalry still hits hard and the +5% discipline path still rewards invested players, but the old expectation that a cavalry wing can win a battle by itself is squarely what Paradox is trimming.

Combine that with faster, cheaper sieges and the shape of 1.4 warfare is: lean on line infantry and artillery, stop expecting flanking alone to decide big battles, and get used to forts falling a little sooner than they used to. Adapting to that shape before the update lands is genuinely the winning move.

title: EU5 Cabinet and Courtiers Explained
metaDescription: EU5 cabinet and courtiers: where characters come from, how marriage grows the candidate pool, and why character skills drive combat, sieges, and institutions.
content:
Every EU5 mechanics guide on this site has bumped into the same unopened door. The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) takes generals and admirals as a given, and its diplomacy math quietly assumes you have characters worth appointing. The [Combat guide](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) mentions that a general's Diplomacy skill contributes to morale, without ever explaining where that general came from or how you end up with a good one. The [Sieges guide](/blog/eu5-sieges-explained/) assumes Diplomacy and Admin skill speed up the fall of a fort, which is a real statement about the character running the siege, not the siege itself. The [Parliament guide](/blog/eu5-parliament-explained/) walks through an activity that raises a brand new character from an estate, and you see that character's stats before committing, which is a great system and also a giant unasked question. And the [Ages](/blog/eu5-ages-explained/) and [Institutions](/blog/eu5-institutions-explained/) articles both point at an advance that unlocks a Promote Institutions cabinet action. All six of those articles reference characters or the cabinet without ever covering the system that produces them. This is that system, and this is the article that finally closes every one of those loops.

The demand for this one is not hypothetical. A Steam Community thread from November 2025 asks, bluntly, "How do I get more Courtiers?" and another from December 2025 asks "I'm running out of people for my cabinet positions??" Both are real players, both are genuinely stuck, and both threads are full of partial answers that never quite close the loop. If you have ever hit the cabinet screen, seen an open slot, and wondered where the qualified people are supposed to come from, this article is written for exactly you.

## What the cabinet actually is

The cabinet is the group of characters your country appoints to run its day-to-day government. Every country starts with just two cabinet seats. More seats unlock over time as the country grows, or through certain Advances, so the cabinet slowly becomes a bigger part of your management loop as the campaign goes on rather than being a fixed-size screen you meet once.

A cabinet member is not a gear you turn. You assign characters to cabinet actions, and how well they perform that action depends on that character's own skills, culture, estate, and religion. That last part is the whole key to this article: the quality of your cabinet is upstream of everything your country does, because every action runs through the character sitting in the seat. A well-matched character in the right seat is a real multiplier. A mismatched one is a silent tax.

How many actions can a cabinet actually perform? The original reveal of the system listed at least 45 confirmed cabinet actions, and the exact count has very likely grown since, because the game has been patched and expanded repeatedly. Treat 45 as the floor from the reveal, not as the current ceiling. If you see a higher number in current materials, that is expected, not a contradiction.

One rule new players get wrong constantly: an empty seat does not disable an action. Cabinet actions still function with the slot unfilled, they just provide a reduced boost instead of the full effect. You never lose access to an action because you have nobody sitting there. You just get less out of it, which is both a relief and a quiet pressure to actually fill the seat.

## What Patch 1.2 changed, and why it matters

Version 1.2 of EU5, the patch called "Echinades" that released May 6, 2026, made changes to the cabinet that are worth knowing as concrete facts rather than vague impressions.

First, characters serving in the cabinet can now gain traits applicable to the country as a result of their service. In plain terms, the characters you appoint are no longer just inputs into your government, they are also outputs. A long-serving cabinet member can pick up a trait that benefits your country, which means keeping stable, long-tenured people in seats has a compounding reward on top of their day-to-day performance. That is a real incentive to let good characters stay in position instead of reshuffling them for short-term gain.

Second, subject nations have one fewer cabinet slot than a fully sovereign nation. This is a direct, structural penalty on vassals and similar subject states, separate from any other limit. If you have ever played as a subject and felt like your government was more cramped than it should be, that is not imagination. The cabinet slot math is literally working against you, on top of the other ways subjecthood already restricts your freedom of action.

## Where characters actually come from, in practice

Here is the part every forum thread asks about. There are a handful of ways to put people into your court and your cabinet, and they are not all equally useful.

Hiring directly is the immediate fix. The cabinet screen has a button that lets you hire an advisor, general, or admiral outright, using Gold. It works, and it is the right answer when you need a specialist right now. It is also expensive, and hiring repeatedly is a long-term drain rather than a sustainable strategy. Sources are deliberately vague on the exact numbers here, and the cost scales with what you are hiring, so treat "real and sometimes significant" as the accurate summary rather than expecting a single fixed price.

Marriage is the core long-term mechanism, and it is where most players either quietly win or quietly fail. Keep marrying off the people already in your court to each other. Within a few decades, the pool grows faster than you can use it, because every marriage produces new characters who grow up and marry in turn. The inverse is also true: an unmarried court produces no new candidates. If your court is full of single adults, you are running a demographic dead end, and no amount of hiring can fix a court that never reproduces. Do not be precious about the matches either. Marrying characters to lowborns is fine and often necessary. The goal is growing the pool, not maximizing prestige on every single union.

There is a built-in auto-correction that makes this whole system friendlier than it looks, and honestly, it is one of the cleverer pieces of quiet game design in EU5. When the number of eligible male candidates in your court drops below double the number of cabinet slots that need filling, the AI automatically starts marrying characters to replenish the pool on its own. That directly explains a pattern players have reported for months: running low on candidates, feeling the squeeze, and then watching the problem mysteriously resolve itself a little later. That is not a coincidence and it is not blind luck. It is the game quietly doing the marriages for you, saving you from a spiral you would almost certainly have blamed on bad RNG. Sometimes a spouse you did not arrange is the game being helpful, not the game being weird.

A specific Parliament activity can raise a brand new character from an estate directly, showing you that character's stats before you commit. This is the ability the [Parliament article](/blog/eu5-parliament-explained/) keeps referencing, and the full session mechanics live over there. For the cabinet question, the short version is that Parliament is a legitimate source of hand-picked talent, just on a slower, session-based timer.

Estate privileges can restrict the cabinet in a way most players never suspect. Certain privilege choices can ban a specific estate from being eligible for cabinet positions entirely. If you have an estate that never produces candidates and you cannot figure out why, go check your privileges. The ban is a real, checkable cause, and it is the kind of self-inflicted problem that is easy to fix once you know where to look. For the fuller picture of how estates wield that power in the first place, the [Estates guide](/blog/eu5-estates-guide/) covers the system from the ground up.

Government type changes the whole picture at the top. A republic without a single ruling dynasty generates cabinet candidates through a different mechanism than a monarchy does, which is a genuine, confirmed nuance rather than a cosmetic difference. The [Government Types guide](/blog/eu5-government-types-explained/) on this site covers how that works in detail. For this article, the honest summary is: if you swap government types, do not assume your candidate pipeline stays the same, it does not.

## Why the cabinet is the load-bearing wall of your entire campaign

It is tempting to treat the court as a side show, an elaborate family tree you visit when a popup demands it. That is wrong, and the rest of this site's mechanics articles prove it by accident.

Combat is the clearest example. A general's Diplomacy skill feeds directly into morale in battle, which the [Combat guide](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) covers in its full math. What that means for this article is simple: the difference between a good fight and a bad one is partially sitting at home in your court, waiting to be married, hired, and appointed. Your army's performance is downstream of your marriage planning.

Sieges work the same way. Diplomacy and Admin skill affect how fast a siege actually progresses, which is one of the reasons the [Sieges guide](/blog/eu5-sieges-explained/) stresses keeping your siege leadership competent. A castle that takes years instead of months to fall is often not a castle problem, it is a personnel problem wearing a wall costume.

Even institutions trace back to the cabinet. An advance called Share of Knowledge, available once your country has embraced the Printing Press institution, unlocks the Promote Institutions cabinet action, which lets a well-staffed cabinet actively accelerate the spread of an institution you care about. That is a direct, mechanical link between the character system and the [Institutions guide](/blog/eu5-institutions-explained/), which covers the full 18-institution picture. The cabinet is how you stop waiting for institutions and start pushing them.

The pattern is the same everywhere: armies, sieges, institutions, and even advancement through the [Ages guide](/blog/eu5-ages-explained/) timeline all draw from the same limited, marriage-dependent pool of characters. Manage your court well, and the whole country hums. Neglect it, and you will keep hitting the same wall in combat, in sieges, and in institutions, never quite sure why your country underperforms its size. The answer is usually at home.

## A court is a compounding machine, not a decorative screen

If you take exactly three things from this article, let them be these. Keep your court married and reproducing, because the candidate pool is the economy everything else runs on. Actually look at your empty cabinet seats, because an empty seat is a reduced boost you are accepting on every single action it touches. And when the game's auto-marriage quietly saves you from a candidate drought, remember that the system is designed to stop you from falling into a spiral, not to mock you for it.

The characters page is not a family tree you occasionally tidy. It is the upstream input to combat, sieges, institutions, and government itself. Every other mechanics guide on this site has been pointing at this one. Now it exists, and the open loop that ran through six articles is finally closed.

title: EU5 Decisions Are Back: The New Content Tab Explained (Update 1.4 Preview)
metaDescription: EU5's update 1.4 brings back Decisions from EU4 through a new Content Tab. Here's everything confirmed so far about how it works.
content:
Update 1.4 is still in preview, and so is everything in this article. The facts below come from a single developer diary, Tinto Talks #120, posted August 12, 2026, and none of it exists in the live build of the game today. If you played EU4, the word that will draw you in here is Decisions, and it deserves a moment: Decisions were a well-known EU4 feature, and EU5 launched without them. Update 1.4 is bringing them back in a new form. Before the nostalgia runs away with you, hold on to one clarification: this is not a straight port. The diary frames Decisions as a returning concept, reworked for EU5 and delivered through a new system rather than being a copy of the old menu. Same idea, new home.

## What the Content Tab actually is

The new Decisions arrive inside what the diary calls the Content Tab. The Content Tab is a single hub that centralizes everything unique to a country: its unique reforms, its advances, its decisions, its policies and laws, its subject types, and its units all in one place. The point of that consolidation matters. In EU4, Decisions lived in their own standalone menu, a screen you went to specifically. In EU5, they are one entry in a fuller picture of the country's unique content, presented as part of the whole rather than as an isolated list.

## How a decision works

The diary describes the mechanical shape of Decisions in four confirmed strokes. A decision can be single-use, firing and then going away, or repeatable, available to use again under the right conditions. It can be country-specific, tied to one nation's unique content, or generic, open to any country that meets the requirements. And every decision shows a visible progress bar that tells you how close you are to meeting its requirements, so the feature is transparent about what it takes rather than hiding preconditions. That is the full extent of the confirmed mechanical detail. The diary did not give worked examples or exact thresholds, and this article does not invent them.

## The design idea: turning passive content into active choices

The reason this system exists at all is the most interesting part. A significant number of 1.4's new decisions work by converting content that used to wait for a random event to fire into player-driven, clickable actions instead. The old pattern asked you to sit and hope a particular event eventually showed up. The new pattern hands you the decision directly. That is a real shift in agency: the game stops being a slot machine of sometimes-relevant events and starts putting the relevant content in front of you at the moment you can act on it. It is a design philosophy with a clear direction, and it is being pointed at the passive event system specifically.

## A first iteration, not the finished system

The diary is explicit that this is the first iteration of a new content delivery system, not a finished, comprehensive one. The developers intend to keep building on it in future updates, and that expectation is written into the feature rather than being an afterthought. That is a legitimate reason to check back after 1.4 lands, because what ships in the beta is a foundation that was designed to grow. For context around everything else confirmed for the update, the site's [1.4 hub article](/blog/eu5-update-1-4-rio-salado/) tracks the whole patch, and the [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) covers the resource many of the patch's systems run through. Decisions and the Content Tab are one more confirmed piece of the 1.4 picture, and this article is the full extent of what has been shown so far.

title: EU5 Estate Private Armies Explained: Noble and Cossack Regiments (Update 1.4)
metaDescription: EU5's update 1.4 gives Nobles and Cossacks their own private army regiments. Here's everything confirmed about how they work and what it costs to use them.
content:
Update 1.4 is still a preview, and so is everything in this article. The facts below come from a single developer diary, Tinto Talks #119, posted August 5, 2026, and none of it exists in the live build of the game today. It is the same preview framing the Political Influence guide used for this exact update, and the same diary that article explicitly set this mechanic aside from as its own feature. Before anything else, the distinction that matters most: estate private armies are not levies. Levies are the population-drawn system already live in the game and already covered on this site. These private regiments are actual regular military units that belong to an estate, not troops pulled from the general population when a war needs bodies.

## What an estate private army actually is

Two estates get private-army privileges in 1.4: the Nobles and the Cossacks. Both can take privileges that let them raise regiments that belong to the estate itself rather than to the crown. The size of that force scales with the estate's population, so a bigger, more populous estate fields a bigger private army, and a smaller one fields a token force. Composition follows the estate's own martial traditions. Nobles raise heavy cavalry, the classic armored charge of the aristocracy. Cossacks raise light cavalry, the fast, mobile horsemen of their frontier tradition. Those are the only two confirmed pairings, and no other estate was shown getting either privilege.

## What the crown can do with them, and what it costs

Private armies are not decorative. The crown can press these estate regiments into royal service, which gives a temporary military boost by putting those troops into the crown's own hands when they are needed. The catch is that pressing them into service costs legitimacy, and that is a real price rather than flavor text. The second catch is the one that feeds the whole existing estate system: a disloyal estate can recall its soldiers. If an estate's loyalty has dropped, it can pull its private regiments back out of royal service, exactly when a war makes you want them most. That recall mechanic is the reason this belongs in the same conversation as the existing [EU5 Estates guide](/blog/eu5-estates-guide/), which covers loyalty and satisfaction from the ground up. Private armies do not replace that system, they extend it: the same estate satisfaction you manage today is the fuse that decides whether these regiments stay with you in a crisis.

## Some countries start with the system already live

One detail worth ending on because it changes how you should read the whole feature: countries with historically documented private-army privileges begin the game with those estates already at full strength. This is not purely a mid-game unlock that every nation grows into. For a handful of countries, the private-army system exists on day one, estates at full power from the very first month. The same update's [1.4 hub article](/blog/eu5-update-1-4-rio-salado/) tracks everything else confirmed for the patch, and the [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) covers the resource this update is built around. Estate private armies are one more confirmed piece of the 1.4 picture, and this article is the full extent of what has been shown so far.

title: EU5 Expeditions Explained: Circumnavigation, Treasure Fleet, and Pilgrimage Preview (Update 1.4)
metaDescription: EU5 Expeditions is a new exploration system coming in update 1.4. Here's everything confirmed so far about Circumnavigation, the Treasure Fleet, and the Hajj.
content:
Update 1.4, code-named Rio Salado, has a new system on its way that this site has not covered until now because it did not exist publicly until very recently: Expeditions. Everything below comes from a single source, Tinto Talks #121, posted August 19, 2026, where Paradox introduced the system in an early look. Before anything else, take that framing seriously, the same way the [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) did for its own 1.4 preview. The developers said it in their own words: Expeditions are still under development, actively being tested and iterated on, and this is an early look. None of this is in the live build of the game today, and numbers and mechanics can change between now and release.

Expeditions are a new system meant to make exploration more engaging. The examples in the diary are part of the free 1.4 update, and they are deliberately flavorful. Paradox says the team went for a more flair-forward approach to art and UI than previous features: 3D character models, unique icons per expedition, animated buttons and dialog containers, and more color and texture in the panels. That is a direct, explicit response to long-standing player feedback that EU5's UI needed more visual feeling. Some other expeditions will be exclusive to the paid "Across the Pillars" Chronicle Pack DLC, the first of that kind for the game, and those have not been shown yet. One more honest note before the three examples: the diary is almost entirely qualitative. Very few hard numbers exist, so this article does not pretend otherwise.

## Circumnavigation: the race around the world

Circumnavigation is a prestigious expedition, a race to be the first country to sail all the way around the world. Along the way the expedition collects resources, with the example given being cloves, which are sold at market price for ducats. The developers describe resources as somewhat abstracted, so this is closer to a story-driven voyage than a full cargo simulation. Provisions matter in the most direct way possible: run out of provisions and morale drops, and low morale risks mutiny, which can end the expedition entirely. Being the first to circumnavigate yields useful bonuses, and no exact numbers were given for what those bonuses are, so the uncertainty is stated openly rather than papered over.

## The Treasure Fleet: a Middle Kingdom exclusive

The second example is unique to the Middle Kingdom, the game's term for China, and it only becomes available through the Age of Treasure Voyages event. It starts through an action in the Middle Kingdom International Organization, where the country picks three things: the target destination, the character who leads the expedition, and how much cargo the voyage carries. The leader's stats are mechanically relevant, and this is the part most players will care about. Military skill reduces cargo loss when negative events hit, and diplomatic skill increases the chance that visited countries make choices favorable to China. The expedition gets its own dedicated GUI view, showing Voyage Cargo, the quantity of Gifts Received, and Countries Visited.

As the fleet travels it stops at prominent ports and triggers events, and each host country chooses between two stances, which is where the system gets genuinely interesting. A submissive stance makes that country a distant member of the Middle Kingdom IO, grants benefits to the Outward societal value, and adds tribute benefits. An arrogant stance instead gains power projection, noble satisfaction, and subject loyalty. Those are two very different deals, patronage and tribute versus pride and internal consolidation, and both are on the table. Some pulse events, the diary notes, can also meaningfully alter local politics on their own during port stops, so the destination is not the whole story.

When the fleet returns, the Middle Kingdom receives a summary of the journey, including gifts received and other notable occurrences, with the example given of an extradited dissident or even a captured foreign ruler. It is diplomacy wearing a fleet costume, and it plugs straight into the systems the [EU5 Diplomacy Guide](/blog/eu5-diplomacy-guide/) on this site covers in depth.

## The Great Pilgrimage (Catholic)

Expeditions also cover religion, with two separate religious expeditions shown in the diary. The first is the Great Pilgrimage for Catholic countries. It tries to visit as many Catholic Holy Sites as possible, and each site visited adds to a running count that increases the expedition's benefits. The journey ends with a visit to Jerusalem, with additional sites possible on the way back. Sites that do not have their own unique events still tally toward that count, and at the end the total feeds a clergy satisfaction and legitimacy reward. It is a numbers-adjacent pilgrimage rather than a purely narrative one, and the reward scales with how many holy places you actually hit.

## The Royal Hajj (Muslim)

The second religious expedition is the Royal Hajj, and it is focused on the journey more than the destination. The ruler themselves departs with an entourage of guards, and the trip must be completed within the same year or the pilgrimage fails outright. Depending on where in the world the journey starts, the expedition aims for one of four destinations: Damascus, Cairo, Baghdad, or Jeddah. The country can pay extra gold before departure for more guards and a more splendid entourage, and the mahmal can be picked up en route, opening extra event options for displaying wealth. The catch is that the mahmal can be lost if the expedition is raided, and more guards protect against exactly that. The one-year time limit is a real constraint, lingering too long on side events can cause the hajj to fail. On successful completion the pilgrim performs the rites at Mecca, and the more splendor accrued along the way, the bigger the prestige reward at the end.

## What is still coming before the open beta

Update 1.4 has no confirmed release date. What is known is that these August developer diaries were in preparation for the open beta, which the developers say will be held not too long after they conclude. Before the beta arrives, Paradox has teased what is next on the docket: Catholicism updates, a small surprise 1.4 feature that was teased without explanation and is not guessed at here, more UI quality of life work, and economy and trade additions. Next week's Tinto Talk was skipped for Gamescom, and the diary also leaves the door open for the Across the Pillars DLC expeditions to be shown off at a later date.

That is the shape of things to come, and it is a good reason to come back when the beta lands. Expeditions are still being tuned from this very preview, the free examples above are the confirmed starting point, and the DLC expeditions are the promised follow-up. This is one of those systems where the numbers will keep moving between now and release, and the site will be right here with the full breakdown once they stop.

title: EU5 Government Types Explained
metaDescription: EU5 government types explained: the five types and their resources, which rulers and succession laws each allows, and how a Tribe can modernize three ways.
content:
Your government type is the least flashy and most load-bearing setting on your country's screen. It decides which estate your ruler and heir sit in, which resource fuels your ruler's actions, and which succession laws you are even allowed to look at. The EU5 political cluster on this site has been assuming that layer exists all along. The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) takes for granted that rulers act through a government-specific resource. The [Parliament guide](/blog/eu5-parliament-explained/) assumes estates have a seat in your government that depends on your type. And the [Estates guide](/blog/eu5-estates-guide/) keeps mentioning which estate holds the ruler without ever stopping to explain why that matters. This article is the foundation those pages lean on, and it was the missing piece in the cluster until now.

So what does a government type actually control, in practice? Paradox introduced the system in Tinto Talks #4, its own dev diary, and said plainly that the type determines a fair bit of what mechanics you get access to. Different types run their rulers on different resources. And the official EU5 wiki frames government as the structure of your Ruler and Cabinet, shaped by Societal Values, Reforms, and Laws, which is exactly the layer this site's [Societal Values guide](/blog/eu5-societal-values-explained/) is about. Every piece of that structure already has a home on this site. The foundation under all of it did not, until now.

## The five types, and the resource each one runs on

- Monarchy: Legitimacy.
- Republic: Republican Tradition.
- Theocracy: Devotion.
- Steppe Horde: Horde Unity.
- Tribe: Tribal Cohesion.

Community data-mining rounds out the at-a-glance picture, and it is worth flagging clearly before trusting it: according to Paradoxpedia, a separate community-run reference site. Monarchies and Theocracies number same-name rulers regnally, so an heir called Henry becomes Henry III rather than another plain Henry. Steppe Hordes and Tribes are the two types that auto-generate a consort for an unmarried ruler. And each type seats its ruler and heir in a default estate: Monarchies with the Nobility, Republics with the Burghers, Theocracies with the Clergy, and both Steppe Hordes and Tribes with the Nobility again.

## Monarchy and Theocracy: the orderly, numbered route

Monarchies are the benchmark the other types are measured against. The ruler rules for life, the heir comes from the dynasty, and Monarchies have Royal Marriages available, which can secure alliances and even inherit foreign countries through Personal Unions. It is why the great monarchist powers of the map end up married to each other, a web of related crowns held together by diplomacy and signed contracts. Legitimacy is the currency of that arrangement, and it is the resource the whole type quietly runs on.

Theocracy is the orderly sibling with a very different tone. Its ruler is chosen by election, almost always for life, and it runs on Devotion instead of a family name. Community data-mining credits Theocracies with two distinct habits: they force-convert subjects when a new ruler is created, and they prefer Liturgical Language as the court language, a small but real cultural current that colors the whole realm. Estate-wise, Theocracies seat their ruler with the Clergy, which tells you most of what you need to know about who actually runs the state behind the title.

## Republic: election, no marriages, less dynasty

Republics run on Republican Tradition, and they trade away the two things monarchist play styles depend on. Rulers are chosen by election, so the throne is a temporary office rather than a birthright, and Republics cannot use Royal Marriages at all, which is Paradox's own example of mechanics being gated by government type. Dynasties matter far less here; the family that sits in the palace today is a faction, not a bloodline entitlement. That shows up in the estate screen too, where a Republic's ruler and heir sit with the Burghers, the commercial class that tends to back whichever candidate benefits trade. If you are weighing EU5 monarchy vs republic vs theocracy early on, the practical split is this: monarchies buy dynastic continuity, republics buy elective control, and both are real, defensible trades.

## Steppe Horde: the government built for war

Steppe Hordes run on Horde Unity, and the mechanic would be doing a disservice if it did not say what that actually means for play. Paradox's dev diary used the Horde as the clearest example of type-driven behavior: a Steppe Horde has a different view of war, peace, and conquest than the settled types do. The estate screen keeps them with the Nobility, and like Tribes they auto-generate consorts for unmarried rulers. It is a lean, aggressive, single-minded government, and understanding it starts with understanding that its resource is about keeping the warband coherent rather than keeping dynasties or elections on schedule.

## The Tribe, and the one real early decision in this system

Tribes run on Tribal Cohesion, and they are the type this guide spends the most space on for a specific reason: a Tribe is the only government type with three different modernization destinations. The others are open roads with signs already planted. A Tribe reaches a fork every time it reforms.

The play feel comes first. Tribes auto-generate consorts for unmarried rulers, and community data-mining credits them with Royal Marriages access, which sits oddly at first until you realize it is about the political network of the clan, not the legal ritual of a court. Community data-mining also lists several always-on Tribe modifiers worth respecting rather than tuning out: a +10% preference for Common Language as the court language, a -50% cost to downgrade a settlement to Rural, a -25% cut to Noble food consumption, and a -75% reduction in diplomatic upkeep. Those read almost like a settlement government wearing warmer clothes, cheap to maintain and slow to churn.

The branch matters more than any modifier. The official wiki says a Tribe can only reform into Monarchy, Republic, or Theocracy, and Steppe Hordes sit in the same restricted lane, while the settled three can reform into each other. That makes a modernizing Tribe the one moment where the game hands you a genuine EU5 monarchy vs republic vs theocracy decision in the middle of a campaign. Modernize into a Monarchy and you are buying into royal marriages, dynasties, and Personal Union games. Modernize into a Republic and you are choosing elections and commercial control. Modernize into a Theocracy and you are picking devotion, clerical rule, and the conversion habits that come with it. Same starting point, three different games layered on top.

## How to change government type in EU5

The official EU5 wiki states the rules for changing government type plainly, and the numbers matter, so they are worth writing in full. A country can change its government type as long as it is at peace, has no active disaster, is not bankrupt, and is not part of a Personal Union. Doing so costs 50 Stability and 25 Government Power, and it changes the country type to Settled if it was not already. A few formable countries change government type when they are formed, and some historical flavor events can change it too. Papal States, Yuan, and any country that is an elector or emperor of the Holy Roman Empire cannot change government type at all.

The asymmetry is the quiet structure under everything: Tribe and Steppe Horde can only reform into Monarchy, Republic, or Theocracy, while those three can reform into each other. In practice that means the tribal ladder is a one-way climb toward one of three destinations, and the settled group is a revolving door among itself. If you are googling how to change government type in EU5, those conditions and the 50/25 cost are the answer. The strategy is the sentence before it: the only fork with three paths is the tribal one.

## A five-type system, not a port of EU4's

If this all feels adjacent to something familiar, it is worth drawing the boundary cleanly. EU4 handles governments with its older four-group arrangement of monarchy, republic, theocracy, and its tribal group, plus a reform track that was overhauled in the Dharma era. EU5 is not that system wearing a new coat. It is a five-type design of its own, with its own resources, its own modernization ladders, and its own succession law menus. The differences are worth reading side by side, and the site's [EU4 vs EU5 guide](/blog/eu5-vs-eu4-differences/) does exactly that without flattening either game into the other.

## Succession laws are the next layer up

Everything in this guide sits underneath one more menu, and that menu is succession law. Succession law is gated entirely by government type, and the counts diverge sharply: 22 available to a Monarchy, 16 to a Republic, 9 to a Theocracy, 5 to a Tribe, and just 3 to a Steppe Horde. Changing a succession law is done from the Government menu, Country page, using the button under the heir's portrait, and it costs 50 Stability and 50 Government Power. It can also be blocked, either by a fixed succession law or by the Nobility estate holding the Right to Inherit privilege. That is a real, deep, next guide's worth of content, and this one is the foundation it will stand on rather than a rushed chapter of it.

Which leaves a single point worth closing the whole thing on, and it is not the one most players expect. The moment that matters most in EU5's government system is not at country creation. It comes later, the campaign where you are running a Tribe comfortably and the game quietly asks whether, and when, to modernize, and into what: Monarchy with its marriages, Republic with its elections, or Theocracy with its devotion. Every other type's branch is decided by history before you arrive. The Tribe is the one where somebody has to decide, and it is you. That small, quiet fork is the real depth of this system, and now the foundation it sits on is on this site where it belongs.

title: EU5 Update 1.4 'Río Salado': Everything Confirmed So Far
metaDescription: Confirmed EU5 update 1.4 'Río Salado' features so far: Political Influence, Decisions, Expeditions, the timeline, and more, from the Tinto Talks previews.
content:
Update 1.4 for Europa Universalis V, code-named Río Salado, is the biggest confirmed batch of changes this site has tracked in a single update, and it has no release date yet. Everything below comes from the official Tinto Talks developer diaries that Paradox publishes weekly, read directly from the game's Steam announcements page. Seven of them are in so far, Tinto Talks 117 through 123, and this page assembles the confirmed picture up to the most recent one. Treat every line as a preview, not live content: none of it is in the current build of the game, and the developers have said repeatedly that preview numbers and mechanics can change. Two clarifications belong at the top because the community keeps tripping over them. Ambitions are not in 1.4; they were explicitly moved out to a future update called Discovery, currently targeted for Late 2027, which will also bring a Colonization rework and a content delivery overhaul. And the update itself is framed as centered on pre-1500s Iberia rather than on the colonization era.

The topics below are grouped by system, and each represents the confirmed state at the time of writing. The diaries did not all land in the order originally announced, so view the topics as confirmed and the announced schedule as history. Because this is a living document, it will be refreshed as new Tinto Talks post, and every section links out to a dedicated article where this site already covers a system in full.

## Politics and diplomacy

The headliner is Political Influence, a new 0 to 100 country currency representing the ruler's political capital, and keeping it high raises base Crown Power by up to 20%. That system already has its own article on this site, so only its shape is repeated here, and the [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) carries the full detail.

Diplomacy gains new actions. Demand War Leadership and Offer War Leadership make war leadership something to negotiate rather than something that just happens. Inheritance Contracts let a paying monarchy buy the right to inherit an heirless monarchy, with the cost scaled by development and running roughly between 50 and 1500 gold. Betrothals turn marriages into promises, available for children aged two and up.

Hegemony antagonism gets flattened: the penalty is now a flat +10% instead of scaling up to +100% when you hold all five hegemonic titles, and each hegemony held grants +1 diplomatic reputation. The diplomacy automation overhaul is large. High-stakes actions like changing religion, primary culture, or succession law, declaring war, forming alliances, and joining International Organizations can no longer be automated at all. Automation now leaves alone the ongoing actions you personally started instead of cancelling them, fixing the automation keeps fighting me complaint, and the diplomat cap rises from 1 to 3. The same diary also introduced estate private armies for the Nobles and Cossacks, which have their own [full guide](/blog/eu5-estate-private-armies/) on this site.

## Decisions and the Content Tab

Decisions return as a feature, and they arrive inside a new Content Tab that centralizes a country's unique reforms, advances, decisions, policies and laws, subject types, and units in one place. Many 1.4 decisions convert content that previously waited on a random event to fire into player-driven, clickable actions, and the developers are explicit that this is the first iteration of a content delivery system they will keep building on. Decisions can be single-use or repeatable, country-specific or generic, and each one shows a visible progress bar toward its requirements. Decisions now have their own [full guide](/blog/eu5-decisions-content-tab/) on this site.

## Expeditions

Expeditions are the newest and most work-in-progress item in 1.4. The developers called them explicitly an early look, with the system still under development and being iterated on, so this section and the dedicated article lean on that warning rather than hiding it. The system has three flavored examples confirmed so far: Circumnavigation, a race to sail all the way around the world; the Treasure Fleet, a Middle Kingdom exclusive; and the Great Pilgrimage and the Royal Hajj, two religious expeditions. Hard numbers are thin everywhere in the diary, so next to no exact figures exist for any of these. Some expeditions will be exclusive to the paid Across the Pillars DLC, EU5's first Chronicle Pack, and none of those have been shown yet. The [full Expeditions guide](/blog/eu5-expeditions-explained/) covers all three confirmed examples in detail.

## Colonization and population

Colonization picks up clarity and direction. Colonial charters now let a player pick the goal up front, Form Colonial Nation, Join Colonial Nation, or Keep as Territory, instead of hitting an event popup at completion. Colonies get migration and ETA indicators plus milestone messages, and a fully self-sustaining colony is explicitly marked Self Sustaining. Conquistadors are built at a homeland port instead of a colonial port, gain auxiliary units to prevent starvation, and joining a conquistador war automatically makes you the war leader.

Population growth now comes from actual food surplus rather than hoarded stockpiles. Spare land no longer speeds growth by itself, growth slows as locations approach capacity, and overcrowded locations lose people. Large cities and harsh winters reduce local food production. A new Egyptian Plague endemic disease models over 50 historical Mamluk-era outbreaks between 1348 and 1517, spawning roughly every few years in the Nile delta and occasionally spreading to the Levant, and it runs on its own resistance track, so Black Death survivors get no immunity.

Cultures get a sharper tier system in the same diary cycle. The old Discriminated tier is renamed to Ignored, and a new level below it takes the Discriminated name. That new tier represents active oppression, dramatically increasing cultural assimilation at the cost of pop satisfaction and increased emigration, and countries dislike you for discriminating. Estates put forward Parliament agendas to accept or discriminate against cultures they like or dislike, which is a natural link to the [Parliament guide](/blog/eu5-parliament-explained/) already on this site. Migration also gets direct tools: an Age of Reformation advance unlocks a Direct Domestic Migration cabinet action that moves pops from one location to another over ten years.

## Mercenaries and combat

Mercenaries get more expensive and more demanding. Hiring costs roughly twice as much upfront and 35% more in monthly upkeep, they consume 50% more food in the field than regulars, and hiring from rival-owned soil carries a 25% default hostile territory surcharge.
