A new Mercenary Market law arrives in the Age of Renaissance with four policy options: Condottieri Business, Open Markets, Restricted Markets, and Unrestricted Market, which is the 1.3 default.

Combat numbers shift down across the board. Cavalry combat power drops from 4 to 3.25, the flanking bonus is cut from +110% for light cavalry and +100% for heavy down to +60% for both, and the Napoleonic Warfare advance is reworked to grant +5% discipline instead of ignoring zones of control. Sieges get a smaller stepping-stone rework: artillery now needs only 2 regiments per bonus point against forts instead of 3, and forts auto-surrender below 5% garrison strength instead of below 10 defenders, ahead of the bigger siege rework the developers say is planned for 1.5. Both systems get their own dedicated [deep-dive on what changes in 1.4](/blog/eu5-1-4-combat-siege-changes/).

## The Campaign Timeline, performance, and pacing

The September 9 diary, Tinto Talks 123, led with a genuinely free feature: the Campaign Timeline. It is free with 1.4 and explicitly not part of the Across the Pillars DLC. It lets you rewind to any point in a campaign and watch the map, one day at a time if you want, with nudge increments from a single day up to 50 years, a play button, and camera jump toggles for specific regions. At launch it also breaks down the primary stats, Population, Economic base, and Tax Base, sortable as pie charts or direct ranks. It lives in the Content Tab and in the top-right UI panel.

The same diary covered performance, and the headline is a pacing change with real consequences: hourly ticks are removed in 1.4. Ticks now run day to day, as they did in EU4, and Speeds 6 and 7 are gone, making speed 5 the maximum again. Removing the hourly tick adds roughly 10 to 15% faster performance on its own. Development also shared an internal observer-mode example, going from 2 minutes 45 seconds to reach January 1339 on 1.3 down to 47 seconds on the latest internal 1.4 build, on high-end hardware and with an honest caveat that exotic office stats should not be taken at face value for every system. The complacency system, the one that penalized growing too large, is removed completely in 1.4.

The same diary rounded out with a batch of balance and state-of-the-game items. An estate sitting above 25% power now puts a small drain on your legitimacy or its equivalent. Low government power is being rebalanced so that collapse hurts similarly across government types, with low devotion weighing harder on clergy and stability for Theocracies, and two new disasters, one for Theocracies and one for Republics, are confirmed as in the works. Theocracies, Steppe Hordes, and Tribes each get their own new capital flavor building. These items are confirmed but still being tuned, which is the normal state of a pre-beta build.

## UI and quality of life

The UI pass is steady, practical stuff. The road builder gets a preview of the road before you build it, plus an option to skip sections where rivers or maritime connections already beat a road. Laws move to their own dedicated vertical panel, out of a cramped subtab. The country and throne-room panel is reorganized, a new Urbanization Panel takes over the old Production Locations screen, the budget panel gains a Tax Base Ratio stat, and a Turmoils Panel centralizes diseases, rebels, and movements in one place. Location building queues become visible and editable, up to six queue types. Two new map modes arrive, War Score and Crown Power, both per location. A Trade Orders UI overhaul is teased but not detailed yet.

## What is still coming before the open beta

The confirmed teases, none of them with dates: Catholicism updates, a small surprise 1.4 feature that has not been explained and is not guessed at here, more UI quality of life, and economy and trade changes, including a new tariff system, per the September diary. Update 1.4 itself still has no confirmed release date. The August and September diaries were explicitly in preparation for the open beta, and the developers say it will be held not too long after. When it does land, this page gets its next regular refresh, because everything above is only what has been shown so far, and the full shape of Río Salado is still being assembled one Wednesday at a time.

title: Crusader Kings 3: By God Alone, Everything Confirmed So Far
metaDescription: CK3's By God Alone expansion confirmed: playable theocracies, College of Cardinals, and Spiritual Fulfillment. Releases September 30, 2026.
content:
Before anything else, the framing that matters for a preview article like this one: Crusader Kings III: By God Alone is an announced but not yet released expansion. It is confirmed for September 30, 2026, and none of what follows is playable in the current build of the game. That date and preview status are stated up front so the rest of the article can be read honestly, as confirmed plans rather than live features.

That said, this preview is on unusually firm ground. Eight independent sources, including Paradox's own official press release, agree on the same core facts, so confidence in what is described here is high even though the content itself is not live yet. When an announcement is this consistent across Paradox itself and the press, hedging every sentence would be noise. The honest frame is: this is real, it is confirmed, and it arrives on September 30, 2026. This page is a living preview: once the expansion is live, it will be refreshed with confirmed playable mechanics, so what is previewed here becomes verified detail after release.

There is also a practical reason this article earns its place right now. This site's existing [Best Religions in CK3](/blog/ck3-best-religion/) article just showed a 1,603% impression spike, which is almost certainly early search interest tied to this exact announcement. People are looking for playable-Pope content before it ships, and CK3 coverage has been comparatively under-developed next to the EU5 cluster on this site. This is the natural, high-interest way to bring the same research rigor to CK3.

## What By God Alone actually is

By God Alone is the core expansion, one of two centerpiece releases in Crusader Kings III's Chapter V content pass. The other is [Silk and Silver](/blog/ck3-silk-and-silver-preview/), a separate, later expansion covering merchant republics and trade, expected by the end of 2026. It is mentioned here in one line only because this article is specifically about the religion overhaul, not the trade one.

## Pricing and the Chapter V pass

The full Chapter V Expansion Pass costs $43.99 / £36.99 / €43.99, and it includes one Major Expansion, one Core Expansion, which is By God Alone, a Music Pack, and a Cosmetic Clothing Pack.

By God Alone is also purchasable standalone at $19.99 / £16.99 / €19.99, so you do not have to buy the whole pass to get the religion system.

One detail worth knowing if you are deciding now: the pass is already purchasable, and buying it immediately unlocks two already-released items, the Symbols of Authority clothing pack and the Songs of the Realm music pack. Both are cosmetic. Neither is the religion content itself, they are the pass's way of giving you something concrete the moment you pay, while the expansion proper waits for its September date.
## The headline feature: playable theocracies

The feature getting the most attention is also the most important one. For the first time in Crusader Kings III's history, players will be directly controlling theocratic landholders, up to and including the Pope himself. Playable realms include landed archbishops and the Papacy, and the press release is explicit that as the Papacy, new resources of power and wealth are at your disposal.

That is worth pausing on, because it is a genuinely significant design shift for the series, not new content bolted onto old systems. For nine years, players of Crusader Kings games have negotiated with religious authority, requested claims and excommunications, paid indulgences, and maneuvered around the Pope, but always from the outside. Letting you become the very religious authority you used to have to negotiate with inverts the assumptions the whole series has been built on. The person holding that power is now you, and everyone else is the one doing the negotiating.

One practical detail from a hands-on Gamescom preview: Popes tend to be old when they take the office, which makes succession a real planning consideration for anyone planning to play the Papacy. It is a concrete, sourced detail rather than a guess, and the kind of thing that matters across a whole campaign.

## The four new interconnected systems

By God Alone rebuilds Christianity through four new systems that the press release and multiple independent sources describe as interconnected. They are the skeleton the whole expansion hangs on.

**Rites** are new ways to customize a character's relationship to their faith. That includes leaning into heretical beliefs that push against orthodox boundaries, and it includes having personal religious preferences gradually accepted through internal church politics. The flavor of the system is negotiation with your own church rather than either pure conformity or total rebellion.

**Archdioceses** give the church a structured hierarchy players can engage with at any level, from a local bishop up to the Pope. Multiple sources describe it as a complex, era-appropriate hierarchy across all regions, not just Catholic Europe. This is the expansion making church structure into a spatial system, religious authority that covers a region regardless of which secular ruler holds the land.

**The College of Cardinals** is where the tension gets sharp. The Pope can appoint Cardinals across Christendom, but secular rulers are not powerless here, they can use their own influence to shape who gets appointed and what direction the College takes. That tug-of-war between secular and religious authority is a genuinely interesting design choice, it means playing as the Church does not remove the conflict between church and state, it just puts you on the church side of it.

**Spiritual Fulfillment** is the emotional core of the whole expansion. A character's traits, actions, and religious tenets combine to reflect their inner spiritual life. A devout ruler who honors vows, supports crusades, and protects the Church builds Fulfillment, earning bonuses to piety, clerical opinion, and potentially dynastic prestige. A hypocritical ruler, someone privately sinning while publicly performing devotion, suffers the reverse, internal crisis events and real reputational costs.

This is the system that makes faith more than a resource bar. By God Alone ties religion to a kind of internal honesty mechanic, the game is watching whether your character's private behavior matches their public devotion, and rewarding or punishing that match. No exact bonus numbers have been confirmed yet, and none are invented here, but the shape is clear and it is the system that gives the expansion its weight.
## The Christian Situation and the 867 Schism

By God Alone adds a persistent Situation that tracks the overall health and unity of the Christian faith across the game world. It is the umbrella that the other systems sit under, a living record of how the church is doing, and it gives players new actions and decisions tied to the development of the Faith.

One honest aside worth including: this shares its name with EU5's own Situations mechanic, which this site has covered in its [Situations guide](/blog/eu5-situations-explained/). The two are separate systems in separate games, not the same feature. The naming echo is worth noting so nobody goes looking for a mechanical connection that does not exist, but that is all it is, a naming echo.

The Situation connects directly to a headline moment. In the 867 start date, the Christian church will eventually reach a crossroads, and that can result in the Great Schism, separating Western Catholicism from Eastern Orthodoxy. Players in an 867 campaign get to steer that fork, either following history into the 1054 split or finding a way to diverge from it.

## Ecumenical Councils and revised tenets

Two more confirmed pieces round out the expansion. Ecumenical Councils are a new venue where players participate in steering the direction of Religious Rites, and they are also the mechanism that can trigger the Great Schism from the 867 start. If the Situation is the health bar of the church, the Councils are where its direction actually gets decided.

And the existing tenet system is being reworked to center on a character's personal relationship to their faith and what counts as acceptable behavior within it, rather than remaining a static bonus list. Heiety and orthodoxy become things a living church negotiates, which is what makes heresies such a natural feature of the expansion, divergence is now a gameplay pressure, not just a background flavor.

## Holy Orders, cathedrals, and holy sites

Two more confirmed pieces round out the picture. Monastic Holy Orders are centers of research and theological power, and hosting one's headquarters grants potent bonuses. Cathedrals gain a second life as focal points of reverence: a cathedral can become associated with a specific saint or holy figure, and that reverence can in turn lead to it becoming a Holy Site. Neither system has had exact numbers confirmed yet, and none are invented here. For how faith works in today's build, the site's [culture and faith mechanics guide](/blog/ck3-culture-faith-mechanics/) covers the system this expansion builds on.

## What this means for this site's existing CK3 advice

This expansion will eventually make parts of the existing [Best Religions in CK3](/blog/ck3-best-religion/) article partly obsolete. That article's advice centers on negotiating with religious authority from the outside, requesting gold and claims from the Pope, worrying about excommunication, and using Catholicism as a tool while dealing with its costs. When By God Alone ships, some of that advice holds and some of it inverts, because you will be able to sit on the other side of that relationship.

That is not a flaw in the older article, it is the natural lifecycle of a guides site when a series gets a system overhaul. When the expansion is live, that article will get a forward-looking update to cover the playable-theocracy reality. Until then, the current advice is still how the game plays today.

## Faith becomes the seat of power

By God Alone is the rare expansion that does not add a new region or a new map mode, it adds a new way to be powerful. Playable theocracies put you inside the church. The College of Cardinals makes church politics a lever instead of a wall. Spiritual Fulfillment makes your character's faith an active, watchful system rather than a static bonus. And the Christian Situation gives the church a pulse that ticks across the whole world.

None of that is playable until September 30, 2026, and that date should hold every expectation you have about this content. But the confirmed shape, eight sources wide, including Paradox's own hand, is that CK3 is finally giving religion the depth it has always been missing, and letting you become the authority this series has spent nine years asking you to negotiate with.

title: EU5 Institutions Explained
metaDescription: EU5 institutions explained: the 18 institutions, embrace thresholds, spawn restrictions, and how institutions unlock advances.
content:
The [Ages article](/blog/eu5-ages-explained/) on this site ended by explicitly deferring this topic. It said a full breakdown of institutions was out of scope, that it was a reference-table task best left to its own article. This is that article. It also closes a functional loop the Ages piece could only gesture at: institutions are what unlock new advances within an Age, so a reader who understands Ages without understanding institutions only has half the picture of how a country actually progresses technologically. Institutions and Ages are two halves of one tech system, and this is the second half.

One sourcing note worth leading with, because it explains how careful this research has been. The core facts below come from the EU5 wiki's own Institutions content, cross-checked against three independently published guides from November and December 2025, well after the game's release. An older Steam Community thread on this general topic initially looked relevant, but it turned out to be about EU4's institution system specifically, not EU5's, different terminology, a 2017 date, and EU4's own app ID. It was excluded rather than blended in. This article covers EU5's current mechanics, no EU4 leftovers.

## The 18 institutions, three per Age

There are 18 institutions total in the game, exactly three for each of the six Ages. Each one is a cultural or technological paradigm shift that appears at a historically fitting location and spreads outward across the map. Once an institution has spread to at least 20% of a country's population, that country can Embrace it at a cost scaled in Stability and Gold.

The embrace cost has a genuinely useful property: it decreases the more of your country has already adopted the institution naturally. An expensive-looking embrace early gets cheaper the longer you wait, which means rushing to embrace the instant you cross 20% is not always the right call. Sometimes letting the institution keep spreading on its own before you pay is the cheaper play, and the tooltip will show you exactly how much you are saving.

Embracing does two concrete things. It unlocks a brand new branch in that Age's advance tree, and it doubles the institution's spread rate going forward. That doubling is the reason institution timing feels so snowbally, the country that embraces first gets its other locations to adopt faster, widening the gap with the country that waits.

## The Age of Traditions special case

Institutions from the Age of Traditions are a special case: they start the game already spawned and already spread from their historical locations, regardless of the game rules you set. Feudalism begins in Aachen, Legalism in Rome, and Meritocracy in Khanbaliq.

That might read as a small mechanical convenience, but it is actually a subtle worldbuilding choice. The game starts in 1337, and the Age of Traditions is already ending as the campaign begins. Of course those institutions are already widespread, history had been running for centuries before you ever pressed start. The pre-spawned Traditions institutions reflect that the world was already in motion, not that the game could not be bothered to spawn them live. It is a quiet way of telling you that by the time you take control, there is already a rich technological present waiting.
## Not every institution can spawn for your country

Here is a real limitation worth stating plainly, because it explains a point of confusion many players hit: later Ages restrict where an institution can even appear, and some nations simply never get a natural spawn point for certain institutions.

Age of Renaissance institutions can only spawn in a location sharing the country's own primary culture. Age of Reformation and Age of Absolutism institutions are even more restricted, they can only spawn in Europe or North Africa. What that means in practice: if you are playing a nation outside Europe and North Africa, the Reformation and Absolutism institutions never appear on your doorstep by themselves. Your only path is to let them spread in from elsewhere, which is exactly why the embrace threshold and the waiting math matter so much for non-European playthroughs.

This is not a bug and it is not your country being shortchanged. It is an intentional claim about history, the Renaissance genuinely was a European phenomenon, and the institutions that followed it were born in specific places with specific cultural prerequisites. The game is reflecting that geography, not hiding a mechanic from you.

## The cabinet can push institutions

Institution management is not purely passive. An advance called Share of Knowledge, available in the Age of Discovery once a country has embraced the Printing Press institution, unlocks a Cabinet Action called Promote Institutions. This lets a country actively push a specific institution's spread rather than passively waiting for it to arrive.

This is confirmed identically across two independent 2025 guides, so it is solid. It is also worth stating plainly, with a forward link to this site's [Cabinet and Courtiers guide](/blog/eu5-cabinet-courtiers-explained/), that institution management is one of the concrete things a cabinet can actively do. When you read about cabinet members being assigned actions, this is a major one: point your cabinet at the institution your country needs most, and it spends its effort spreading it for you.

## What actually drives spread rate

Beyond the embrace math, it helps to know what makes an institution spread faster into your locations. The practical factors, confirmed across multiple sources, are all intuitive once you see them.

An institution spreads faster into locations that are more developed, and faster into locations that are closer to a place that already has it. Friendly borders and coastlines that already host the institution accelerate it, and trade connections through a shared market help too. A more technical secondary source adds that spread also scales with a country's control over the relevant territory, echoing a point the Ages article already made, that control matters to how institutions behave in your country.

That last one is worth internalizing. Development and proximity you can influence by building and expanding. Control you can lose during wars or unrest. The countries that embrace institutions fastest are not just the ones that happen to sit near where they spawn, they are the ones that keep their territories well-controlled and developed enough for the spread to take root quickly.

## This is EU5's system, not EU4's

One final clarification, since the mechanics share a name with a familiar older game. EU4 had an institution system too, and it was built on its own rules, its own spawn logic, and its own spread math. This article is specifically about EU5's current system, which is confirmed by the wiki and by the post-release guides cited above. If you are coming from EU4, treat the similarities as surface-level and relearn the specifics, the example many players trip over is assuming EU4's insta-reform-spawn behavior or its spawn mechanics carry over, when EU5's calendar-driven, 20%-threshold, control-scaled system is its own thing entirely.

## The map is the curriculum

Institutions are where the Age system stops being a timeline and becomes a map. Three per Age, appearing in historically meaningful places, spreading through development, proximity, borders, trade, and control, and usable only once one-fifth of your population has adopted them, institutions are the reason the same calendar makes different countries progress at different speeds. The Ages article gave you the timeline. This article gives you the geography. Together they are the full picture of how technological progress actually moves in EU5, and how a country either rides that current or gets left behind by it.

title: EU5 Ages Explained
metaDescription: EU5 ages explained: the six eras, research costs, focuses, institutions, and what each age unlocks.
content:
Four articles on this site have opened loops that only make sense once you know what an Age is. The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) described the Absolutism versus Liberalism societal value axis granting monthly Political Influence at both extremes, without ever saying when that axis becomes available. The [Societal Values guide](/blog/eu5-societal-values-explained/) noted that some axes are gated by Age without explaining what an Age actually is. The [Government Types guide](/blog/eu5-government-types-explained/) mentioned Age-gated reforms without a number. And the [Sieges](/blog/eu5-sieges-explained/) and [Combat](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) guides describe mechanics that shift meaningfully across eras, including the fact that war score gained from battles drops in later Ages. This article is the timeline the rest of the political and military cluster runs on, and it is long overdue.

One confidence note up front. The numbers in the first half of this article come directly from the EU5 wiki's Age pages, several of which cite the game's own internal code constants rather than player tests or forum guesses. That is about as primary a source as this project has ever had, so the research costs, start years, and institution rules below are written with confidence. A second set of figures later in the article comes from Paradoxpedia, a separate reference site, and it is exactly as solid, but it is still a secondary source, so those numbers are flagged as such rather than presented with the same certainty.

## Institutions unlock new branches

Each Age introduces three Institutions that appear at historically fitting locations and spread outward along trade routes and borders. They are the game's way of making knowledge geographic, a discovery in Venice is not a discovery in London until it travels there.

Once an Institution has spread to roughly one-fifth of a country's territory, that country can Embrace it at a cost scaled in Stability and Gold. The exact threshold is a game-code constant, around 20%, rather than a number displayed prominently in the UI, so check your own institution panel before planning around it. Embracing does two clear things: it unlocks a brand new branch in that Age's advance tree, and it doubles the Institution's spread rate going forward. The spread bonus even has a caveat, if you lack control over the relevant territory, the doubling shrinks.

The practical shape of this is that each Age is really three institutions, three new research branches, and three spread timers running in parallel. A country that embraces institutions early researches more of its Age's tree; a country that ignores them falls behind on the same calendar everyone else shares.

## The direct callback: Age of Absolutism

The Age of Absolutism, starting in 1637, is the specific era that unlocks the Absolutism and Liberalism societal values. That is the same axis the Political Influence article described as granting monthly Political Influence at both extremes, and this article should settle what that article left open: that axis does not exist from turn one. It becomes available only once a country reaches this specific Age.

That reframes a detail you may have misread. The Political Influence guide's mention of the Absolutism versus Liberalism axis sounds like something you could engage with in 1337, but it is actually a 17th-century option, gated behind a century and a half of calendar before a single law can touch it. Locking a prominent-sounding mechanic behind an era is a genuinely interesting way to keep the early game feeling different from the late game, but it is the kind of thing that can silently mislead a new player who assumes every listed resource is available from day one.

The Age of Absolutism also shifts the economy. It raises the maximum market price ceiling to 500% and holds market price stability at 4%, which matters if you are used to earlier Ages with tighter price bands and more volatile markets. Markets in the Age of Absolutism can swing much further before they hit a cap, which changes how aggressive you can be with trade-heavy economies.

## Broader shifts across the Ages

Beyond the wiki-confirmed mechanics, a secondary reference site, Paradoxpedia, catalogs several structural shifts across the Ages that are worth carrying into your planning. These are flagged as secondary because they come from that reference rather than the wiki's own numbers, but they are consistent with everything else on this page.

The Hegemon system, where the great power leading in a given field can be proclaimed Hegemon and earn bonuses, only becomes available in 4 of the 6 Ages. It is not a permanent feature of the late game.

Mercenary availability shrinks substantially in later Ages, down to around a 90% reduction by the latest ones. If your early game relies on buying armies, expect that option to be almost gone by the late game, a real planning consideration most players do not start budgeting for.

War score gained from actual battles decreases in later Ages, by as much as 80% at the far end. That shifts the practical emphasis toward occupying territory directly rather than winning field battles, which is a genuinely useful strategic note to connect back to the Sieges article, since sieges and occupation are exactly how that occupation-first strategy executes.

And the direct, quantified version of what the Government Types article gestured at without a number: roughly 130 government reforms require reaching a specific Age before they are available at all. Your government's reform pool is not static, the calendar quietly unlocks most of it over time.

## The calendar is a silent co-governor

The Ages are the least talked about, most load-bearing structure in EU5. Political Influence's most distinctive societal value axis is locked behind the Age of Absolutism. Societal values are gated by era. Government reforms are gated by era. Even war strategy shifts with the Ages, from battles toward occupation as the centuries roll forward. Every one of those is a loop this site opened in another article, and this is the timeline that closes them.

The practical read is a quiet one. You cannot opt out of the Ages and you cannot speed them up, so the winning move is to plan with them instead of against them. Bank research before an Age turns. Embrace institutions to keep your advance tree open. Know that the Height of Absolutism is where the political systems really open up, and know that by the Age of Revolutions, mercenaries and battle-based war score will not carry you the way they did at the start. The calendar is the silent co-governor of every campaign, whether you were paying attention to it or not.
## The six Ages, and the calendar you cannot argue with

EU5 runs on six Ages: Traditions, Renaissance, Discovery, Reformation, Absolutism, and Revolutions. They begin respectively in year 1, 1342, 1437, 1537, 1637, and 1737, and each lasts roughly a century.

The structural fact worth stating plainly: every country transitions between Ages at the same moment, the instant the game clock hits that year. This is not something an individual country can rush, delay, or opt out of. There is no button that hurries your realm into the Renaissance and no lever that holds it back in Traditions. You do not choose when your country enters the next Age, the calendar does, and it does so for every nation on the map simultaneously.

That simultaneous transition is more than trivia. It means every realm is researching under the same constraints at the same time, and the relative advantages of being early or late to an Age are locked in by the world clock, not by player skill.

## Each Age, you pick a Focus

At the start of every Age after Traditions, a country selects one of three Focuses: Administrative, Diplomatic, or Military. That single choice determines the actual shape of the advance tree available to research for the entire Age.

This is a real, once-per-Age strategic decision, not a minor toggle. Pick Military for the Age of Discovery and your available advances skew toward martial options for the whole era; you are not revisiting that choice until the next century turns over. And if the three-way Administrative, Diplomatic, Military split sounds familiar, it should, the same division already runs through how governments are built and how Political Influence is spent. The Age system is echoing a core design rhythm the rest of the game shares.

## How research actually works

The research system sits on top of the Ages, and its numbers are wiki-confirmed. The base cost for any advance is 25 Research Progress. Each Age after Traditions adds a cumulative 15% to that base cost, so Renaissance-era advances cost 15% more, scale up from there, and reach a full 75% more by the Age of Revolutions.

There is a partial offset worth knowing. Once a country has moved into a new Age, advances left over from previous Ages get a flat discount of 8 Research Progress off their cost. Finishing your Traditions-era backlog in the Renaissance is cheaper than it would have been while it was current, which quietly rewards clearing old trees rather than abandoning them.

A country not actively researching anything can stockpile up to 12 months of research progress, and that banked value carries straight into the next advance you start. This is the number worth remembering if you are tempted to glance at research as a pure on/off: pausing research briefly is not a wasted opportunity. It banks. Twelve months of stored progress is waiting for you the moment you pick something to spend it on.

title: EU5 Societal Values Explained
metaDescription: EU5 societal values explained: societal value axes, diminishing returns, conditional axes like Mysticism and Sinicized, and how they shape laws and diplomacy.
content:
Two articles on this site have already pointed at societal values without ever explaining what they are. The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) mentioned that the Absolutism versus Liberalism axis now grants monthly Political Influence at both extremes, without defining what an axis is. The [Situations guide](/blog/eu5-situations-explained/) walked through a worked example that ends in a choice between two societal value outcomes, again without unpacking the system behind it. This article is the answer to both. It is the missing explanation that turns a passing reference into something you actually manage.

One confidence note before the deep dive: this article is on firmer ground than most in the cluster. The core mechanics here are confirmed identically across four independent sources, the EU5 wiki's Government page, a detailed Steam community guide, and two third-party reference sites. That is stronger corroboration than most mechanics pieces in this project have had, so the framework below is written with confidence. Specific bonuses and exact scale values still get tuned between patches, but the shape of the system is well established.

## What a Societal Value actually is

A Societal Value is an axis with two opposite poles, and both ends are capped at 100. A country's position on that axis is primarily shaped by its Laws, Government Reforms, Estate Privileges, and Cabinet Actions, and it drifts slowly over time toward whichever pole those forces are pushing it toward.

The key thing to understand is that progress is gradual, not instant. As a country moves toward a pole, it gains bonuses and penalties that scale up smoothly from zero to their full listed value. There is no flip switch moment where you suddenly become one thing or the other. Your country is always somewhere on the spectrum between the two poles, and what you feel is the cumulative weight of how far you have drifted.

That makes societal values feel like a current rather than a destination. You are not setting a value and being done. You are continuously being pulled in one direction, and the pull only matters as much as the forces behind it keep pushing.

## The diminishing returns ceiling

Here is the mechanic worth featuring prominently: progress toward a pole stalls at a ceiling determined by how many total factors are currently pushing in that direction. The further a country has already moved toward one pole, the more additional factors it needs to push it any further.

That single rule has a real consequence. It is the mechanical reason a country cannot just pick a direction once and coast. Early in the game, a handful of aligned laws and reforms will move you noticeably. Later, once you are already deep toward a pole, those same factors move you much less, and you need a growing pile of reinforcement just to hold ground, let alone advance.

This is a subtle but real reason players who chase one extreme late in the game find it slower going than it was early on. The system is quietly rewarding sustained commitment and quietly punishing anyone who tries to rush a pole at the last minute. If you want to sit at an extreme, you have to build the whole country around it for the whole game, not just flip a law in the endgame.

## It is a background layer touched by almost everything

One detailed community guide makes a point worth carrying into every campaign: societal values are influenced by surprisingly indirect things. How much a country spends on army, fort, and navy maintenance. The proportion of its population that are Nobles versus Burghers versus Soldiers. Even how much Art the country has produced.

That list matters more than the specific entries. It tells you this is not a menu you visit occasionally. Societal values are a background layer shaped by almost everything you do, which means you are always steering them whether you mean to or not. A player who ignores them entirely is still moving them with every maintenance slider, every decision about which pops to favor, and every Art-producing building they build. You might as well be deliberate about it, because you cannot opt out of influencing them.
## Not every axis is available to every country

Here is the single most useful, non-obvious fact in this article, and it directly answers a confusion you are likely to hit: societal values are not a uniform, identical menu for every nation. Your country's religion, location, and current era genuinely change which axes you are even managing.

Some axes are conditional. The Mysticism versus Jurisprudence axis is only available to countries whose primary religion belongs to the Islamic, Druze, or Yazidi religion groups. The Sinicized versus Unsinicized axis is only available to countries outside the Chinese culture group whose capital sits in the China or Southeast Asia subcontinent, or who are subjects of China. And some axes are gated by Age, the game's era-progression system, only becoming available once a country reaches a specific era.

The conditional axes also have a gotcha worth internalizing. Switching away from a religion or status that grants one of these axes does not preserve your progress if you later switch back. When you lose the axis, whatever progress you had is gone, and re-gaining the axis restarts you from the middle of it, not from where you left off. A country that converts away from an Islamic religion and later converts back does not resume its old Mysticism rating. It starts over.

That directly answers the "why don't I have this option" confusion. If another country has a societal value you do not see, the answer is usually that their religion, location, or era qualifies them for it and yours does not. It is not a bug and it is not a missing feature on your end.

## What a societal value shift actually looks like

The clearest concrete example is the one the Situations article already referenced without explaining. During the Nanbokucho Jidai situation, countries at war with a member of the Japanese Shogunate can get an event offering a choice between two outcomes: a change of +5 toward the Belligerent pole at a cost of 10 Purity, or a change of +5 toward the Conciliatory pole at a cost of 5 Prestige.

That is the entire mechanic in miniature. A real choice, a real directional shift on an axis, and real opposing costs attached to each direction. Choosing Belligerent makes your country more aggressive as a society at the price of its spiritual purity. Choosing Conciliatory does the opposite, softer national character for a cheaper but still real cost to your prestige. Neither option is free, and neither is purely good, which is exactly why societal values feel like a genuine trade-off rather than a free bonus.

This is the piece that closes the loop with the Situations article. When it said a situation ends in a choice between societal value outcomes, it was describing exactly this kind of moment: an event where the direction of your country's current is one of the things on the table.

## The diplomatic consequence

Societal values are not only an internal bonus system. They measurably affect how other countries treat you. Player discussion around EU5's Antagonism mechanic notes that societal value differences between two countries are one of the direct inputs into their mutual antagonism score, sitting alongside differences in government type, religion, culture, and language.

Higher antagonism does real work against you. It can trigger hostile effects in shared locations and it worsens how the other country views you. This is worth one clear paragraph because it means the choices you make on your societal value axes leak out into the diplomatic map. A country at odds with you on values is a country that starts the relationship closer to hostility, not because of anything either of you did recently, but because of the slow drift your two societies have been on for years.

## A background system worth respecting

Societal values are the connective tissue this site has been circling for two articles. The Political Influence guide referenced the Absolutism versus Liberalism axis producing monthly Political Influence at both extremes. The Situations guide ended its worked example on a societal value choice. Both were pointing at a system that rewards sustained, deliberate, whole-realm commitment and quietly taxes anyone who ignores it or tries to rush it late.

The practical read is simple. Pick a direction that fits the country you are building, keep reinforcing it with laws, reforms, privileges, and cabinet choices, accept that late-game movement is slower than early-game movement, and remember that your values are also diplomacy. You are never not steering this system, so you might as well steer it on purpose.

title: EU5 Situations Explained
metaDescription: EU5 situations explained: historical arcs that play out as geopolitical events, Nanbokuchō Jidai worked example, and how they connect to Political Influence.
content:
The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) already told you that interacting with Situations costs Political Influence. What it never explained is what a Situation actually is. This article is that explanation, the missing piece that turns a line-item cost into something you understand before you spend on it.

One quick caveat before the deep dive, the same one worth giving for any mechanics piece this far into a live-service Paradox title: the wiki's Situations page is tagged both "Potentially outdated" and "Pre-release," and named situations have already been through several balance passes. The framework here is real and confirmed, the idea that EU5 plays out historical moments as living systems. Treat the specific historical situations and their exact numbers as subject to tuning in later patches, and check in-game prompts before betting a war on a figure.

## What a Situation actually is

A Situation is a historical arc the game plays out as a connected, ongoing event rather than an isolated one-off trigger. Think the Hundred Years' War, the Guelphs versus Ghibellines struggle in Italy, the Reformation, the Black Death, the Rise of the Turks, or Japan's Nanbokuchō Jidai civil war. Each of those isn't a single event firing once and then vanishing, it's a story with phases, participants, and choices that unfold across years of in-game time.

That might sound abstract until you remember why EU5 starts in 1337 in the first place. EU4 started in 1444, more than a century later, which means a lot of its most famous historical moments were already underway or over before you ever loaded in. EU5 deliberately pushes the start date back more than a century specifically so you can experience some of these situations from their actual historical beginning instead of joining partway through. That is a genuinely different design philosophy from EU4, and it changes how you approach the opening of any campaign.
## The worked example: Nanbokuchō Jidai

The clearest way to see how a Situation actually functions is the Nanbokuchō Jidai, the 1337 Japanese civil war between two imperial courts. Worth acknowledging up front: every Situation is built differently, some include their own sub-systems like the Leagues in the Italian Wars, so treat this as one strong illustration of the pattern rather than a universal template. But it shows the bones of the mechanic better than anything else in the game.

When the situation starts, every involved country is placed into one of two sides, the Jimyōin Court supporters or the Daikakuji Court supporters, or else it stays neutral. Countries on the same side cannot declare war on each other, which immediately turns the diplomatic map of medieval Japan into a hard-coded faction split.

Then comes the real decision. Each involved country chooses to support the side it historically supported, support the opposing side, or remain neutral, and each choice carries a real, named cost:

- Supporting your historical side grants +5 Prestige. If the game's Historical AI setting is on, every AI-controlled country automatically makes this choice.

- Supporting the opposing side costs 12 Stability and 15 Honor, a serious bill for trying to rewrite history.

- Staying neutral costs 2.5 Stability and 5 Honor, cheaper than flipping sides but still not free, there is no side-option without strings attached.

And it doesn't end when the situation starts. Any country that is at peace can later change its position. Moving to neutral costs 10 Stability and Honor, and flipping to the opposing side costs 30 Stability and Honor, so the exit doors are expensive too. One specific nation involved, Ashikaga, cannot make that later switch at all, they're locked in from the moment the situation begins.
## Situations run at every scale

Not every Situation is a continent-spanning war. The same mechanic powers smaller, more granular moments too. Take the Rise of the Turks situation, which gives its strongest Beylik access to unique situation actions. If any location has the Conquered integration status, there is a 4% chance each month that a triggered event offers a real choice: gain 20 integration progress plus a 5-point shift in societal values toward Communalism, or gain 10 integration progress plus 7 Stability instead.

That is the same skeleton as Nanbokuchō Jidai, historical context, sides or factions, and a choice with concrete costs and rewards, just scaled way down to a single province rather than a whole region. It's worth including here because it shows Situations aren't only the big headline wars. They're a layer of the game that operates at every level, and the mechanic rewards actually reading the prompt and weighing the two sides before you click.

## Situations get balanced, and some contain Leagues

Everything above isn't a dusty system Paradox shipped once and forgot. The patch notes for several releases confirm named situations have received direct balance changes, including the Rise of the Turks, the Hundred Years' War, the Red Turban Rebellions, and the Italian Wars. One of those changes specifically improved how countries in the Italian Wars situation choose whether to join Leagues within that situation.

That confirms Leagues are a sub-mechanic inside some situations, alliance-like groupings tied to the specific historical conflict rather than a global alliance system. It varies from situation to situation, so there's no single rule to memorize here, just know they exist and are worth watching for in whichever conflict you get pulled into.

## What Situations mean when you actually play them

The [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) referenced Situations as a spending category without ever unpacking them. Now the loop is closed. Political Influence is spent on Situation interactions, and those interactions are real historical arcs with real sides, real choices, and real Stability and Honor costs attached to picking wrong. When you see a Situation fire in your campaign, you're not watching a scripted cutscene, you're standing inside a system that wants you to make a decision and live with its consequences.

title: EU5 Naval Warfare Guide: Ships, Fleets, and Sea Battles Explained
metaDescription: EU5 naval warfare guide: heavy ships, galleys, and light ships, the cannons vs hull formula, frontage, blockades, and how to build a fleet that wins.
content:
Land combat at least has a paper trail. There's a wiki page, unreadable as it is, and a forum thread that field-tested the actual math. Naval combat doesn't even get that much attention. The wiki buries its ship formulas underneath the land army formulas like an afterthought, most build guides mention ships only to say "build some for exploration," and even the best community combat write-up treats the navy as a footnote tacked onto the end of a land-warfare essay. Nobody's laid out why your battle fleet keeps losing, or why the navy you're paying to maintain in peacetime is quietly bleeding your treasury for nothing in return. That's what this one is for.

One caveat before the deep dive, the same one worth giving for any mechanics piece this far into a live-service Paradox title: the numbers below come from the current wiki cross-checked against a detailed, well-regarded community breakdown from shortly after launch. The game has moved through several balance passes since, most recently update 1.4 "Rio Salado." Treat which ship does which job as the durable part. Treat exact percentages as "true as tested," and check your own combat tooltips before betting a war on a specific number.

## The three ship types are not interchangeable

EU5 gives you four ship categories, but only three of them fight: Heavy Ships, Galleys, and Light Ships. Transports exist to carry regiments across water and have a token combat stat (Transport Power) that nobody should ever plan around.

The other three split into three completely different jobs, and building the wrong one for the job you need is the single most common way to waste treasury on a navy that does nothing.

**Heavy Ships** carry the most Cannons and the biggest Hull. They are, without qualification, the best ships in a straight fight. They're also expensive to maintain and bad at the two things that make a navy useful in peacetime, which we'll get to. The right call is usually to build them for war and mothball a chunk of the fleet when you're not using it, but budget for a slow wake-up call. The wiki confirms repair draws on Sailors and Gold without giving a timeframe, but a detailed community test from shortly after launch clocked mothballed ships dropping to 10% strength and regenerating only about 10% of that per month, so it takes the better part of a year to bring a fleet back from nothing. That test is from an early patch and hasn't been reconfirmed since, so treat it as "recovery is genuinely slow" rather than a fixed nine-month deadline. Either way, unmothballing is something you plan ahead of a war, not something you do in reaction to one.

**Galleys** are the budget option. They're cheap, and because they cost less Frontage than a Heavy Ship, you can field more of them in the same space. In Narrows they get a real damage bonus, and they pick up a smaller one in Inland Seas. Take them into open Ocean or Deep Ocean and the exact same terrain modifier flips against them hard: a straight damage penalty in the open sea. That makes Galleys a genuinely good regional choice if you're fighting in the Mediterranean, the Baltic, or similar enclosed waters, and a genuinely bad choice anywhere else.

**Light Ships** lose straight combat to almost everything. Their real job isn't fighting; it's Maritime Presence, trade protection, and blockading enemy ports, and they're the best ship type at all three even though they're the worst at combat. If a fight breaks out while you're using a Light Ship for one of those jobs, keep it in reserve and let your Galleys or Heavies do the dying.

## How a ship actually deals damage

Ship damage doesn't work like land combat's "manpower times combat power." It compares Cannons on the attacking ship against Hull Size on the defending ship. The bigger the gap in the attacker's favor, the bigger the damage bonus. Concretely: a ship with 9 Cannons attacking a ship with 6 Hull gets roughly a 50% damage bonus, because 6 would need to grow by half to match 9. Flip the ratio and the same math turns into a penalty instead of a bonus. This is why Hull Size matters as much for a ship's survivability as raw firepower does for its offense, and why pairing a high-Cannon ship against a low-Hull target (light ships and galleys, mostly) is where the real damage spikes happen.

From there, several familiar multipliers stack on top, all multiplicative with each other:

- **Current ship strength** scales damage output directly. A ship down to 50% strength deals roughly half its normal damage. A limping ship isn't just fragile, it's also barely contributing, which is a real argument for pulling damaged ships out rather than leaving them to soak more hits while doing nothing.

- **Ship Experience** cuts incoming damage the same way it does on land: up to 50% reduction at 100% experience. Veteran crews are mechanically tankier, not just flavor text.

- **Flanking Ability** rewards attacking a section the enemy isn't defending, same concept as land combat. Light Ships get a flat +20% bonus when flanking; Galleys sit at a mild edge over baseline. Neither is the reason you win a naval war, but they matter on the margins.

- **Naval Damage Done** stacks up to roughly 20% from a skilled admiral and select advances, and **Naval Damage Taken** works as a flat reduction on the defensive side, similar in spirit to a nation's starting naval bonuses or penalties.

- Attacking a ship that hasn't engaged yet gives the attacker a modest edge, a 10% Strength damage bonus and a 20% Morale damage bonus. That's the same shape as land combat's disengaged-unit penalty, and worth knowing since it means straggling ships are a real liability, just not a catastrophic one.

## Frontage is why raw ship count lies to you

Every ship type costs a different amount of the location's available Frontage: Heavy Ships cost the most per hull, Light Ships sit in the middle, and Galleys cost the least, meaning you can physically fit more Galleys into the same battle. It's tempting to read that as "Galleys can swarm Heavies with numbers," and it's wrong.

Take a concrete case: eight Age IV Heavy Ships (Galleons, roughly 60 Cannons and 30 Hull each) fill about the same Frontage as thirteen Galleasses (a Galley type with roughly 16 Cannons and 10 Hull each), even fighting in coastal waters where Galleasses get their terrain bonus. Work through the Cannons-vs-Hull math for both sides and the Galleasses come out dealing under a quarter of the damage the Galleons do, despite outnumbering them by more than half and technically fitting into a similar Frontage footprint. More hulls sound like more damage. What actually decides the fight is Cannons against Hull, and Heavy Ships win that comparison badly enough that Frontage efficiency doesn't come close to closing the gap.

The practical read: if you expect to actually fight a rival navy, Galleys are a stopgap for early game or a specialist choice for enclosed waters, not a numbers strategy against someone building Heavies.

## The job nobody builds a navy for: presence and blockades

Combat isn't the only thing a navy does, and for a lot of the game it isn't even the main thing. Maritime Presence, the stat that determines how much naval influence you project in a sea zone and feeds directly into Proximity for colonization and trade, comes overwhelmingly from Light Ships. Blockading an enemy port during a siege, which speeds up the siege dice roll, is also a Light Ship specialty.

Galleys can pitch in on Maritime Presence reasonably well, just not as well as Light Ships, but they're a poor choice for blockading specifically. The practical logic: a real blockade works like a standing physical barrier that can sit on station for a long time, and that favors a hull built for endurance over a galley built for short, oar-powered bursts of speed. Heavy Ships are worst at both jobs and are also your most expensive maintenance line, which is the second reason (Frontage-inefficient combat being the first) that leaving a full Heavy fleet active in peacetime is usually just burning treasury.

That split gives you a genuinely simple rule of thumb: Heavies fight your wars, Light Ships run your peacetime navy and your blockades, and Galleys fill in wherever the water is enclosed enough to make them cheap and viable.

## What this means for your fleet

Building a navy is a smaller decision than building an army, but it follows the same logic your army composition already runs on: match the tool to the job and the terrain, don't default to whichever unit looks biggest on paper. A few things worth taking away:

- Keep a lean, mostly-Light-Ship peacetime navy for presence and trade protection, and build up Heavy Ships specifically ahead of a war you're planning, since mothballed Heavies take months to bring back to fighting strength.

- Don't mix Light Ships into a battle fleet expecting them to contribute damage. Their job is staying alive to keep doing their real job, not trading blows with Heavies.

- Galleys are a legitimate strategy if your wars happen in enclosed seas. They're a losing one the moment the fighting moves into open ocean.

- A damaged ship is doing less work than its hull count suggests, since its strength percentage scales its own output down. Pull it before it becomes dead weight in the formation.

None of this replaces knowing your actual numbers in a live game, since Paradox has already shown with land combat's Secure Flanks and disengaged-unit penalty that hidden multipliers get rebalanced hard between patches without much announcement. But the shape of the naval system, what each ship type is actually for, is the part that's held steady, and it's the part most players are currently guessing at.

*Related reading: [EU5 Combat Explained](/blog/eu5-combat-explained/) for the land side of this same system, [EU5 Army Composition Basics](/blog/eu5-army-composition/) for the ground-force equivalent of this guide, and [EU5 Beginner's Guide: Trade and Merchants](/blog/eu5-trade-guide/) for how Maritime Presence feeds into the trade system.*

title: EU5 Parliament Explained
metaDescription: EU5 Parliament explained: the session this site has referenced across three guides, agenda pass/fail stakes, the neglect penalty, and why location matters.
content:
Parliament is the mechanic this site keeps referencing without ever explaining. The Political Influence guide mentions spending 75 Political Influence for 25 Parliament support. The Estates guide covers estate power without covering what estates actually do with it in the chamber. And the court conversation around raising a new character from an estate points at a Parliament activity that never gets unpacked. This article is the piece that connects all three, and it's about time it got its own explanation.

One quick caveat before the sessions begin. The EU5 wiki's Parliament page and its Government pages are both tagged by their editors as potentially outdated, with sections last verified for a pre-release build, and a Patch 1.3 changelog entry confirms Parliament mechanics are actively being tuned. The shape of the system is solid, so treat it as a reliable map. But specific numbers may shift between patches, and that's expected rather than a flaw in the guide.

## What calling Parliament actually lets you do

A session of Parliament is not a single-purpose screen. When you call your estates together, you can use the session to create a Casus Belli, raise taxes, increase your Army Levies and Naval Levies, or change any of your current laws. That makes it a genuinely multi-purpose tool, one session can resolve a problem that would otherwise cost you several separate resources.

You don't get unlimited sessions. Parliament can be called every five years, so each one is a scarce opportunity rather than a button you press whenever something annoys you.

## Agendas, and the support wall you have to climb

Before any estate will pledge its support to your session, that estate may have a Parliament Agenda that has to be resolved. You can't just walk in and expect a blank check. Whether an agenda passes or fails depends on estate power, each estate either supports or opposes the issue, and whichever side it picks, it adds its estate power to that side of the scale. The estate that originally proposed an issue always supports it automatically.

There's also a hard cap on how much any single estate can push. Each estate can propose up to two Parliament issues at a time, so a powerful estate can flood the agenda, but only so far. If you want the full picture on how that power is built and balanced in the first place, the [Estates guide](/blog/eu5-estates-guide/) has the deep dive, this is where that power actually gets spent.

## The stakes are concrete, and they're not symmetric

If a Parliament agenda passes, the country gains a bonus. If it fails, the country loses a flat 7 Stability. That is the single number worth remembering from this whole system, failure is not a shrug and a move on, it is a meaningful stability hit that costs real resources to recover.

What a passing agenda can actually do is deliberately varied. Accepting an agenda costs varying amounts of Stability, and in exchange it can shift societal values, enact a policy, affect opinion with another country, or reduce taxes on the supporting estate for five years. There is no single fixed reward, so don't plan around one number. The range is the point, sometimes you're shaping your nation's values, sometimes you're buying a diplomatic opening, and sometimes you're quietly paying off the estate that keeps your treasury full.

## The neglect penalty that sneaks up on you

Parliament has a timer in the background that most players never look at. If Parliament hasn't been called within the last 120 months, that's 10 years, then every month after that, all estates lose 1% Satisfaction Equilibrium. It's a slow bleed rather than a cliff, which is exactly why it's easy to ignore until it has already cost you real estate satisfaction.

That quiet tax is the kind of mechanic this genre is full of. It never makes a scene, it just makes every estate slightly unhappier than it should be, month after month, and ten years later you wonder why your realm feels harder to manage than it used to. A single Parliament session every decade is a cheap insurance policy against the slow grind.

## Location matters, and so does the war map

You don't have to hold Parliament in your capital. It can take place in the capital or in another location, and holding it elsewhere gives that location some small extra benefits. Choosing a seat is a real decision, not a cosmetic one.

The risk is that if the chosen location becomes occupied during a war, the Parliament fails outright. Calling a session in a border province while you're fighting an active war is a genuine gamble. If that province gets taken, you lose the session and whatever you were trying to accomplish with it. If you're planning to use Parliament to raise taxes or change a law right when a war starts, that's a strong argument for holding it somewhere that won't be on the front line.

## Parliament type decides who gets a voice

Which estates can propose agendas depends on your Parliament type, and that type is something you choose and can change. It costs 50 Government Power to switch, so it's not something you'll be toggling every session, but it's a real lever when your realm's balance changes.

One constant cuts across every type: the Nobility estate can always suggest agendas, regardless of what kind of parliament you run. Even if you pick a type that explicitly favors commoners or the clergy, the nobles still get their seat at the table. That's worth knowing before you build your whole strategy around shutting them out.

## The Crown Power link you should actually use

Initial Parliament Support is raised mainly by Crown Power, with laws, government reforms, and advances able to add to it as well. And here's the link the [Political Influence guide](/blog/eu5-political-influence/) already set up without this article existing to close it: Political Influence is what raises Crown Power in the first place. A well-managed Political Influence economy makes your Parliament sessions go more smoothly before you even walk into the chamber, because the support you're starting with is higher when your crown is strong.

That's the connective tissue this site has been pointing at for three separate articles. Political Influence feeds Crown Power, Crown Power feeds initial Parliament support, estate power decides whether your agendas pass, and the whole loop sits on top of the estate management the Estates guide covers. It all runs through this one screen.

## The Holy Roman Empire does its own thing

One acknowledgment before the summary, because it's a genuinely separate system. The Holy Roman Empire has its own, more elaborate Parliament called the Imperial Diet, with seven special statuses that carry voting power and its own set of laws that only the organization's leader can propose changing, each requiring a full year of debate. If this site ever covers the HRE in depth, that breakdown belongs in its own article. For now, the short version is: if you're playing inside the Empire, don't assume your normal Parliament rules apply, you're dealing with a different game entirely.

## A Parliament routine worth keeping

The practical takeaway from all of this is that Parliament rewards a routine, not a drama. Call it at least once every decade to keep the neglect penalty from bleeding your estates dry. Hold it somewhere defensible if there's even a chance of war. Keep your Political Influence healthy so your Crown Power starts every session ahead. And remember that each estate can only propose two issues but the Nobility always gets a vote, so spend your estate power where it actually decides an outcome.

The three articles that referenced Parliament on this site were all correct. Political Influence really does buy support, estate power really does decide agendas, and the court really does use Parliament to raise characters. Now that this guide exists, the loop between them has a home.

title: EU4 Trade Companies Explained
metaDescription: EU4 trade companies explained: what they are, eligibility rules, the 51% merchant threshold, and when to choose a trade company over a full state.
content:
Trade companies are one of those EU4 systems people keep reinventing the wrong way. Confusion about them turns up consistently from 2014 through 2024, a full decade, with the same recurring questions: how do you actually create one, should that distant colony become a trade company or a full state, and what are the real benefits and tradeoffs. This article is the third piece in a set with the interactive trade node map and the trade power guide, and it answers the question those first two leave open: what do you actually do with overseas territory once you understand how the network and its merchants work.

## What a trade company actually is

A trade company is a collection of provinces in a designated trade company region. Compared to including those same provinces in a state or a territory, a trade company gives you less tax, manpower, and sailors, but more trade power, more trade goods including production income, and more naval force limit. It also eats less governing capacity than a state would.

That last point deserves a direct correction while we're here. An older, frequently-repeated player claim says production income is untouched by trade company status. The current wiki page states the opposite: trade companies actually increase trade goods and production income compared to full statehood. This guide sides with the wiki on that one, since we leaned on the current wiki page over older forum comments wherever the two disagree.

## Who is eligible

The rules are specific. Only provinces on a different subcontinent from your capital can be part of a trade company. Trade company regions don't include the Americas at all, colonial nations handle those instead. A province can't be part of a state and a trade company at the same time, so only provinces not currently in a state are eligible to be added, and if a province already in a trade company later becomes part of a state, it gets automatically removed.

To create one, you can add eligible provinces all at once through the trade node's own interface, or province by province through each province's own interface.

## One thing to know before you start

Trade companies require the Wealth of Nations DLC at minimum. If you don't own it and you've been hunting for the trade company option without finding it, that's why. You're not missing something, the feature itself is locked behind that DLC, a fact confirmed directly by players who bought it specifically to unlock the feature.

## The 51% merchant threshold

Here's the most repeated, most concrete fact in all the discussions: once trade company provinces control more than 51% of the total trade power in that trade company's region, the owner gains an additional merchant. Players have confirmed this independently years apart, in 2017 and again in 2024.

That single threshold is a genuinely strong incentive on its own. It explains why experienced players obsess over pushing a region over the halfway mark. A bonus merchant is a big deal, and reaching it turns an ordinary overseas region into something you actively want to grow.

## The scaling bonus that almost nobody explains

There's a mechanic most guides skip entirely, and it's one of the most underexplained parts of the whole system. Trade companies give a scaling goods-produced bonus to every province in that trade company region that is NOT itself part of a trade company, regardless of who owns it.

Here's what actually drives it. The size of that bonus scales with what percentage of the region's total trade power sits inside trade companies, and with how many institutions the trade-company-forming nation has embraced. So the bonus grows stronger later in the game, as your trade power share climbs and you embrace more institutions.

This deserves far more attention than it usually gets, because it changes the calculus on what you do with territory you don't control. Pushing trade company share in a region isn't just about your own provinces. It silently boosts production everywhere in that same region, even in provinces owned by other nations.

## A common misconception about Expand Overseas

The generic Expand Overseas mission requires owning at least 5 provinces in each of three separate trade company regions, 15 total. Here's the part the mission's own wording gets wrong: those provinces do not need to actually be organized into trade companies to satisfy the requirement. Simply owning them in those regions is enough.

This is a real, repeated point of confusion, and it costs people real effort. Players over-convert provinces into trade companies unnecessarily, chasing a requirement they already met, just because the mission text implies it. Own the land in the right regions and the mission counts it.

## Trade company or full state

The consistent community answer across years of threads is that trade companies are generally the better choice when a province is culturally or religiously different from your main group, geographically distant from your capital, or not valuable enough on its own to justify full integration. Full statehood makes more sense for closer provinces that are easy to integrate and genuinely worth the state slot.

There's a well-established practical tip that goes with that. Convert a province's religion or culture before adding it to a trade company, not after. Players consistently describe a heavier conversion penalty for provinces already inside a trade company. I'll flag this as practical advice rather than a precise mechanic, since the exact penalty size isn't independently confirmed on the wiki, but it's repeated often enough that it's worth taking seriously.

## One risk to know about

There's a negative event-driven country modifier called Trade Company Trouble that reduces trade efficiency by 10% for a period of years. The wiki page describing it is tagged by the wiki's own editors as potentially outdated, referencing an older patch, so the exact odds and duration aren't guaranteed current numbers. Treat it as a warning that trade company life has occasional headaches, without taking those specifics as gospel.

## What it means for your campaign

The full three-part picture now goes like this. The trade node map shows you the shape of the network. The trade power article explains how power and merchants move value inside it. This piece covers what to do with the territory once you're out there expanding. Trade companies tie most of that logic together, since the whole point of building a trade empire is to control and steer more value through the network.

If you're running a nation far from home, look hard at the trade company option before reaching for the state button. The extra merchants, the trade dominance, and the scaling goods bonus usually outweigh what you'd otherwise get from stating. Combined with the steering chains from the trade power guide, a well-run set of trade companies feeds a very healthy home economy.

title: EU5 Combat Explained
metaDescription: EU5 combat explained in plain language: battle phases, engagements, flanking, frontage, terrain penalties, and the defensive stats that win fights.
content:
EU5 combat has a transparency problem. The game's own wiki page is a wall of nested multiplication formulas, math notation, and unlabeled variables. It's genuinely correct and genuinely detailed, and genuinely unreadable for anyone who isn't already deep into the mechanics. A separate forum thread explains the real mechanics brilliantly, but it's written for people who already understand the basics. Nobody has taken the middle ground and made this system accessible. That's what this article is for. It's also the natural follow-up to the army composition guide, since this is what actually happens once the army you built steps onto the field.

One quick caveat before the deep dive. The wiki's combat page is tagged by its editors as potentially outdated, last verified for version 1.0, and the game has moved on through at least a 1.3 patch. The core systems here, phases, sections, engagement, flanking, frontage, are fundamental and unlikely to have changed shape. But treat specific numbers as illustrating how the system behaves rather than guaranteed current values.

## How a battle starts

One side attacks, one side defends. If the location has no fort, whichever army arrived first becomes the defender. If it does have a fort, the fort's controller is always the defender, regardless of who got there first.

That's the whole opening setup. It means the defender isn't always the player who wants to defend, and it rewards thinking about who controls the forts in the path of your advance before you commit to a fight.

## Phases, and the artillery opening

Combat is broken into repeating phases, each lasting five hours. In each phase, both sides roll a die, and the result determines how much damage gets dealt until the next phase rolls around.

If either side has artillery, the battle opens with a separate five hour Bombard Phase first. During it, artillery gets a chance each hour to strike a regiment before the main fighting even starts. So a force with artillery gets free shots at the enemy before any regular unit has swung a weapon, which is another reason the army composition guide pushes artillery so hard.

## Sections, and what engagement really means

Every battle has a center, a left flank, a right flank, and a reserve. You assign your units to these positions before the fight begins.

Units placed in reserve aren't just waiting around safely, and that's the part people get wrong. The real mechanic to understand is engagement. A unit in the center or on a flank has an hourly chance to become engaged, meaning it locks onto a target and starts actually fighting. Until that happens it stays disengaged, and disengaged units take extra morale damage when attacked. The wiki lists this as a 1.2 multiplier for land units, twenty percent more morale damage.

I want to single that number out because a specific claim floating around community discussions says this is a flat two times, a double penalty. The current wiki text says 1.2 times for land combat. Use that number, and treat the two times figure as the rumor it is.

## Frontage decides how many can actually fight

Here's the mechanical reason a bigger army doesn't automatically win. Only so many units can be engaged simultaneously in a given location, and that limit is shaped by the terrain itself. A large army just means more units waiting their turn or sitting disengaged and vulnerable, not more units hitting the enemy at the same moment.

So combat width is a real constraint, and it rewards quality over raw numbers once you're past it. Bring enough to fill the front and hold the flanks, and funnel the rest where terrain lets them matter.

## Terrain has real, specific costs

The wiki gives a clean example that makes this concrete. A mountainous woods location gives the attacker a -3 penalty to their dice rolls, -2 from the mountains and -1 from the woods, and reduces possible frontage for both sides by -6. Rivers cost an attacker -1 to their dice roll for crossing, and straits cost -2.

Those numbers illustrate why attacking across bad terrain into a prepared defense is such a brutal proposition. The dice penalty compounds every phase, and the frontage cut prevents you from bringing your numeric advantage to bear.

## Flanking rewards maneuvering, not just numbers

Attacking a section your opponent isn't actively defending lets your Flanking Ability stat apply as a damage bonus. The wiki states it plainly: 200% flanking ability is a full two times damage multiplier, while 100% means no bonus at all.

This is a real mechanical reason to actively think about where you're attacking, not just how much you're bringing. Hitting an undefended flank is worth dramatically more than piling onto a defended center, because the flank lets a modest advantage become a swing.

## Levies vs the professionals
