When levies attack Regulars, a Levy Combat Efficiency modifier applies, with a base value of 0.5. That's the concrete number behind the general advice already in the army composition guide, levies genuinely punch below their stats specifically when fighting professional troops.

It also means army quality isn't just about stacking more troops. A smaller force of regulars can hold its own against a much larger levy swarm, and converting levy numbers into regular quality is one of the strongest upgrades available.

## The defensive stats that quietly win fights

Military Tactics divides incoming damage. The wiki's own example states that a Tactics value of 2 is a 50 percent damage reduction. Army Experience works the same way, at 100 percent experience that's also a 50 percent reduction in damage taken.

Veteran troops are mechanically tankier, not just better on paper. When the trade power of two armies is close, the one with higher tactics and experience absorbs half again the punishment, and that advantage snowballs across a long war.

## Secure Flanks rewards balanced deployment

Having friendly troops in an adjacent section gives a defensive bonus, 10 percent for infantry in the center, 5 percent on the flanks, and it doubles if both flanks are secured. This is concrete encouragement to spread out across all three sections deliberately rather than stacking everything in the middle.

A balanced line isn't just tidy, it's statistically safer. Leaving a flank empty because you want a bigger center is giving away a permanent defensive bonus you could have kept.

## The morale finding that changes how you pick generals

There's a genuinely surprising community analysis worth taking seriously. A detailed breakdown on the official Paradox forum worked through a real combat example and found that morale damage is calculated using the attacking unit's current Morale multiplied into the damage formula. A unit with high morale can deal dramatically more morale damage than raw troop losses would suggest, roughly fifteen times more in the example, despite the actual kill count only differing by about 2.6 times.

The same analysis noted that max Morale scales with a general's Diplomacy skill, which means that stat might matter far more than most players assume. I'll flag this honestly as one detailed player's tested analysis, not an official developer-confirmed number, since it isn't stated directly on the wiki. But it's exactly the kind of finding that changes how you'd actually pick a general, not just flavor text.

## What this means for your next war

Combat in EU5 is a system of layered constraints and bonuses. Terrain cuts your dice and your frontage, flanks reward a numerical overhang on the right spot, levies fold against regulars at a known rate, tactics and experience halve incoming damage, and sometimes a high-morale army simply floors the enemy before casualties even tell the story. Sieges are a separate system entirely, and they deserve their own article, but the field battle is where all of these pieces collide.

None of this says you can ignore army composition. It says the army you build is just the raw material, and how you deploy it, where you hit, who leads it, and how much morale it carries decides what that material actually accomplishes. Build the right force, and then spend as much time aiming it as you did building it.

## Try It Yourself

The best way to internalize these mechanics is to see them fight. Our **[EU5 Army Battle Lab](/tools/eu5-army-simulator)** lets you build an army against an AI opponent with equal resources, watch the fight resolve phase by phase, and get an autopsy of what worked and what did not.

title: EU5 Sieges Explained
metaDescription: EU5 sieges explained: how sieges work, the dice roll table, assault mechanics, artillery, blockade penalties, and what's different from EU4.
content:
The combat guide ended on a promise: sieges are a separate system, and they deserve their own article. This is that article. Sieges are one of the most confusing parts of EU5 for new players, and the confusion is real, there's a Steam Community thread literally titled "WTF IS THE SIEGE SYSTEM??" full of genuine, unresolved questions. The replies in that same thread also contain some of the best tactical advice found anywhere in the research for this piece, assembled here into one actual guide for the first time. Combined with the army composition guide, this closes out the full picture of what happens when your armies go to war.

Same caveat as the combat article: the wiki's Combat page, where the siege rules live, is tagged by its editors as potentially outdated, last verified for version 1.0, and the game has moved on through at least a 1.3 patch. The fundamentals here are stable, but treat specific numbers as illustrating how the system behaves rather than guaranteed current values.

## How a siege starts

When an army stops in an enemy location that isn't defended by its own army, a siege begins automatically. Every location has a Garrison number, and the siege is won once that garrison is either killed or its morale collapses entirely.

The siege just runs once you sit there. You don't need to issue a special order, you need to be present in force, and the garrison number tells you what you're up against.

## The minimum force requirement

To make progress at all, you need at least as many soldiers besieging as the location has in its garrison. For an unfortified location, at least 100 men will occupy it in 15 days, though various factors can change that timeline.

This is why the army composition guide keeps hammering on force size. If you show up to a siege under-strength, you don't slowly chip away, you simply don't progress until you bring in more men.

## Assault, the fast but bloody option

The attacker can order an assault at any point. It speeds up siege progress dramatically, but it costs soldiers, and once ordered, it cannot be cancelled. Up to three Breaches can occur during a siege, and each one reduces how many soldiers die in an assault.

That last part matters more than it looks. A siege that's gone on longer and produced breaches makes a later assault safer than an early one would have been. Rushing an assault before any breaches exist is the bloodiest possible way to take a fort.

## Phases and the dice roll table

Each siege phase lasts 30 days by default, adjustable by various factors. Every phase rolls a die, and the result drives what happens. Fort Level reduces that roll, so harder forts resist longer. Each Breach increases it by 2, and artillery can add a further bonus. Here's what the roll actually produces, in plain language:

- A roll of 1 triggers a Disease Outbreak.
- Rolls 2 through 4 mean nothing changes, the status quo holds.
- Rolls 5 through 11 cause a Supplies Shortage for the defender.
- Rolls 12 through 13 cause a Food Shortage.
- Rolls 14 through 15 cause a Water Shortage.
- Rolls 16 through 19 cause defenders to desert.
- A roll of 20 means outright Surrender.

Notice what this table is really saying. Progress toward a win is a climb, and most rolls land somewhere in the middle, chipping away at the defender through shortages before desertion and surrender become possible. Sieges in EU5 are a lottery ticket you can tilt, not a button you press.

## The blockade detail that actually matters

A coastal location that isn't blockaded gives the attacker a -1 penalty to the dice roll each phase. That's a specific, real number, and it directly confirms the advice you'll see in every serious siege discussion: blockading a coastal fort isn't just generally helpful, it's removing a penalty you'd otherwise eat every single phase.

If your target is on the coast and you can get ships there, blockading should be near the top of your to-do list. It's the difference between rolling normally and rolling at a permanent disadvantage.

## What artillery contributes

Artillery helps, but how much depends on its condition. Each artillery regiment contributes to the siege dice roll based on its strength and the fort's level, a full-strength artillery unit contributes meaningfully, a heavily depleted one contributes very little or nothing at all.

The plain-language version: stronger, fuller artillery units meaningfully speed up a siege, while a badly depleted artillery regiment barely helps. Dragging a half-strength artillery stack to a siege is a lot of travel for almost no gain, one more reason to keep your artillery healthy between battles.

## Tactics the community has actually tested

This next batch comes from player experience, not the wiki, and it's the best stuff in this guide. Treat it as community-tested knowledge rather than officially documented developer statements.

The AI doesn't pay to keep forts fully staffed during peacetime. Garrisons are typically only around 33% strength the moment a war begins, which is a shock to anyone assuming they need to prepare for full-strength defense.

The timing of your declaration matters. Declaring war on the first day of a month reportedly gives roughly 30 days where assaulting forts is close to free, because the garrisons are at their lowest and haven't ticked up yet.

Regulars are strong at assaulting. A full stack of regular troops can reportedly take 3 to 5 forts in the first month of a war using those assault bonuses, before the garrisons recover.

Generals matter here too. A general's Diplomacy and Admin skills can boost siege effectiveness, in some cases up to 100%. This connects straight back to the combat article's finding about Diplomacy affecting morale, the pattern is consistent, generals are mechanically more important across multiple systems than their flavor text suggests.

Ships can participate directly. From a certain ship tech level onward, naval units in adjacent sea tiles can join battles and sieges directly, and blockading a coastal fort can massively cut down siege time.

And starving the defender out is a legitimate strategy. Buying up or controlling a besieged nation's food supply is a real, usable tactic, not just flavor text, and it compounds with the Food Shortage rolls on the table above.

## What's different from EU4

If you're coming from EU4, a few habits will actively mislead you here, and these differences trace back to the game's lead designer, per reliable player discussion. There is no instant create a wall breach button the way EU4 had, that shortcut is gone. Assaulting burns through an army's morale much faster than it did in EU4, so it can't be spammed the same way you could there. Food logistics are now a real constraint during a siege, a besieging army that isn't fed can starve and desert, which never worked that way in EU4.

Most importantly, the system is intentionally built to be uncertain. The design intent, per the lead designer, is that sieges should be RNG-driven on purpose, both to simulate the psychological uncertainty of a real siege and to make it genuinely possible for the besieger to fail outright.

That last point deserves to be said plainly to any EU4 veteran: don't expect siege outcomes to be as predictable as they were in the previous game. That unpredictability is a deliberate design choice, not a bug. And honestly, it's a choice that will either frustrate or delight you depending on how much you liked the old system's predictability.

## What this means for your war plans

The full picture across three articles now runs together. The army composition guide builds the force, the combat guide explains what happens when that force fights in the field, and this guide covers the sieges that follow. Bring enough men to match the garrison, keep a healthy artillery stack, blockade coastal targets, and time your assaults to the first days of the war. Whatever the dice roll, you've given yourself the best chance the system allows, and for the forts you really can't afford to roll poorly on, you can starve the garrison out before the lottery even starts.
## Try It Yourself

Want to feel the lottery before you bet a war on it? Our **[EU5 Siege Lab](/tools/eu5-siege-simulator)** lets you pick a fort, a garrison, and your army, then rolls the 30-day dice phase by phase, showing you the modifier math and an autopsy of exactly why the fort fell or held. It's the fastest way to internalize why artillery, breaches, and blockades matter more than raw siege length.

title: EU4 Trade Power, Merchants, and Steering Explained
metaDescription: EU4 trade power, merchants, and steering explained: how trade value is created, what merchants actually do, and how a steering chain compounds income.
content:
Ask around the EU4 community and you'll find something that doesn't happen with most other systems: players with hundreds of hours in the game quietly admitting they still don't understand trade. It's not their fault. Threads asking almost exactly this question turn up in 2014, 2015, 2018, 2020, 2023, and 2024, sometimes from people with over 500 hours on the clock. The individual pieces are simple enough, but the way they combine obscures everything. This article is the mechanical explanation behind the interactive trade node map on this site, and the answer to a question players have been asking for over a decade: what is trade power, what do merchants actually do, and how does steering work?

## Where trade value comes from

Every province in EU4 produces a trade good: cloth, wine, iron, gold, whatever sits on that land. The province's trade value is a straightforward calculation, its local goods produced multiplied by the current price of the good it produces. That's the value that enters the trade network from that province.

Two details here surprise people. Production efficiency doesn't touch this number, and local autonomy doesn't either. Trade value is its own separate calculation, which is why a province can look unimpressive as a producer on paper yet still pump serious value into its node.

## What a merchant actually does

A merchant placed at a trade node does one of two things. It collects, converting your percentage share of that node's value directly into income. Or it steers, also called transferring, pushing the node's value onward toward a connected node instead.

That's the entire job description. Merchants don't generate trade value out of thin air, they either cash in your existing share of a node or move it along the network. Most of the confusion around trade clears up once you hold onto that basic distinction.

One restriction worth knowing: a merchant can only reach nodes within your country's trade range. You can't place one anywhere on the map, geography and range decide where you can operate.

## The flat merchant bonus

Here's a detail that's easy to miss because it applies no matter what the merchant is doing. A merchant present at a node gives a flat +10% trade efficiency and +2 trade power at that specific node, whether it's collecting or steering there. That baseline is confirmed and stable.

The practical takeaway is that every merchant you field is worth a little something even before you decide where to point it. Exact numbers can shift slightly between patches, so for big decisions it's worth checking the current in-game tooltip, but the underlying system here has held for a decade across the sources.

## The steering chain

This is the single most important strategic concept in trade. The wiki's own trade strategy guide is explicit about it: the most profitable way to grow trade income is to place merchants in a chain across nodes you control, so that each merchant compounds the value being passed to the next one downstream.

Value doesn't just add up along that chain, it multiplies at each step where a merchant is actively steering it forward. That's the mechanical reason experienced players talk about building a trade empire rather than just picking one good node. A long, merchant-controlled chain leading to your home node is worth dramatically more than the same nodes generating value in isolation.

## The home node collection penalty

Here's the cost that trips everybody up. Collecting at any node that isn't your designated home or primary trade node comes with a base -50% trade power penalty. That number is stable and well known, showing up identically in player discussions from 2015, 2020, and 2024. It wasn't patched away.

But there's a second cost tucked behind the first one, and it's the part that keeps confusing people even after they've heard about the 50% penalty. Collecting anywhere outside your home node also forfeits a separate stacking bonus. Every merchant you have transferring trade toward your home node normally adds a percentage trade power bonus there, and that bonus only applies as long as you aren't collecting elsewhere.

So the real cost of collecting off-node is two losses stacked together, not just one. You take the direct penalty at the node you're collecting from, and you lose the bonus back home. That's exactly why "why did collecting from that node barely earn anything" keeps showing up in threads year after year. Honestly, this is a much harsher cost than most new players expect, and it completely changes the math on where to send your merchants.

## The different kinds of trade power

If you've ever grabbed a trade power modifier and wondered why it didn't seem to do anything, the answer is usually in which category it belongs to. These aren't official wiki terms, they're widely used community shorthand, but they explain most of the confusion:

- Provincial trade power, a flat percentage boost from province-level modifiers, stacks with mercantilism.
- Domestic trade power, only affects nodes where you actually control territory.
- Foreign trade power, only affects nodes where you don't control any territory.
- Global trade power, applies everywhere, the most broadly useful category, but often more expensive or harder to get than the others.
- Trade steering, specifically increases your weight in determining which direction a node's value flows, and it does nothing in a node without an active merchant steering trade.
- Trade efficiency, unlike the categories above, doesn't touch your trade power or share at all. It's a flat multiplier on what you actually collect once your share is determined, capped at 200%.

## Steer Trade vs Transfer Trade Power

Two diplomatic tools, one short note because they're commonly confused. Per the wiki's diplomacy page, Steer Trade tells a target nation's merchants to redirect where they're pointed, but if that merchant is already sitting in its own home node, this can end up doing effectively nothing, since no real trade power changes hands. Transfer Trade Power is generally the more reliable of the two for actually getting value moved in your direction.

## Building your trade empire

Trade companies interact with all of this too, but that's a distinct topic worth its own guide later. For the core system, the picture is simple. Value enters from provinces, merchants either collect it or push it onward, steering compounds it along a chain, and collecting away from home stacks two penalties onto you.

The most important number to remember is that off-home collection costs you far more than the obvious -50%, and the strongest growth comes from a long chain of steering merchants feeding your home node. That combination is the whole game. Trade power categories just explain why individual modifiers behave the way they do, and now they shouldn't surprise you anymore.

The interactive EU4 trade node map shows the network all of this runs on, and this guide covers the mechanics underneath it. They're meant to be read together, the map shows you the shape of the system, and this article tells you how to make it work for you.

title: EU5 Political Influence: What Update 1.4 'Rio Salado' Adds
metaDescription: EU5 Political Influence is a new 0-100 country currency coming in update 1.4. Everything confirmed so far about how you gain and spend it.
content:
Europa Universalis V is adding a unified political resource in upcoming update 1.4, codenamed "Rio Salado." Before that raises your hopes too high, read this part carefully: everything below comes from a recent Tinto Talks developer diary, and it is a preview, not live content. None of this exists in the current version of the game right now. The developers have explicitly said that numbers and mechanics can change before release, so treat every detail here as subject to change.

## Why Political Influence exists

To understand Political Influence, you first need to see the problem it solves. According to the developers, the current game has a lot of places with wildly inconsistent costs. Some actions cost gold, some cost legitimacy, some cost stability, and it is not always obvious which one applies where. They described this as a balancing problem that, in their view, did not really exist in EU4. Political Influence is their answer, one consolidated currency instead of that patchwork.

This reads like a genuine attempt to fix a named, specific complaint rather than change for its own sake. Grand strategy games get messy when several currencies pile up with overlapping uses, and folding them into one readable resource is exactly the kind of cleanup a mature game benefits from.

## What Political Influence is and does

Political Influence is a country-level currency that runs from 0 to 100. Think of it as your ruler's accumulated political capital, credence with the institutions and estates of your realm. It sits alongside legitimacy and stability, but it is more flexible because you actually spend it rather than just holding it.

Keeping it high matters. When Political Influence stays high, it increases your base Crown Power by up to 20 percent. Crown Power is already load-bearing in EU5, so that single bonus is reason enough to pay attention to the resource even before you look at how it gets spent.

## How you gain Political Influence

The diary names two main sources of Political Influence. The primary one is your ruler's own abilities and stats, a capable ruler simply generates more of it. The secondary one is the active abilities of your cabinet, which feed the resource over time. On top of both, certain laws and privileges adjust how quickly it builds up.

The exact gain rate has not been detailed yet. The shape is clear, though. Better ruler, better cabinet, better laws, and Political Influence rises faster.

## What you spend it on

This is the most useful part of the diary, a confirmed list of the things Political Influence buys. Let me go through them.

Instituting a new estate privilege. Important footnote here, revoking a privilege still costs Stability, and that has not changed. Political Influence applies to the creation side, not the revocation side.

Estate interactions, which arrived in an earlier patch. Spending Political Influence on these temporarily lowers Crown Power, so there is a trade-off to budget for.

Culture and identity actions. You spend it to tolerate or accept a culture, to discriminate against one, to change your primary culture, and to grant urban rights to a region.

Governance and court. Moving your capital, appointing cabinet members, hiring courtiers, and interacting with Situations all draw on the same currency.

Parliament. Applying political pressure in Parliament has one hard confirmed number: 75 Political Influence buys you 25 support.

That is a broad span that reaches across your entire nation. It touches estates, culture, your court, your capital, and your Parliament. In practice that makes Political Influence a resource you always budget, because so many separate actions draw from the same well.

## A few changes that sit alongside it

The same source groups several related changes worth keeping in mind. The Absolutism versus Liberalism axis now produces extra monthly Political Influence at both extremes, an attempt to reward committing to either end of the spectrum instead of staying in the middle. If you tend to sit the gap, this is a nudge toward picking a side.

Societal-value Parliament agendas now cost Stability to enact instead of extra prestige. That unifies the cost across all of them, closing another of the inconsistent-cost gaps the developers keep mentioning.

There is also a separate feature called [Estate Private Armies](/blog/eu5-estate-private-armies/) in the same update, where the Nobles and Cossacks can take privileges to raise their own regiments separate from the crown's army, and those can be pressed into royal service at a legitimacy cost. I want to keep this separate and not blur the line, because Private Armies are their own mechanic, and mixing it into a Political Influence explainer would just muddy both ideas.

One more change worth listing: any estate that holds more than 25 percent power now drains Legitimacy, or the equivalent resource, intended to discourage building one estate up above all the others.

## What is coming

If this ships as described, Political Influence becomes one of the smoothest resources you manage on top of the usual constraints. The practical takeaway is that a good ruler and a good court are worth more than their face value, because they supply the currency that buys so many of these actions. And the 25 percent estate threshold is no longer just a soft suggestion, since overfunding one estate now lets legitimacy drain away.

The most concrete number in the whole update is 75 to 25, what it costs to pressure Parliament into supporting you. That single swap is worth remembering, because once Political Influence lands it becomes one of the clearest descriptions of how much raw influence can buy.

Remember that none of the above is active in the build you can play right now. When 1.4 "Rio Salado" actually arrives, we will see how the details get tuned. Until then, file Political Influence under likely coming soon, and treat nothing here as gospel for your live campaign.

title: Understanding the EU4 Trade Node Network (Interactive Map)
metaDescription: EU4 trade nodes explained: how value flows through the network, why it splits across routes, and how to use our interactive trade map to understand it.
content:
I've played EU4 for years, and trade has always confused me. For a long time I wasn't able to take full advantage of it simply because I never had a clear understanding of how it worked. I built this tool to give you a quick visual guide, the kind of thing I wish I'd had, to help you see how trade actually flows in a much easier and more intuitive way.

## What Are Trade Nodes?

Every province in EU4 feeds its trade value into a **trade node**. Trade nodes are the hubs of the global economy. They collect value from the provinces around them, and that value either gets collected by a nation with trade power in the node, or it flows onward to the next node.

Think of it like a river system. Provinces are the streams that feed into the river (the trade node). The river flows downstream, and at each junction, the water splits based on how much control each branch has. Some of the water gets diverted (collected by nations), and the rest keeps flowing toward the sea.

## The Three End Nodes

The trade network has three **end nodes**, the "seas" where trade value finally settles:

- **English Channel:** the richest end node in the game, fed by trade from the New World, Africa, and Northern Europe
- **Genoa:** the Mediterranean end node, fed by trade from the Middle East, North Africa, and the Atlantic
- **Venice:** the eastern Mediterranean end node, fed by trade from the Levant, the Balkans, and beyond

Once value reaches an end node, it stays there. It doesn't flow anywhere else. It just sits, waiting for a nation to collect it. This is why controlling an end node is so powerful: you're at the end of the line, and everyone's trade has to pass through you.

## How Value Flows

Here's the key mechanic that confuses most new players: **trade value doesn't pick one path. It splits across every available route.**

If a node has three outgoing connections, the value flowing out of that node splits across all three, proportionally to the trade power each downstream node has. If you control 50% of the trade power in one downstream node, you capture 50% of the value that flows there.

This means:
- **Trade power matters everywhere**, not just in your home node
- **Controlling the path** is often as important as controlling the source
- **Merchants** can steer trade toward your preferred route, but they can't stop the split entirely

## Why This Matters for Your Campaign

Understanding the trade network changes how you play:

**1. Your home node is your foundation.** The node where your capital sits is where you collect trade. The more trade power you have there, the more of the value you capture.

**2. Expand toward the end nodes.** The closer you are to an end node, the more value flows through your territory. A nation in the English Channel collects far more than a nation in the middle of the network.

**3. Trade power compounds.** The more provinces you control in a node, the more trade power you have, which means you capture more value, which means you can afford more provinces. It's a snowball effect.

**4. Don't ignore upstream.** Even if your home node is downstream, controlling key upstream nodes lets you steer more value toward yourself.

## Explore It Visually

Understanding trade flow from text is hard. It's a network, and networks are best understood visually. That's why we built a free interactive tool:

**→ [Explore the interactive EU4 trade node map](/tools/eu4-trade-map)**

Click any node to see:
- What feeds into it
- Where its value flows
- Which end node it eventually reaches
- How the value splits across routes

The map has four views: Simple (12 key nodes), Europe (29 nodes), Asia (31 nodes), and Global (78 nodes), plus a search function to jump to any node by name.

Trade in EU4 is a network, not a line. Value flows from provinces into nodes, splits across every available route, and eventually settles in one of three end nodes. The nations that understand this network, and position themselves to capture the flow, are the ones that build the richest empires.

If you've ever wondered why your trade income is lower than it should be, or why the English Channel is so valuable, the interactive map will show you exactly how it all connects.

title: How Estates Work in EU5 and Why They Matter
metaDescription: EU5 estates explained: how the estate system works, what each estate wants, and why managing them is key to a stable and prosperous realm.
content:
Estates are one of the most important internal systems in EU5, and one of the most different from EU4. In EU4, estates were a side system you interacted with occasionally. In EU5, they're central to how you manage your realm. Here's what you need to know.

## What Are Estates?

Estates are the powerful social groups within your realm: the nobility, clergy, burghers, and other classes who hold power and influence. They have their own interests, their own demands, and their own ways of helping or hindering you. EU5's estate system is deeper than EU4's, with more estates, more interactions, and more meaningful consequences.

## Why Estates Matter

Estates aren't optional. You can't ignore them. They control significant portions of your realm's economy and military. How you manage them determines whether your realm is stable and prosperous, or beset by rebellion and infighting.

**What estates provide:**
- **Nobility:** military power, generals, and manpower
- **Clergy:** stability, conversion, and legitimacy
- **Burghers:** trade income, tax revenue, and economic growth

Each estate provides these bonuses at full strength when they're loyal, and withholds them, or worse, actively opposes you, when they're unhappy.

## Estate Influence

Each estate has an **influence** level: how much power they wield in your realm. Influence is affected by:

- **Privileges:** granting an estate privileges increases their influence
- **Actions:** some actions increase or decrease estate influence
- **Events:** events can shift the balance of power between estates

**High influence** means the estate can demand more from you and is harder to control. **Low influence** means they're weaker but also less helpful.

## Estate Loyalty

Estates also have a **loyalty** level: how happy they are with your rule. Loyalty is affected by:

- **Privileges:** granting privileges makes an estate more loyal
- **Actions:** fulfilling their demands increases loyalty; ignoring them decreases it
- **Events:** events can change estate loyalty

**High loyalty** means the estate provides their bonuses at full strength. **Low loyalty** means they withhold their support, and may even support rebels or refuse to pay taxes.

## The Privilege System

Privileges are the main tool for managing estates. Each privilege grants an estate more power and influence in exchange for a bonus to your realm.

**The trade-off:** Privileges are useful because they give you bonuses, but they're hard to revoke. Grant a privilege and the estate's influence grows, making them harder to control. Grant too many privileges and you've created a monster.

**How to use privileges wisely:**
- Grant privileges that give bonuses you actually need
- Don't grant privileges casually. Think about the long-term influence cost
- Revoke privileges when you can afford the loyalty hit

## Estate Agendas

Estates have **agendas**: tasks they want you to complete. These are marked in the estate interface, and completing them is almost always worth it.

**Why agendas matter:**
- Completing an agenda improves estate loyalty
- Agendas give you clear goals and direction
- They're often easy tasks like "build a church in this province" or "win a war against this rival"

## Managing Estates Effectively

**1. Don't let one estate dominate.** A nobility with too much influence can challenge your authority. Keep estates balanced.

**2. Grant privileges strategically.** Privileges give estates more power in exchange for bonuses. They're useful, but they're hard to revoke. Don't grant privileges you'll regret.

**3. Complete estate agendas.** Agendas are easy bonuses. Completing them improves loyalty and prevents problems.

**4. Watch the balance of power.** If one estate becomes too powerful, take actions to reduce their influence, even if it makes them unhappy in the short term.

## Common Mistakes

- **Ignoring estates entirely.** Ignored estates become disloyal, which means lost bonuses and potential rebellion.
- **Granting too many privileges.** Privileges are a slippery slope. Each one makes the estate harder to control.
- **Letting one estate dominate.** A single dominant estate is a threat to your authority.
- **Not completing agendas.** Agendas are easy bonuses. Ignoring them wastes free value.

Estates are the internal politics of EU5. They're not a side system. They're central to how your realm functions. Manage them well, and they'll be your strongest supporters. Manage them poorly, and they'll be the greatest threat to your rule.

The key is **balance**: keep your estates happy enough to provide their bonuses, but not so powerful that they can challenge your authority. Get this right and your realm stays stable through even the hardest wars. Get it wrong and you'll be dealing with internal crises on top of everything else.

title: Europa Universalis 5 Diplomacy Guide: Alliances and Rivals
metaDescription: EU5 diplomacy guide: how alliances, rivals, and diplomatic reputation work, and how to navigate the diplomatic web to your advantage.
content:
Diplomacy is the art of getting what you want without fighting for it. In EU5, it's just as important as it was in EU4. Alliances, rivals, and diplomatic reputation shape every campaign. Here's how to master the diplomatic game.

## The Basics of EU5 Diplomacy

The core diplomatic systems in EU5 are similar to EU4: you can form alliances, declare rivals, improve relations, and negotiate peace deals. The fundamentals carry over, but there are new tools and adjustments that reward careful attention.

**The key diplomatic actions:**
- **Alliances:** mutual defense pacts. Your ally will join your wars, and you'll join theirs.
- **Rivals:** nations you're competing with. Rivalry gives you bonuses but makes the rival hostile.
- **Improve relations:** send diplomats to improve your standing with other nations.
- **Royal marriages:** for monarchies, a marriage creates a bond between two nations.

## Alliances: Your Shield

Alliances are the most important diplomatic tool. A strong alliance can deter attackers, give you military support, and provide diplomatic cover.

**How to build alliances:**
- **Improve relations first.** Nations are more likely to ally you if they like you. Send diplomats to improve relations before asking for an alliance.
- **Match your interests.** Nations with common rivals or common goals are more likely to ally you.
- **Watch your reputation.** A nation with a bad reputation (high aggressive expansion, broken truces) will struggle to find allies.

**How to use alliances:**
- **Don't call allies into every war.** Calling an ally into a war costs favors and can strain the relationship. Save it for wars that matter.
- **Honor your alliances.** Breaking an alliance damages your reputation and makes other nations trust you less.
- **Use allies as a deterrent.** A strong alliance network makes enemies think twice before attacking.

## Rivals: Your Enemies

Rivals are nations you're competing with. Declaring a rival gives you bonuses: power projection, prestige, and a casus belli. But it also makes that nation hostile toward you.

**How to choose rivals:**
- **Pick rivals you can beat.** A rival you can't defeat is just a source of stress.
- **Pick rivals that matter.** Rivalry is most useful against nations that are actually competing with you for territory or influence.
- **Don't over-rival.** Having too many rivals spreads your diplomatic attention thin.

**How to use rivalry:**
- **Use the rivalry casus belli.** Rivalry gives you a CB to humiliate or take territory from your rival.
- **Watch your rival's alliances.** Your rival's allies are your enemies. Plan accordingly.

## Diplomatic Reputation

Your diplomatic reputation is how other nations perceive you. It's affected by:

- **Aggressive expansion:** conquering too much territory makes other nations fear you
- **Broken truces:** breaking a truce damages your reputation severely
- **Diplomatic actions:** some actions improve your reputation, others damage it

**The key insight:** A good reputation makes diplomacy easier. Nations are more willing to ally you, less likely to form coalitions against you, and more likely to accept your peace deals.

## Practical Diplomacy Tips

**1. Always have diplomats working.** An idle diplomat is a wasted diplomat. Improve relations, fabricate claims, and build your diplomatic network.

**2. Watch your aggressive expansion.** High AE is the fastest way to lose friends and gain enemies. Spread your conquests around and let AE decay.

**3. Use your rivals strategically.** Rivalry is a tool, not just a declaration. Use it to gain bonuses and justify wars.

**4. Think about who benefits.** When you go to war, think about who gains and who loses, not just you, but your allies and rivals. Diplomacy is a web, and every action ripples through it.

Diplomacy in EU5 is about building relationships and managing your reputation. Strong alliances protect you, well-chosen rivals give you bonuses, and a good reputation makes everything easier.

The key is to be proactive, not reactive. Don't wait for diplomatic opportunities to come to you. Create them. Improve relations before you need allies, declare rivals before you need the bonuses, and manage your reputation before it becomes a problem.

title: EU5 vs EU4: What Changed for Returning Players
metaDescription: EU5 vs EU4: the biggest changes for returning players, from the pop system to trade, estates, and diplomacy. Here's what you need to unlearn.
content:
If you've spent hundreds of hours in EU4, EU5 is going to feel familiar but different. The core DNA is the same. You're still managing a nation, fighting wars, and painting the map, but many of the systems you mastered have been reworked. Here's what changed and what you need to unlearn.

## The Pop System: The Biggest Change

The single biggest difference is the pop system. In EU4, provinces were abstract numbers: development, tax, production, manpower. In EU5, provinces are populated by pops. Individual groups with social classes, cultures, religions, and happiness levels.

You can't just conquer territory and forget about it. You need to manage the people in your provinces. Keep them happy, promote them to better classes, and convert their culture and religion. It's more work, but it makes the game feel more alive.

## Trade: Reworked

EU4's trade system was based on static trade nodes. You steered trade from node to node toward your home node. EU5's trade system is more dynamic, based on supply and demand that shifts as economies change. Goods flow along routes determined by what's being produced and consumed, rather than following predetermined paths.

**What this means for you:** Your EU4 trade instincts may not apply. Don't assume that the same trade nodes are valuable or that the same strategies work. Experiment and learn the new system. Want to see the EU4 trade network visually? Check out our [interactive trade node map](/tools/eu4-trade-map).

## Estates: More Complex

EU4's estates were relatively simple. Three estates with influence, loyalty, and a few privileges. EU5's estates are a core part of your internal management, with more interactions, more consequences, and a deeper relationship with your pop system.

**What this means for you:** You can't just set your estates and forget them. You need to actively manage them. Grant privileges carefully, complete their agendas, and keep them balanced.

## The Military: Levies and Professionals

EU4's military was fairly straightforward. You built regiments and they were your standing army. EU5 splits your military into **levies** (temporary, citizen militias raised for war) and **professional troops** (your permanent, trained standing army). This changes how you think about military spending and warfare significantly.

**What this means for you:** Your EU4 military habits don't carry over. You need to learn how to balance these two forces. When to rely on levies, when to invest in professionals, and how to manage the cost.

## Diplomacy: Similar but Different

Diplomacy in EU5 is broadly similar to EU4. Alliances, rivals, wars, peace deals. The core systems remain recognizable.

**What this means for you:** Your EU4 diplomatic instincts are mostly still valid. Alliances are still important, aggressive expansion still matters, and you still need to watch your reputation.

## What's the Same

Some things haven't changed:

- **The map.** Still province-based, still the same world.
- **War.** Still about armies, sieges, and peace deals.
- **Expansion.** Still about conquering territory and managing the consequences.
- **The goal.** Still about building your nation's power over centuries.

EU5 is EU4's successor, not its replacement. The core game is the same, but the systems have been modernized and deepened. The pop system is the biggest adjustment. You're managing people now, not just numbers.

Give yourself time to unlearn your EU4 habits. Don't assume that what worked in EU4 works in EU5. Experiment, read the tooltips, and be willing to try new approaches. The game rewards players who adapt.

title: Understanding the Pop System in Europa Universalis 5
metaDescription: EU5 pop system explained: how populations work, what social classes exist, and how to manage your pops for a stronger economy and stable realm.
content:
The pop system is the biggest new addition in Europa Universalis V, and it changes how the game plays in fundamental ways. If you're coming from EU4, where provinces were abstract numbers, EU5's pops will take some getting used to. Here's what you need to know.

## What Are Pops?

Pops are the individual population groups that live in your provinces. Each province has multiple pops, and each pop has:

- **A social class:** what they do (farmers, artisans, nobles, clergy, etc.)
- **A culture:** which cultural group they belong to
- **A religion:** what they believe
- **A size:** how many people are in the pop
- **A happiness level:** how content they are

The pop system is inspired by games like Victoria, Paradox's other pop-based grand strategy, but adapted for the early-modern setting of EU5.

## Why Pops Matter

Pops are the engine of your economy. They produce the goods, pay the taxes, and provide the manpower that your nation runs on. But they're also the source of your problems. Unhappy pops cause unrest, refuse to pay taxes, and can even rebel.

**The key insight:** In EU4, you managed provinces. In EU5, you manage pops. It's a more granular, more personal system.

## The Social Classes

Each pop class has a different role:

- **Farmers:** produce food and basic goods. The backbone of your economy.
- **Artisans:** produce manufactured goods. More valuable than farmers but need resources.
- **Burghers:** the merchant class. Generate trade income and tax revenue.
- **Nobles:** the ruling class. Provide manpower and military bonuses but demand privileges.
- **Clergy:** the religious class. Provide stability and conversion but demand influence.

Different classes also respond differently to events. A tax increase hurts farmers more than nobles, while a war benefits the nobility at the expense of everyone else.

## Managing Your Pops

**1. Keep pops happy.** Unhappy pops cause unrest and produce less. Watch their happiness levels and address the causes of discontent.

**2. Promote pops strategically.** You can promote pops to higher classes, turning farmers into artisans, for example. This increases their output but costs money and can cause short-term unrest.

**3. Convert culture and religion.** Pops of a different culture or religion are harder to keep happy. Use your clergy and administrators to convert them over time.

**4. Balance your classes.** A province with too many farmers and not enough artisans is underperforming. A province with too many nobles is unstable. Aim for a balanced mix.

## The Economic Impact

Pops change how you think about your economy:

- Development is different. Instead of abstract development points, your economy is based on what your pops actually produce.
- Buildings matter more. Buildings improve pop output. A workshop makes your artisans more productive.
- Trade is connected. Pops produce the goods that flow through your trade routes.

The pop system is the heart of EU5. It makes the game more complex, but also more rewarding. You're managing people, not just numbers. Keep your pops happy, promote them strategically, and balance your social classes, and your economy will thrive.

The key adjustment from EU4: think in terms of people, not provinces. Every decision you make, whether war, taxation, or buildings, affects your pops. Manage them well, and your nation will prosper.

title: EU5 Army Composition Basics: A Beginner's Guide
metaDescription: EU5 army composition explained: how the levy vs professional troop system works, how to balance your forces, and how to manage your military.
content:
Building and managing an army in EU5 is different from EU4 in one crucial way: EU5 uses a **dual army system** with levies and professional troops. Understanding the difference between these two forces is the most important thing a beginner needs to know about EU5 combat. Here's how it works.

## The Two Armies: Levies and Professionals

**Levies** are the citizen militias that rally to your banner when you go to war. They're the bulk of your early army, and they have distinct characteristics:

- **They're temporary.** Levies are summoned when war breaks out and disband when it ends.
- **They're plentiful but weak.** You can raise large numbers of them, but they're poorly trained and equipped compared to professionals.
- **They spawn from your provinces.** Your levy pool comes from your population, so a larger population means more levies.
- **They're cheap.** Levies cost little to maintain during war, which makes them attractive for early-game economies.

**Professional troops** are your standing army. Trained, equipped, and always ready:

- **They're permanent.** Professionals stay in your army during peace and war alike.
- **They're expensive.** Professionals cost significantly more to maintain than levies, both in gold and in upkeep.
- **They're reliable.** Professionals fight far better than levies, with higher discipline and morale.
- **They're limited by your economy.** You can only maintain a certain number of professionals based on your budget and military infrastructure.

## Why This Matters

The levy/professional split changes how you think about war in EU5:

**Early game.** You'll rely mostly on levies, with a small core of professionals. Your army is large but fragile. You can win wars, but you need to win them quickly before your levies' morale collapses or they take unsustainable casualties.

**Mid game.** As your economy grows, you transition toward a professional core. Your armies get smaller but stronger. You can fight longer wars because your professionals don't disband.

**Late game.** A fully professional army is the goal. It's expensive to maintain, but it's the most reliable fighting force in the game.

## Building Your Army

With the two-army system in mind, here's what a balanced military looks like:

**Early game:**
- A small professional core (a few thousand men)
- Large levy armies raised for specific wars
- Accept that your levies are expendable. They're there to win the war, not to survive

**Mid game:**
- A growing professional army as your backbone
- Levies used as auxiliary forces or for defensive wars
- Invest in military buildings that improve both your levy pool and your professional capacity

**Late game:**
- A fully professional army as your main force
- Levies kept as a reserve for emergencies
- Professional armies are expensive, but they win wars

## Managing Your Military

**1. Don't waste your professionals.** Professional troops are expensive to replace. Use them for decisive battles, not for garrison duty or siege support.

**2. Levies are expendable, use them that way.** Levies are there to absorb casualties and win wars. Don't be precious with them.

**3. Watch your economy.** A professional army can bankrupt you if you build it too fast. Grow your professional core as your economy allows.

**4. Use terrain and tactics.** Defending in mountains or across rivers gives you a massive bonus. Let the enemy attack you in bad terrain, regardless of which army type you're using.

## Common Beginner Mistakes

- **Treating levies like professionals.** Levies are not your real army. They're a force multiplier. Don't expect them to fight like trained soldiers.
- **Building too many professionals too early.** A professional army is expensive. Build it as your economy grows, not before.
- **Ignoring your levy pool.** Even in the late game, levies are useful as reserves. Don't let your levy pool sit unused.
- **Forgetting maintenance.** At peace, lower your maintenance costs. Raise it to full before going to war.

The levy/professional system is the defining feature of EU5's military. Learn to use both forces effectively. Use levies for scale and expendability, professionals for quality and reliability. As your economy grows, transition toward a professional core while keeping your levies as a reserve.

The key insight: EU5's military is about resource management, not just army composition. You're managing two different forces with different costs, different strengths, and different roles. Master both, and you'll have a military that can handle anything.

## Try It Yourself

Want to see how composition decisions play out? Our **[EU5 Army Battle Lab](/tools/eu5-army-simulator)** gives you and an AI opponent the same 100-point budget to build armies, then fights the battle and explains what happened. It is a great way to feel why Regulars beat Levies and why Artillery changes the opening.

title: Best Starting Nations for New Players in EU5
metaDescription: The best EU5 starting nations for new players: from the safest pick Hungary to the expansion-friendly Ottomans. Here's who to choose and why.
content:
Picking your first nation in EU5 is a big decision. Pick someone too weak and you'll be crushed. Pick someone too complex and you'll be overwhelmed. The sweet spot is a nation that's strong enough to survive your mistakes but simple enough to learn the game. Here are the best starting nations for new EU5 players, based on what the community has learned since launch.

## The Safest Pick: Hungary

Many current guides rank Hungary as the single safest starting nation for new players, and it's easy to see why:

- **Land-focused and forgiving.** Hungary is a land-based power with no naval complexity to worry about. You learn the core systems: economy, military, expansion. No juggling fleets.
- **Strong starting position.** Hungary sits in the middle of Europe with plenty of expansion room in the Balkans and against weaker neighbors.
- **Teaches core systems well.** Hungary's position lets you learn diplomacy, war, and internal management at your own pace, without the pressure of being a major power.

The downside is that Hungary isn't flashy. But for learning the game, that's exactly what you want.

## The Tutorial Pick: Portugal

Portugal has been the classic beginner nation since EU4, and it remains a great choice in EU5:

- **Safe position.** Portugal is on the edge of Europe, protected by the ocean and its neighbors. No one can easily invade you.
- **Clear goals.** Portugal's path is obvious. Expand overseas, build a colonial empire, and dominate trade.
- **Strong economy.** Portugal has access to good trade routes and can build a strong trade economy early.

The Portugal run is straightforward: build your economy, colonize the New World, and become a trade power. It's the closest thing the game has to a guided campaign.

## The Expansion Pick: The Ottomans

The Ottomans are frequently recommended for new players, but not because they're the strongest nation in the game. EU5 starts in 1337, much earlier than EU4's 1444, and the Ottomans begin with less territory than their EU4 incarnation. What makes them great for beginners is their **neighbors**:

- **Weak neighbors.** The Ottomans are surrounded by smaller, weaker states that are ripe for conquest. You can expand steadily while learning the ropes.
- **Strong military traditions.** The Ottoman military is still excellent, giving you a comfortable edge in early wars.
- **Expansion in every direction.** Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa are all open to you.

The key difference from EU4: the Ottomans are a strong *starter* nation because of their opportunities, not because they start near-total. It's a satisfying rags-to-empire experience.

## The Trade Pick: Venice

Venice is a small but wealthy nation, and it's a great pick for beginners who want to focus on trade:

- **Trade powerhouse.** Venice is one of the richest trade nations in the game.
- **Small and manageable.** Venice is a small nation, which means less to manage while you learn.
- **Clear focus.** Venice's path is clear. Dominate trade in the Mediterranean.

The downside is that Venice is small and surrounded by larger powers. You'll need to be careful with your diplomacy.

## The Second Campaign Pick: France

France is a great nation, but it's usually recommended as a *second* campaign, not a first. Here's why:

- **Major power pressure.** As one of Europe's largest nations, France draws constant attention. Coalitions, rivalries, and diplomatic pressure come early.
- **Complex management.** A large realm means more provinces, more pops, and more internal systems to manage while you're still learning.
- **Strong when you're ready.** Once you understand the basics, France is one of the most powerful nations in the game. You can dominate Europe.

If you're coming from another Paradox game and feel confident in the fundamentals, France is excellent. If this is your first grand strategy game, save it for campaign number two.

## What to Look For in a First Nation

If you don't want to pick one of these specifically, here's what to look for:

- **A safe position.** You want room to make mistakes without being crushed.
- **A clear path.** Whether it's colonization, trade, or conquest, a defined goal gives you direction.
- **A manageable size.** A medium-sized nation is easier to manage than a sprawling empire.
- **A strong economy.** A good economy gives you room to recover from errors.

For your first EU5 campaign, pick **Hungary** if you want the safest, most forgiving learning experience. Pick **Portugal** if you'd rather learn through colonization and trade. Once you're comfortable with the basics, try **France** for a more powerful, more demanding campaign, or **The Ottomans** for steady expansion.

The key is to pick a nation that gives you room to learn. You'll have plenty of time to play the hard starts once you know what you're doing.

title: How to Manage Unrest in Europa Universalis 5
metaDescription: EU5 unrest explained: what causes rebellions, how to keep your population happy, and how to stabilize newly conquered territory.
content:
Unrest is one of the most important internal threats in Europa Universalis V. Unlike EU4, where unrest was a simple province modifier, EU5 ties unrest directly to your population. Different pop groups in your realm have their own concerns, and when they're unhappy, they let you know. Here's how to keep your realm stable.

## How Unrest Works in EU5

Unrest in EU5 is tied to your **populations**. Each province contains pop groups with their own culture, religion, and social class. When those pops are unhappy, they generate unrest, and enough unrest in a province can lead to rebellions that threaten your control.

**Key factors that drive unrest:**

- **Cultural differences:** pops of a different culture than your primary culture are more restless. The larger the cultural gap, the more unrest they generate.
- **Religious differences:** pops of a different religion are harder to keep content. Converting them takes time, but it's worth it for long-term stability.
- **Taxation:** high tax rates generate unrest, especially among lower-class pops who bear the brunt of the burden.
- **Recent conquest:** newly conquered territory has elevated unrest for years. The pops remember who they used to belong to.
- **War exhaustion:** long wars wear down your population's patience and increase unrest across your entire realm.

## Stabilizing New Territory

This is the most common source of unrest problems for beginners. You conquer territory, and suddenly you have a rebellion problem. Here's how to handle it:

**1. Take territory in manageable chunks.** Conquering too much territory too fast creates a massive unrest problem that can spiral out of control. Take what you can stabilize, not what you can conquer.

**2. Prioritize corruption reduction.** Corrupt provinces generate unrest and are harder to manage. Deal with corruption before it spreads.

**3. Station troops.** Having soldiers in a rebellious province deters rebellion and reduces the chance of uprisings. But this costs money, so use it strategically.

**4. Lower taxes temporarily.** If a province is on the edge of rebellion, lowering its tax rate can buy you time to stabilize it through other means.

## Long-Term Unrest Management

For permanent stability, you need to address the root causes:

**1. Convert culture.** Your administrators can gradually convert pops to your primary culture. This is slow but permanent. Converted pops stop generating cultural unrest.

**2. Convert religion.** Similarly, your clergy can convert pops to your state religion. Religious converts are much easier to manage.

**3. Watch your war exhaustion.** Long wars destabilize your entire realm. If your war exhaustion is high, consider making peace even if the deal isn't ideal.

**4. Balance your economy.** An overtaxed population is an unhappy population. Keep tax rates sustainable rather than squeezing every last coin.

## Rebels and Revolts

When unrest reaches its breaking point, rebels appear. Here's what to expect:

- **Rebel armies** spawn in provinces with high unrest
- They'll try to seize control of the province and may spread to neighboring territory
- You can crush them militarily, but that's a temporary fix. The underlying unrest remains
- **The real solution** is addressing what caused the unrest in the first place

Unrest in EU5 is a management challenge, not a punishment. It's the game telling you that your population isn't happy, and it's giving you a chance to fix the problem before it becomes a rebellion.

The key principles: don't overextend, convert culture and religion over time, keep taxes sustainable, and watch your war exhaustion. Do those four things consistently, and unrest will stay manageable.

The important difference from EU4: unrest isn't just a number to be suppressed. It's a signal about what's wrong with how you're ruling your people. Listen to it, and you'll be a better ruler.

title: EU5 Beginner's Guide: Trade and Merchants Explained
metaDescription: EU5 trade and merchants explained: how trade routes work, how to use merchants effectively, and how to build a strong trade economy.
content:
Trade in Europa Universalis V is one of the most important systems in the game, and also one of the most different from EU4. If you're coming from EU4, you'll need to unlearn some habits. The trade system has been significantly reworked. Here's what you need to know to get started.

## How Trade Works in EU5

The core concept is that goods are produced in provinces and flow through trade routes to where they're needed. The key difference from EU4 is that EU5 uses a more dynamic trade system based on supply and demand, rather than EU4's static trade nodes. Goods flow along routes based on what's being produced and what's being consumed, which means trade patterns can shift over time as economies change.

The key thing to understand is that trade is about connecting production to demand. Provinces produce goods, and those goods flow to places where they're needed. Your job as a ruler is to position yourself to capture value from that flow. If you're coming from EU4, you can see how the old trade node network worked visually with our interactive trade node map.

## Merchants

Merchants are your agents in the trade system. They're assigned to trade routes and trade centers, and they help you capture more value from the goods flowing through your realm. Merchants are obtained through trade-related buildings, ideas, and certain nation bonuses.

**The basics:**
- Assign merchants to the most valuable trade routes you have access to
- Merchants in your home region are more effective than those far away
- You can move merchants between routes, but there's a cooldown

## Building a Trade Economy

Here's a practical approach to building a strong trade economy as a beginner:

**1. Focus on your home region first.** Before you expand trade networks abroad, make sure your home region is well-connected. Build trade buildings in your capital and key provinces.

**2. Control production.** Trade is only as valuable as the goods being produced. Invest in production buildings in provinces with valuable goods: cloth, wine, iron, and other high-value resources.

**3. Expand into trade routes.** As you conquer territory, look for provinces that sit on important trade routes. Controlling the route is often more valuable than controlling the production.

**4. Use your merchants wisely.** Don't spread your merchants thin. Focus them on the 2-3 most valuable routes and move them only when you have a clear reason.

## Common Beginner Mistakes

- **Ignoring trade entirely.** Trade income can be a huge portion of your economy. Even a small investment in trade buildings pays off.
- **Spreading merchants too thin.** One merchant on a minor route is worth less than two merchants on your best route.
- **Not building production.** Trade without production is like a shop with nothing to sell. Build both.
- **Expanding into poor trade territory.** Not all conquests are equal. Prioritize provinces that add trade value.

Trade in EU5 is a system that rewards attention. You don't need to master every detail to benefit. Just understand that production feeds trade, trade feeds income, and merchants are your tools for capturing that income. Build your home economy first, expand into good trade territory, and keep your merchants focused on the best routes.

As you play more, you'll develop a feel for which routes are worth fighting for. But for now, these basics will keep your economy healthy while you learn the rest of the game.

title: The Clausewitz Engine Explained: What It Means for EU4, EU5, and CK3
metaDescription: The Clausewitz engine explained: the game engine behind EU4, EU5, and CK3, and what it means for how these games play and mod.
content:
If you've played more than one Paradox grand strategy game, you've probably noticed they feel similar under the hood. That's not a coincidence. They all run on the Clausewitz engine, Paradox's in-house game engine. Here's what that means for how these games play, how they mod, and what to expect from future Paradox titles.

## What Is the Clausewitz Engine?

Clausewitz is Paradox's proprietary game engine, named after the Prussian military theorist Carl von Clausewitz. It's been in development since the late 2000s and has powered every major Paradox grand strategy game since: EU4, CK3, EU5, and others like Hearts of Iron and Victoria.

The engine is designed specifically for grand strategy games. It handles the map, the province system, the character system, the event system, and the modding tools that make Paradox games so customizable.

## What the Engine Means for Gameplay

Because EU4, EU5, and CK3 share an engine, they share certain fundamental characteristics:

**The map.** All three games use a province-based map. The world is divided into provinces, and each province has its own characteristics: development, terrain, resources, and so on. This is the foundation of all Paradox grand strategy.

**The event system.** All three games use a scripted event system. Events fire based on conditions, and your choices have consequences. This is how Paradox delivers content, through events, decisions, and missions.

**The modding tools.** This is the big one. The Clausewitz engine is designed to be moddable. The game data is stored in text files that modders can edit, and the engine supports custom content, new mechanics, and even total conversions. This is why EU4 and CK3 have such massive modding communities.

**The performance profile.** The engine is known for being CPU-heavy, especially in the late game. As your empire grows and the number of provinces, characters, and events increases, the game slows down. This is a known characteristic of all Clausewitz games.

## What the Engine Means for Modding

The Clausewitz engine's moddability is one of its greatest strengths. Here's what it enables:

**Total conversions.** Mods like Anbennar (EU4) and the various CK3 total conversions completely replace the game's content. New maps, new mechanics, new events. The engine supports this level of modification.

**Mechanic mods.** Mods that add or change mechanics. New government types, new succession laws, new trade systems. The engine's scripting language makes this possible.

**Content mods.** New events, decisions, and flavor. This is the easiest type of mod to make, and it's how most modders start.

The downside is that the engine's scripting language has a learning curve. It's not as accessible as some modern engines, but the community has built extensive documentation and tools over the years.

## EU5 and the Engine

EU5 runs on an updated version of the Clausewitz engine. Paradox has made significant improvements: better performance, improved graphics, and new systems like the pop system that weren't possible in the older engine versions.

The key question for EU5 is whether the modding community will be able to do the same things they did with EU4. The engine is more modern, which should mean more capability, but it also means modders need to learn new tools and systems. It'll take time, but the foundation is there.

The Clausewitz engine is the reason Paradox games feel like Paradox games. It's the shared foundation that makes EU4, EU5, and CK3 feel related. The map, the events, the modding, the performance quirks. It's also the reason these games have such thriving modding communities.

Understanding the engine helps you understand the games. When you know that the map is province-based, that events are scripted, and that modding is supported, you understand why these games play the way they do. And when EU5's modding scene matures, it'll be because the engine supports it.

The Clausewitz engine has been Paradox's workhorse for over a decade, and it's not going anywhere. It's the foundation of the grand strategy genre.

title: How Prestige and Renown Work Across Paradox Games
metaDescription: Prestige and renown across Paradox games: how these reputation systems work in EU4, EU5, and CK3, and what they mean for your playstyle.
content:
Prestige is one of those words Paradox loves. It shows up in EU4, EU5, and CK3, and it means something slightly different in each game. If you're coming from one Paradox game to another, the differences can be confusing. Here's how prestige (and its cousin, renown) works across the three big grand strategy titles.

## Prestige in EU4

In EU4, prestige is a **national resource**. It belongs to your nation, not your ruler. It's a number from -100 to +100 that affects:

- **Diplomatic reputation:** higher prestige makes other nations like you more
- **Trade power:** higher prestige gives you a trade bonus
- **Military morale:** higher prestige gives your armies a small morale boost
- **Monthly gain:** you gain prestige over time based on your actions

You earn prestige by winning wars, completing missions, and making good decisions. You lose it by losing wars, breaking truces, and making bad decisions.

**The key difference from CK3:** EU4 prestige is a **national** stat. It's not tied to a character. It's tied to the nation itself. It's also a **modifier**, not a currency. You don't spend it. It just makes you better or worse at various things.

## Prestige in EU5

EU5's prestige system is still being refined, but it follows EU4's model. It's a national resource that affects your diplomatic standing and various bonuses. The exact mechanics are still being tuned as the game gets patched and expanded.

**The key takeaway:** If you're coming from EU4, EU5's prestige will feel familiar. It's a national stat that reflects your nation's reputation and affects your interactions with other nations.

## Prestige in CK3

CK3's prestige is completely different. It's a **personal resource**. It belongs to your current ruler, not your dynasty or your realm. It's a currency you spend on:

- **Men-at-arms:** hiring and maintaining elite troops
- **Casus bellis:** declaring wars
- **Decisions:** many decisions have a prestige cost
- **Court actions:** some interactions cost prestige

You earn prestige by winning wars, holding events, and being a successful ruler. When your ruler dies, their prestige is gone. Your heir starts fresh.

**The key difference from EU4:** CK3 prestige is a **personal currency**. It's tied to your character, it's spent on actions, and it resets on succession. It's a much more active resource than EU4's passive modifier.

## Renown in CK3

Renown is CK3's **dynasty resource**. It's separate from prestige and it's the long-term resource that makes your dynasty stronger over generations. You earn it from your dynasty's achievements: members holding titles, winning wars, living long lives. You spend it on:

- **Legacy perks:** permanent bonuses for your entire dynasty
- **Disinheriting:** removing children from the succession line

**The key takeaway:** Renown is the resource that compounds over time. It's the difference between a dynasty that grows stronger with each generation and one that resets every succession.

## The Big Picture

Here's the simplest way to think about it:

- **EU4 prestige** = a national reputation stat. Passive, affects your standing.
- **EU5 prestige** = similar to EU4, still being refined.
- **CK3 prestige** = a personal currency. Active, spent on actions, resets on succession.
- **CK3 renown** = a dynasty resource. Long-term, invested in permanent bonuses.

The common thread is that all of these systems reward success. Win wars, make good decisions, and your reputation grows. Fail, and it shrinks. The difference is in how that reputation is used. As a passive modifier in EU4, or as an active currency in CK3.

If you're moving between Paradox games, the biggest adjustment is understanding that prestige means different things in different games. In EU4, it's a national stat you don't think about much. In CK3, it's a personal currency you're constantly spending. And renown is the long-term resource that makes your dynasty stronger over generations.

Once you understand which system you're dealing with, you'll know how to use it.
