title: EU4 vs EU5 vs CK3: Which Paradox Grand Strategy Game Should You Start With?
metaDescription: EU4 vs EU5 vs CK3: which Paradox grand strategy game should you start with? We compare difficulty, focus, and fun factor for new players.
keywords: best paradox grand strategy game for beginners
content:
Paradox Interactive makes some of the deepest strategy games in existence, and if you're new to the genre, picking your first one is genuinely intimidating. EU4, EU5, and CK3 are the three most popular, but they're very different games. Here's a breakdown to help you decide which one to start with.

## The Three Games at a Glance

**Europa Universalis IV (2013)** is the classic. It's a map-painting, nation-management game set from 1444 to 1821. You play as a nation, not a person, and manage its economy, military, diplomacy, and expansion over centuries. It's the most "grand strategy" of the three, with a focus on trade, war, and diplomacy.

**Europa Universalis V (2025)** is the newest. It's a modernized take on EU4's formula, with a new pop system, updated trade mechanics, and a fresh coat of paint. It's still being expanded with DLC, so it's less content-rich than EU4 but more modern.

**Crusader Kings III (2020)** is the character-focused one. You play as a dynasty. Individual rulers who live, die, and are succeeded by their heirs. It's about family, intrigue, marriage, and personal relationships as much as it is about war and conquest. It's the most roleplay-heavy of the three.

## Difficulty

**CK3 is the easiest to learn.** The character-focused gameplay is more intuitive. You're managing people, not abstract systems. The tutorial is excellent, and the game does a good job of guiding you. It's still deep, but the learning curve is gentler.

**EU4 is the hardest to learn.** It's a decade of accumulated mechanics: trade nodes, monarch points, aggressive expansion, estates, government reforms. There's a lot to absorb. The learning curve is steep, but the depth is unmatched.

**EU5 is somewhere in between.** It's more modern and streamlined than EU4, but it's still a nation-management game with complex systems. It's easier to get into than EU4 but harder than CK3.

## Focus

**CK3 is about people.** Your characters have personalities, relationships, and ambitions. You'll spend as much time managing your family as you will your realm. It's the most personal of the three.

**EU4 is about nations.** You're playing as France, or the Ottomans, or Japan. Your ruler is a stat block, not a character. The focus is on the nation's growth: economy, military, diplomacy, expansion.

**EU5 is about nations, but with more depth.** The pop system adds a layer of internal management that EU4 doesn't have. You're managing not just the nation but its people.

## Fun Factor

**CK3 is the most immediately fun.** The character drama, marriages, betrayals, schemes, succession crises, is inherently entertaining. You'll have stories to tell after your first session.

**EU4 is the most rewarding long-term.** The satisfaction of building a small nation into a world power over 400 years is unmatched. It's a slower burn, but the payoff is huge.

**EU5 is the most promising.** It's new, it's modern, and it's going to get better with DLC. But right now, it has less content than its older siblings.

## Which Should You Start With?

If you want the easiest entry point, start with **CK3**. It's the most accessible, the most fun immediately, and it teaches you the core grand strategy concepts: managing resources, making decisions, dealing with consequences. All in a more approachable package.

If you want the classic grand strategy experience, start with **EU4**. It's the definitive Paradox grand strategy game. The learning curve is steep, but it's the game that defines the genre. And it's cheap. You can pick it up on sale for a few dollars.

If you want the newest thing, start with **EU5**. It's the future of the series, and it's a good time to get in on the ground floor. Just be aware that it's less content-rich than EU4 right now.

There's no wrong answer. All three are excellent games. But if you're a beginner, **CK3** is the best starting point. It's the most accessible, the most fun, and it'll teach you the genre's fundamentals. From there, you can graduate to EU4 or EU5 once you're comfortable with the core concepts.

And if you're still not sure, try them all. They're all on sale regularly, and they all offer hundreds of hours of gameplay. You can't really go wrong.

title: How Renown and Prestige Work in Crusader Kings 3
metaDescription: CK3 renown and prestige explained: how they differ, how to earn them, and what to spend them on for maximum dynasty growth.
content:
Renown and prestige are two of the most important resources in CK3, and they're easy to confuse. They sound similar, they're both earned through your actions, and they both unlock things. But they're completely different systems with different purposes. Here's how they actually work.

## Prestige: The Personal Resource

Prestige is your character's personal reputation. It's earned through your actions: winning wars, hosting feasts, holding grand events, and generally being a successful ruler. It's spent on:

- **Men-at-arms:** you need prestige to hire and maintain elite troops
- **Casus bellis:** declaring wars costs prestige
- **Decisions:** many decisions have a prestige cost
- **Court actions:** some court interactions cost prestige

Prestige is a **short-term resource**. It's tied to your current character, and when they die, their prestige is gone. Your heir starts fresh (though they inherit some based on your legacy).

**The key insight:** Prestige is about your current ruler's ability to act. It's the fuel for your military and diplomatic actions. You want to keep it high so you can declare wars and hire men-at-arms when you need to.

## Renown: The Dynasty Resource

Renown is your **dynasty's** reputation. It's earned through your dynasty's achievements: your dynasty members holding titles, winning wars, and living long lives. It's spent on:

- **Legacy perks:** the dynasty legacy tree, which gives permanent bonuses to your entire dynasty
- **Disinheriting:** removing a child from the succession line costs renown
- **Renaming dynasty members:** a minor but fun use

Renown is a **long-term resource**. It accumulates over generations and is shared across your entire dynasty. It's the resource that makes your dynasty stronger over time, not just your current ruler.

**The key insight:** Renown is about your dynasty's long-term growth. It's the resource that makes your family stronger with each generation. You want to invest it in legacy perks that compound over time.

## How to Earn Prestige

Prestige comes from being a successful ruler. The main sources:

- **Winning wars:** the bigger the war, the more prestige
- **Holding events:** feasts, hunts, tournaments, and grand weddings all give prestige
- **Being a good ruler:** high vassal opinion, successful schemes, and good decisions all contribute
- **Your rank:** kings and emperors earn more prestige passively than counts and dukes

The best way to earn prestige is to be active. Hold events, win wars, and make decisions that boost your reputation.

## How to Earn Renown

Renown comes from your dynasty's achievements. The main sources:

- **Dynasty members holding titles:** the more titles your dynasty holds, the more renown you earn
- **Dynasty members winning wars:** wars won by any dynasty member contribute
- **Dynasty members living long lives:** long reigns generate renown
- **Legacy perks:** some legacy perks boost renown gain

The best way to earn renown is to **spread your dynasty**. Marry your children into powerful families, grant titles to your dynasty members, and make sure your family is well-positioned across the map.

## What to Spend Prestige On

Prestige is a resource you should be spending actively. The best uses:

- **Men-at-arms:** this is the most important use. A strong army is the foundation of your power.
- **Wars:** don't be afraid to spend prestige on casus bellis. Wars are how you grow.
- **Decisions:** many decisions give powerful bonuses. If a decision costs prestige and gives a good bonus, take it.

The key is to keep your prestige high enough to act when you need to, but not to hoard it. A ruler with 10,000 prestige sitting idle is wasting potential.

## What to Spend Renown On

Renown is a resource you should be investing for the long term. The best uses:

- **Legacy perks:** this is the most important use. The legacy tree gives permanent bonuses to your entire dynasty. Prioritize the perks that match your playstyle.
- **Disinheriting:** if you have a problematic heir, disinheriting them is worth the renown cost. It's cheaper than dealing with a succession crisis.

The key is to invest renown in legacy perks early and consistently. The bonuses compound over generations, and a dynasty with a well-developed legacy tree is dramatically stronger than one without.

Prestige and renown are two sides of the same coin. One is your personal reputation, the other is your dynasty's. Prestige is short-term and spent on actions. Renown is long-term and spent on growth.

The best players manage both: keep prestige high for military and diplomatic flexibility, and invest renown in legacy perks that make your dynasty stronger with every generation. Master both, and your dynasty will be unstoppable.

title: Best CK3 Starting Characters for Beginners
metaDescription: The best CK3 starting characters for beginners: from the tutorial-friendly Murchad to the powerful Duke William. Here's who to pick and why.
content:
Picking your first CK3 character is a big decision. Pick someone too weak and you'll be crushed. Pick someone too powerful and you'll be overwhelmed by the mechanics. The sweet spot is a character who's strong enough to survive your mistakes but not so strong that you don't learn the game. Here are the best starting characters for beginners.

Not sure which one fits you? Try the interactive [CK3 Start Selector](/tools/ck3-start-selector/) tool, which asks you three questions, plots the same five starts on a map, and hands you a recommendation with difficulty and a first goal.

## The Tutorial Pick: Murchad, Duke of Munster (Ireland, 1066)

Murchad is the game's recommended starting character, and for good reason. He's the Duke of Munster in southern Ireland, and his situation is perfect for learning:

- **No strong neighbors.** Ireland in 1066 is a patchwork of small counts and dukes. No one can crush you early.
- **Room to expand.** The other Irish rulers are weak enough that you can conquer them one by one.
- **No major threats.** You're not next to England, France, or the Vikings. You can learn at your own pace.

The classic "tutorial Ireland" run is to unite Ireland as Murchad, then expand into England and Scotland once you're comfortable. It's the perfect first campaign.

## The Strong Pick: Duke William of Normandy (France, 1066)

William is the famous one. William the Conqueror. He starts as the Duke of Normandy with a claim on the English throne. He's a strong pick for beginners who want a bit more action:

- **A clear goal.** You have a claim on England. Press it, win the war, and you're the King of England.
- **Strong military.** William has excellent stats and a strong army. You can win the war against Harold Godwinson if you play it right.
- **A powerful position.** Once you're King of England, you have a strong base to build from.

The war for England is a real challenge. You'll need to manage your army, your allies, and your finances. But it's a great learning experience.

## The Relaxed Pick: King Sancho of Castile (Spain, 1066)

Sancho is the King of Castile, one of the Christian kingdoms in Spain. He's a good pick for beginners who want a more relaxed start:

- **Strong position.** Castile is one of the more powerful Christian kingdoms in Iberia.
- **Clear expansion path.** You can expand into the Muslim south or unite the Christian kingdoms.
- **Manageable challenges.** The Iberian struggle adds flavor, but it's not overwhelming.

Spain in 1066 is a complex region with multiple competing powers. It's a bit more to manage than Ireland, but it's still very doable for a beginner.

## The Powerful Pick: Emperor Basil of the Byzantine Empire (867)

Basil is the Byzantine Emperor, and he's one of the most powerful characters in the game. He's a good pick for beginners who want to feel powerful:

- **Massive realm.** The Byzantine Empire is huge, with a strong economy and military.
- **Strong ruler.** Basil has excellent stats and a long reign ahead of him.
- **Interesting position.** You're the bulwark of Christendom against the Muslim powers to the east.

Managing an empire is more complex than managing a kingdom. You have more vassals, more factions, and more to keep track of. It's a good second or third campaign, but maybe not the first.

## The Fun Pick: Count Eudes of Anjou (France, 867)

Eudes is a small count in France, and he's a great pick for beginners who want a challenge:

- **Small start.** You're a single county, which means you learn the basics of survival.
- **Room to grow.** France in 867 is fragmented, and there's plenty of room to expand.
- **Interesting position.** You're in the heart of Europe, with opportunities in every direction.

A single-county start is harder. You'll need to manage your liege, build alliances, and expand carefully. It's a great learning experience, but it's more challenging than the other picks.

## What to Look For in a First Character

If you don't want to pick one of these specifically, here's what to look for:

- **A clear goal.** Whether it's uniting Ireland or conquering England, a clear goal gives you direction.
- **A manageable realm.** A kingdom is easier to manage than an empire. Save the empire for later.
- **No immediate existential threat.** You want to be able to make mistakes without being instantly crushed.
- **Good stats.** A ruler with decent stats makes the early game much easier.

For your first campaign, pick **Murchad of Munster** and unite Ireland. It's the classic beginner experience for a reason. It teaches you the game without punishing you too harshly. Once you've done that, try **William of Normandy** for a more action-packed campaign, or **Sancho of Castile** for a more relaxed one.

The key is to pick a character who gives you room to learn. You'll have plenty of time to play the hard starts once you know what you're doing.

title: CK3 Intrigue Guide: Schemes, Spies, and Secrets
metaDescription: CK3 intrigue guide: how schemes work, how to use your spymaster, and how to murder, seduce, and scheme your way to the top.
content:
Intrigue is the dark side of CK3, and it's one of the most powerful tools in the game. You can murder your way to a throne, seduce your way into an alliance, or blackmail your way into a council seat. It's not always pretty, but it's effective. Here's how the intrigue system actually works.

## The Basics: Schemes

Schemes are the core of intrigue. They're long-term plots you start against a target, and they progress over time until they either succeed or fail. There are several types:

- **Murder:** kill your target. The classic.
- **Seduce:** start a romance with your target.
- **Fabricate Hook:** create a hook on your target.
- **Claim Throne:** press a claim on a title you have a claim to.
- **Abduct:** kidnap your target.

Each scheme has a success chance, which is affected by your intrigue skill, your target's intrigue skill, the scheme's secrecy, and various other factors.

## Scheme Success Chance

Your scheme's success chance is the number you're trying to maximize. Here's what affects it:

- **Your intrigue skill:** higher is better
- **Your target's intrigue skill:** higher is worse
- **Scheme secrecy:** if your scheme is discovered, it fails. Keep it secret
- **Agents:** you can recruit agents to help your scheme. Each agent adds to your success chance, but they also risk exposing the scheme
- **Lifestyle perks:** the Intrigue lifestyle tree has perks that boost scheme success

The key insight: **agents are the most important factor.** A well-staffed scheme with good agents is dramatically more likely to succeed than a solo effort. But every agent is a potential leak, so choose carefully.

## The Spymaster

Your spymaster is your most important councilor for intrigue. They do two things:

- **Find secrets:** your spymaster can discover secrets about characters in your realm or abroad. Secrets are leverage
- **Protect you:** your spymaster can also protect you from schemes targeting you

**Using your spymaster to find secrets** is one of the most powerful actions in the game. Secrets can be used to:

- **Blackmail:** get a hook on someone, which lets you force them to do things
- **Expose:** ruin someone's reputation
- **Imprison:** if the secret is a crime, you can imprison them

## Hooks

Hooks are the currency of intrigue. A hook is leverage you have over someone, and it lets you force them to do things they wouldn't otherwise do. Hooks can be:

- **Strong hooks:** you can force almost anything
- **Weak hooks:** you can force limited things

You get hooks from blackmailing people with secrets, from the Fabricate Hook scheme, and from various events. Hooks are incredibly powerful. You can use them to:

- **Force a council seat:** get yourself on the council
- **Force a marriage:** marry someone who wouldn't otherwise accept
- **Force a title grant:** get a title from your liege
- **Force an alliance:** get an alliance without a marriage

## The Intrigue Lifestyle

The Intrigue lifestyle tree is the skill tree for schemers. The key perks:

- **Schemer:** boosts scheme success chance and secrecy
- **Torturer:** boosts dread, which makes people afraid of you
- **Seductress/Seducer:** boosts seduction schemes and gives you hooks from lovers
- **Truth is Relative:** makes it harder for others to discover your secrets

The Intrigue tree is powerful, but it's not for everyone. It's best for characters who want to play the political game rather than the military one.

## Practical Intrigue Tips

- **Always have your spymaster finding secrets.** An idle spymaster is a wasted spymaster.
- **Don't scheme against everyone.** Every scheme you run risks exposure. Focus on the ones that matter.
- **Use hooks before they expire.** Hooks can expire, so use them while you have them.
- **Dread is your friend.** High dread makes vassals afraid to scheme against you. It's a defensive tool as much as an offensive one.
- **Be careful with murder.** Murdering a powerful ruler can backfire if you're caught. Make sure your scheme is well-staffed and secret.

Intrigue is one of the most powerful systems in CK3, and it's often overlooked by new players who focus on military and economy. But a well-played intrigue game can accomplish what armies can't. Removing a rival, securing a claim, or forcing a marriage. Master the scheme system, keep your spymaster busy, and collect hooks like they're going out of style.

Just remember: what goes around comes around. The same schemes you use on others can be used on you. Keep your own secrets close and your spymaster closer.

title: CK3 DLC Roundup: What Each Expansion Adds
metaDescription: Every CK3 DLC explained: what each expansion, flavor pack, and event pack adds to the game and whether it's worth buying.
content:
Crusader Kings 3 has been out since 2020, and it's built up a solid collection of DLC over the years. Some of it is essential, some of it is nice-to-have, and some of it you can safely skip. Here's a rundown of every major CK3 DLC and what it actually adds.

## The Major Expansions

These are the big ones: the expansions that add major new mechanics and content.

**Royal Court** (2022) is the first major expansion, and it's a big one. It adds the Royal Court itself: a 3D throne room where you hold court, receive petitions, and interact with your vassals. It also adds artifacts, which are powerful items you can collect and pass down through your dynasty. The court system adds a lot of flavor and some genuinely useful mechanics, like the ability to gain prestige and renown from holding court.

**Tours & Tournaments** (2023) adds travel and events. You can now go on tours of your realm, attend tournaments, and participate in grand weddings. It's a flavor-heavy expansion, but it also adds some useful mechanics. Tours can boost your vassal opinion, and tournaments are a great way to build relationships with your knights and courtiers.

**Legends of the Dead** (2024) adds legends: a system where you can create and spread legends about your dynasty. Legends give you bonuses and can be used to claim titles and boost your prestige. It's a unique system that adds a new layer to the game.

**Roads to Power** (2024) is the most recent major expansion. It adds the ability to play as a landless adventurer. You can start with no titles and build your way up through mercenary work, adventuring, and eventually carving out your own realm. It's a completely new way to play the game and one of the most innovative additions to CK3.

## The Flavor Packs

These are smaller than the expansions but add significant content for specific regions.

**Northern Lords** (2021) is the first flavor pack, and it's all about the Norse. It adds new Norse events, decisions, and mechanics, including the ability to go on Viking raids and the Varangian adventure. If you play as a Norse character, this is essential.

**Fate of Iberia** (2022) focuses on the Iberian Peninsula. It adds the Struggle for Iberia mechanic, a unique regional system that tracks the conflict between Christian and Muslim powers in Spain. It's a deep, engaging system that makes Iberia one of the most interesting regions in the game.

**Friends & Foes** (2022) is an event pack that adds new events and interactions between characters. It's lighter on mechanics and heavier on flavor. If you enjoy the roleplay side of CK3, it's worth picking up.

**Wards & Wardens** (2023) is another event pack, this time focused on children and guardianship. It adds new events for raising children, which is a nice addition if you enjoy the family management side of the game.

**Legacy of Persia** (2023) is a flavor pack focused on the Persian region, adding new events, decisions, and mechanics for the area, including the Iranian Intermezzo struggle system. It's a solid choice if you want to play in the Middle East, with depth that rivals the bigger expansions.

**Fate of Iberia** and **Northern Lords** are the standout flavor packs, while the event packs (Friends & Foes, Wards & Wardens) are more of a "buy if you want more flavor" proposition.

## What's Worth Buying

Here's my honest take on what's worth your money:

**Essential:** **Royal Court** and **Tours & Tournaments** add the most content and mechanics. If you're only buying two DLCs, get these.

**Strong:** **Roads to Power** is a genuinely innovative expansion that adds a whole new way to play. **Northern Lords** is essential if you play Norse. **Fate of Iberia** is essential if you play in Iberia.

**Situational:** **Legends of the Dead** is interesting but not essential. The event packs (Friends & Foes, Wards & Wardens) are nice-to-have but skippable if you're on a budget.

CK3's DLC has been consistently good, and the game has grown significantly since launch. If you're new to the game, start with the base game and add **Royal Court** and **Tours & Tournaments**. Those two add the most value. From there, pick up the flavor packs for the regions you play most.

And as always, wait for a sale. Paradox DLC goes on discount regularly, and you can pick up the essentials for a fraction of the full price.

title: CK3 Culture and Faith Mechanics Explained
metaDescription: CK3 culture and faith mechanics explained: how traditions, tenets, and doctrines shape your realm and how to use them to your advantage.
content:
Culture and faith are two of the most important systems in CK3, and they're also two of the most misunderstood. They're not just flavor. They're mechanical systems that shape everything from your military to your economy to your succession. Here's how they actually work. If you are here because of the upcoming By God Alone expansion, the site's [By God Alone preview](/blog/ck3-by-god-alone/) covers every mechanic it confirms, including how theocracies change what this system means.

## Culture: The Basics

Your culture determines your cultural traditions, your innovations (tech), and your cultural acceptance with other cultures. It's the "civilization" layer of your realm.

**Cultural Traditions** are the passive bonuses your culture has. Each culture starts with a set of traditions, and you can add more as you progress through the eras. Traditions can give you bonuses like:

- **By the Sword:** cheaper conquest casus bellis
- **Maritime Mercantilism:** bonus to coastal development and trade
- **Stalwart Defenders:** bonus to defense in your home territory
- **Warrior Culture:** bonus to men-at-arms

Traditions are powerful. They shape your playstyle more than almost anything else.

**Innovations** are your tech tree. You unlock innovations over time, and they give you access to new buildings, new men-at-arms, new succession laws, and new mechanics. Your innovation speed depends on your development and your cultural fascination.

**Cultural Acceptance** is how well your culture gets along with other cultures. High acceptance means fewer penalties for having foreign-culture vassals and provinces. Low acceptance means more unrest and more difficulty managing a multicultural realm.

## Faith: The Basics

Your faith determines your religious doctrines, your tenets, and your relationship with other faiths. It's the "spiritual" layer of your realm.

**Doctrines** are the core beliefs of your faith. They determine things like:

- **Clergy:** do you have a religious head? Are your priests appointed or hereditary?
- **Marriage:** can you have multiple spouses? Can you divorce?
- **Crime:** what's considered a crime? Adultery? Witchcraft? Homosexuality?
- **Gender:** can women inherit? Can they hold titles?

**Tenets** are the special bonuses of your faith. Each faith has three tenets, and they can be anything from:

- **Communion:** vassals pay you for indulgences
- **Monasticism:** reduced stress, a way to deal with spare children
- **Warmonger:** bonus to army size and holy war CBs
- **Pacifism:** reduced stress gain

## How They Interact

Culture and faith interact in important ways:

- **Cultural and religious differences** both contribute to vassal opinion penalties. A vassal of a different culture *and* a different faith is going to be much harder to manage than one who shares both.
- **Holy wars** are religious. You can declare them against neighbors of a different faith. Your culture doesn't matter for this.
- **Cultural acceptance** affects how easily you can convert provinces to your culture. Religious conversion is a separate mechanic.

## Using Culture to Your Advantage

Here's how to make culture work for you:

- **Pick traditions that match your playstyle.** If you're a conqueror, take military traditions. If you're a merchant, take economic traditions. Don't just take whatever looks cool. Think about how it fits your campaign.
- **Focus your innovations.** Your cultural fascination determines which innovation you research faster. Pick the one that matters most for your current goals.
- **Manage cultural acceptance.** If you're conquering foreign territory, you'll have cultural unrest. You can increase acceptance through your steward's "Promote Cultural Acceptance" task, or by having foreign-culture courtiers and councilors.

## Using Faith to Your Advantage

- **Reform your faith.** If you're a pagan or a heretic, you can reform your faith to pick the doctrines and tenets you want. This is one of the most powerful tools in the game.
- **Convert provinces.** Your chaplain can convert provinces to your faith. This reduces religious unrest and makes your realm more stable.
- **Use holy wars.** Holy wars are the most powerful CB in the game. They let you take entire duchies at once. If your faith supports them, use them.

Culture and faith are the two systems that define your realm's character. They're not just flavor. They're mechanical systems that reward planning and management. Pick traditions and tenets that match your playstyle, manage cultural acceptance and religious conversion, and use holy wars and cultural bonuses to your advantage.

The players who master culture and faith are the players who build the most powerful realms. It's worth the time to understand how they work.

title: How to Survive as a Small County in Early Game CK3
metaDescription: How to survive as a small county in early game CK3: from managing your liege to building your economy and expanding without getting crushed.
content:
Starting as a single county in CK3 is the classic underdog experience. You're weak, your neighbors are stronger, and your liege (if you have one) might decide to revoke your title at any moment. But it's also one of the most rewarding ways to play. Building a dynasty from a single county to an empire is the heart of CK3. Here's how to survive the early game.

## Pick the Right Start

Not all single-county starts are created equal. Some are genuinely brutal, others are surprisingly comfortable. When you're picking your start:

- **Look for a county with good development.** High development means more taxes and levies. The counties in Italy, France, and the Byzantine Empire are generally strong.
- **Check your liege.** If you start as a vassal, your liege matters a lot. A weak liege means you can expand within the realm without much interference. A strong liege means protection but also more oversight.
- **Consider your neighbors.** You want neighbors you can beat, or at least neighbors who won't immediately attack you. A county surrounded by stronger counts is a death sentence.

## Manage Your Liege

If you start as a vassal, your relationship with your liege is your lifeline. Here's how to manage it:

- **Send gifts.** A small gift goes a long way toward keeping your liege happy. It's worth the gold.
- **Join their wars.** Even if you don't contribute much, joining your liege's wars gives you a relationship boost and shows loyalty.
- **Don't scheme against them early.** You might be tempted to join a faction to install a new liege, but early on, you're too weak to benefit. Focus on building your own power first.
- **Watch your obligations.** If your liege increases your tax or levy obligations, it hurts. Keep your relationship high to discourage this.

## Build Your Economy

Your economy is your foundation. A single county doesn't generate much, so you need to make every coin count:

- **Build economic buildings first.** The farmlands and tradeport buildings are your bread and butter. Prioritize buildings that boost tax income.
- **Develop your capital.** Spending gold on development is a long-term investment, but it pays off. A developed capital means more taxes, more levies, and more men-at-arms.
- **Don't overspend on men-at-arms.** You need some military, but don't bankrupt yourself. A small, well-equipped force is better than a large, poorly-funded one.
- **Marry for money.** Marrying a rich spouse can give you a significant income boost. Look for spouses with high stewardship.

## Expand Carefully

Expansion as a small county is a delicate balance. You need to grow, but you can't afford to overextend:

- **Fabricate claims.** Your chancellor can fabricate claims on neighboring counties. This is your primary expansion tool early on. It takes time, but it's reliable.
- **Marry for claims.** Marrying someone with a claim on a neighboring county gives you a way to press that claim. This is a powerful expansion method.
- **Attack weak neighbors.** Look for neighbors who are at war, have low troop counts, or are dealing with internal revolts. That's your window.
- **Don't take on too much.** Conquering one county at a time is fine. Conquering three at once will stretch your resources and make your neighbors nervous.

## Build Alliances

Alliances are your shield. A strong alliance can deter attackers and give you the military support you need to expand:

- **Marry your children into powerful families.** This is the most reliable way to build alliances. Marry your heir to a powerful duke's daughter, and you have a powerful ally.
- **Marry yourself well.** If you're unmarried, a good marriage can bring an alliance immediately.
- **Use your alliances.** Don't just sit on them. Call your allies into your wars. They'll do the heavy lifting while you take the territory.

## Survive the First Crisis

Every small county campaign hits a crisis. A war you can't win, a liege who wants your title, a faction that wants you gone. Here's how to survive:

- **Surrender if you have to.** Losing a war isn't the end. You lose some territory or gold, but you live to fight another day. A dead ruler is a game over.
- **Buy time.** If you're being attacked, raise your levies, hire mercenaries if you can afford them, and call your allies. Even a losing battle can buy you time for reinforcements.
- **Go into debt if you must.** Debt is recoverable. A lost title is not. Don't be afraid to take loans to survive.

Surviving as a small county is about patience and smart management. Build your economy, manage your liege, expand carefully, and build alliances. Don't try to do everything at once. Focus on surviving the first few decades, and the growth will come.

The early game as a small county is the hardest part of CK3, but it's also the most rewarding. Stick with it, and you'll be amazed at what a single county can become.

title: Best Religions for Stability in CK3
metaDescription: The best religions for stability in CK3: which faiths keep your realm peaceful, your vassals loyal, and your dynasty secure.
content:
Religion in CK3 isn't just about roleplay. It's a mechanical system that affects everything from vassal opinion to stress gain to how easily you can declare holy wars. Some faiths are dramatically better at keeping your realm stable than others. Here's a breakdown of the best religions for stability, and what makes them good.

## What "Stability" Means in CK3

Before we get into specific faiths, let's define what we're optimizing for:

- **Vassal opinion:** happy vassals don't rebel
- **Stress management:** low stress means your ruler doesn't have a breakdown mid-campaign
- **Succession stability:** fewer succession crises
- **Religious unity:** fewer heretic uprisings and holy wars against you

A faith that's good at these things is a faith that keeps your realm running smoothly.

## Catholicism

Catholicism is the default for most European starts, and it's genuinely one of the best for stability. Here's why:

- **The Pope.** You can request gold, claims, and even excommunications from the Pope. Excommunicating a troublesome vassal gives you a free imprisonment reason. That's a huge stability tool
- **Crusades.** The Pope can call crusades, which are a great way to get rid of problematic neighbors and give your spare sons something to do
- **Wide cultural compatibility.** Catholicism is the dominant faith in Western Europe, so you'll rarely face religious revolts if you're playing in that region
- **The downside:** The Pope can also excommunicate *you*, and he gets cranky if you're too aggressive. But for most campaigns, the benefits outweigh the risks

## Orthodoxy

Orthodoxy is the Eastern Christian faith, and it's arguably even better for stability than Catholicism:

- **The Ecumenical Patriarch** is more controllable than the Pope. You have more influence over him, and he's less likely to cause problems
- **Autocephaly.** You can make your own church head, which means you control excommunication. That's a massive stability tool
- **No crusades against you.** The Orthodox don't have crusades, which means fewer holy wars coming your way

**The downside:** Orthodoxy is less widespread than Catholicism, so if you expand into non-Orthodox territory, you'll face religious revolts.

## Islam (Sunni and Shia)

Islam is excellent for stability, particularly for conquest-focused campaigns:

- **Jihad.** Like crusades, jihads are a great way to redirect your aggressive vassals outward
- **Religious head.** The Caliph can grant claims and excommunicate, similar to the Pope
- **Polygamy.** This is a double-edged sword. More children means more succession problems, but it also means more alliance opportunities
- **The downside:** The Sunni/Shia split can cause internal religious tension if you're not careful

## The Reformed Pagan Faiths

This is where things get interesting. If you start as a pagan faith (Norse, Slavic, Tengri, etc.), you can reform it into a custom faith that's tailored for stability. This is arguably the most powerful option in the game.

When you reform a pagan faith, you pick doctrines that shape it. For stability, you want:

- **Temporal head of faith.** You become the religious head, which means you control excommunication and can declare holy wars at will
- **Lay clergy.** Your priests are appointed by you, not by a religious head, which gives you more control
- **Theocratic or Temporal leadership.** Either works, but Temporal is more powerful

The beauty of reformed paganism is that you can build exactly the faith you want. Want a faith that makes your vassals love you? Pick doctrines that boost vassal opinion. Want a faith that lets you holy war everyone? Pick the right tenet.

## The Tenets That Matter

Regardless of your faith, certain tenets are excellent for stability:

- **Communion.** Your vassals pay you gold for indulgences. It's a money printer and it gives you a reason to interact with your vassals positively
- **Monasticism.** Reduces stress gain and gives you a way to deal with spare children. Send them to a monastery
- **Pacifism.** Reduces stress gain significantly, which is great for long reigns
- **Warmonger.** Increases your army size and makes your vassals happier when you're at war. Great for conquest campaigns

For most players, **Catholicism** is the best starting faith for stability. It's well-supported, has the Pope as a tool, and works well in the most common starting regions. **Orthodoxy** is a strong alternative if you're in Eastern Europe or the Byzantine area.

If you're willing to put in the work, **reforming a pagan faith** with the right doctrines is the most powerful stability option in the game. You get to design your faith around your playstyle, and the control you gain over excommunication and holy wars is unmatched.

The key takeaway: religion isn't just flavor in CK3. It's a tool. Pick a faith that gives you tools for stability, and your realm will be much easier to manage.

title: Crusader Kings 3 Succession Laws Compared
metaDescription: CK3 succession laws compared: from Confederate Partition to Primogeniture. Here's how each one works and when you should switch.
content:
Succession is the thing that ends more CK3 campaigns than any war. You build a great kingdom, your ruler dies, and suddenly your realm is split between your sons like a pizza. Understanding succession laws, and how to work around them, is the difference between a dynasty that grows and one that collapses every generation.

## The Basics

Your succession law determines what happens to your titles when your ruler dies. The default for most starts is Confederate Partition, which is the worst one. As you progress through the game, you unlock better options through innovations and cultural traditions.

The key thing to understand is that succession is about **titles**, not just land. Your primary title (your highest-ranked title) goes to your primary heir. Your other titles get distributed among your other children. The more titles you hold, the more there is to split.

## Confederate Partition

This is the default, and it's the one that causes the most pain. Here's how it works:

- Your titles are split equally among your eligible children
- **New titles are created automatically** to make the split "fair." This is the killer. If you're a king with one kingdom title and you have two sons, the game will create a second kingdom title for your second son, splitting your realm in two
- Your primary heir gets your primary title and the best share, but you'll lose territory

**When it's good:** Never, really. It's the starting law and you should be working to get rid of it as soon as possible.

**How to survive it:** The classic strategies are:
- **Have fewer children.** Disinherit, take the celibacy decision, or just don't have more kids than you need
- **Give your spare sons titles before you die.** If they already hold titles, they'll inherit those instead of taking a share of your realm
- **Kill your spare sons.** It's grim, but it's a time-honored CK tradition

## Partition

Partition is the upgrade from Confederate Partition, unlocked through the Hereditary Rule innovation. The difference:

- Your titles are still split among your children
- **But new titles are NOT created automatically.** If you're a king with one kingdom title and two sons, your second son won't get a new kingdom created for him. He'll just get some of your duchies and counties

**When it's good:** It's a strict upgrade from Confederate Partition. You'll still lose some territory, but you won't have your realm split into multiple kingdoms.

## High Partition

High Partition is the next step up, unlocked through the Royal Prerogative innovation. The key difference:

- Your primary heir gets **at least half** of your titles
- The rest is split among your other children

**When it's good:** This is where succession starts feeling manageable. Your primary heir keeps the core of your realm, and you only lose the fringes. It's a significant quality-of-life improvement.

## Primogeniture

Primogeniture is the endgame of succession laws. Unlocked through the Late Medieval innovations, it's the one you're working toward:

- **Your primary heir gets everything.** All titles go to your firstborn (or your designated heir)
- No more splitting, no more losing territory on succession

**When it's good:** Always. This is the goal. Once you have Primogeniture, succession stops being a crisis and becomes a non-issue.

## Ultimogeniture

Ultimogeniture is the reverse of Primogeniture. Your **youngest** child inherits everything. It's available in the same era as Primogeniture.

**When it's good:** It's a niche choice. Some players prefer it because your youngest child is likely to be younger when you die, meaning a longer reign. But it has the same problem as Primogeniture in reverse. You need to make sure your youngest child is actually the one you want.

## House Seniority

House Seniority makes the oldest member of your dynasty inherit. It's available through the Early Medieval innovations.

**When it's good:** It's a weird one. Your heir is unpredictable. It could be your uncle, your cousin, or your great-grandson. It's useful if you want to keep the realm together and don't care who runs it, but it makes long-term planning very difficult.

## Elective Laws

Elective laws (Feudal Elective, Saxon Elective, etc.) let your vassals vote on who inherits. They're available through various innovations and cultural traditions.

**When it's good:** Elective laws are powerful if you can control the vote. If you have strong relationships with your electors, you can get your preferred heir elected, and you can use it to bypass the partition problem entirely. The downside is that if you lose control of the vote, you could end up with a random vassal on the throne.

## Practical Tips

- **Check your succession tab regularly.** It shows you exactly what will happen when your ruler dies. Don't be surprised on death day.
- **Designate an heir.** If you have the right cultural tradition or innovation, you can designate which child inherits your primary title. This is huge for controlling your succession.
- **Disinherit problem children.** It costs renown, but it's often worth it to keep your realm together.
- **The Partition problem is a feature, not a bug.** The game is designed to make succession difficult. Working around it is part of the challenge.

Your succession law is one of the most important decisions in CK3. Start with Confederate Partition, work toward Partition and High Partition as you unlock innovations, and make Primogeniture your long-term goal. In the meantime, manage your family size, designate heirs when you can, and don't be afraid to disinherit a troublesome son or two.

title: Best EU4 DLC Ranked: Which Expansions Are Worth Buying
metaDescription: The best EU4 DLC ranked from essential to skippable. Here's which expansions are worth your money and which you can safely ignore.
content:
EU4 has a lot of DLC. Like, a lot. Over a decade of expansions, immersion packs, and content packs have piled up, and if you're new to the game, figuring out what's worth buying is genuinely overwhelming. The good news is that you don't need everything. Here's my ranking of the EU4 DLC, from essential to skippable.

## The Essentials

These are the DLCs that add core mechanics you'll interact with in every single campaign. If you're only buying a few, start here.

**Art of War** is the single most important DLC in the game. It adds the ability to transfer occupation of provinces to allies, which is essential for coordinated wars. It also adds the League War, which is a major late-game event, and a bunch of quality-of-life features like army templates and the ability to drill armies. If you buy one DLC, make it this one.

**Common Sense** is the other essential. It adds development: the ability to spend monarch points to increase a province's development. This is a core mechanic that affects everything from your economy to your force limit. Playing without it feels like playing a different, worse game.

**Rights of Man** adds great power mechanics, which are important in the late game. It also adds ruler traits, which add flavor and depth to your monarchs. The ability to abdicate and disinherit rulers is a huge quality-of-life feature.

## The Strong Additions

These DLCs add significant mechanics that enhance the game, but they're not as universally essential as the top three.

**Mandate of Heaven** is essential if you want to play in Asia. It adds the Mandate of Heaven system for China, the Age mechanics (which are actually global), and the ability to use the "Unify China" CB. The Age mechanics alone make this worth it. They add objectives and bonuses that change how you play each era.

**Cradle of Civilization** adds army professionalism, which is a global mechanic that affects all nations. It also adds the ability to drill armies and a bunch of Middle Eastern flavor. The army professionalism system is a nice addition, but it's not game-changing.

**Dharma** is essential if you want to play in India. It adds the government reform system (which is actually global), trade companies, and a bunch of Indian content. The government reforms are a major addition that affects every nation.

**Emperor** is a big one. It reworks the Holy Roman Empire, adds the Council of Trent, and adds a bunch of European content. If you play in Europe, this is essential. If you play elsewhere, it's less important.

## The Good But Situational

These DLCs are good, but they're only worth buying if you play the regions or mechanics they focus on.

**Golden Century** is for Iberia and colonization. It adds the ability to create trade companies in the New World, which is nice for colonial nations. If you play Spain, Portugal, or a colonial nation, this is worth it. Otherwise, skip it.

**Rule Britannia** is for Britain and naval play. It adds the ability to promote cultures, which is a nice mechanic, and a bunch of British content. If you play Britain, it's worth it. Otherwise, skip it.

**Mare Nostrum** is for the Mediterranean and naval play. It adds naval missions, espionage improvements, and a bunch of Mediterranean content. If you play a naval nation, it's worth it. Otherwise, skip it.

**Leviathan** is controversial. It adds monuments, which are powerful but can be unbalanced, and a bunch of Asian content. The monuments are actually a lot of fun, but the DLC had a rough launch and some players still avoid it. If you want monuments, it's worth it. Otherwise, skip it.

## The Skips

These DLCs are either too niche or too weak to recommend.

**Conquest of Paradise** is for native American nations. It adds a few mechanics for playing as natives, but it's pretty thin. Unless you specifically want to play as a native nation, skip it.

**Wealth of Nations** is for trade. It adds trade companies and a few trade mechanics, but most of its content has been absorbed into other DLCs over the years. Skip it.

**Res Publica** is for republics. It adds a few republic-specific mechanics, but it's very thin. Skip it.

## The Content Packs

The content packs (like the various unit packs and music packs) are purely cosmetic. They add new unit models, music, and flavor events. They're nice to have if you want more flavor, but they don't add any mechanics. Buy them only if you have money to spare.

EU4 DLC goes on sale constantly. Wait for a Steam sale and you can pick up the essentials for a fraction of the full price. There's no rush, the game is still great with just the core DLC.

title: EU4 Government Reforms Explained
metaDescription: EU4 government reforms explained: how the reform system works, which reforms to pick, and how to progress through the tiers efficiently.
content:
Government reforms are one of those EU4 systems that seems complicated at first but is actually pretty straightforward once you understand it. They're essentially a tech tree for your government. You earn reform progress over time, and you spend it on reforms that give you permanent bonuses and unlock new mechanics. Here's how it all works.

## The Basics

Every nation in EU4 has a government type: monarchy, republic, theocracy, tribe, and so on. Government reforms are a set of tiers (1 through 12) that you progress through over the course of the game. Each tier has a choice of reforms, and each reform gives you a permanent bonus.

You earn reform progress passively over time. The rate depends on your government type and a few other factors. You can also get reform progress from certain events, ideas, and decisions. Once you have enough progress, you can pick a reform from the next tier.

## The Reform Tiers

The tiers are numbered 1 through 12, and they unlock as the game progresses. Higher tiers are locked behind both reform progress and, in some cases, the in-game date. You can't rush to tier 12 in the first 50 years. The game gates it.

Each tier offers a choice of reforms, and the choices are usually themed around your government type. A monarchy might choose between different types of royal courts or administrative structures, while a republic might choose between different electoral systems. Some reforms are clearly better than others, and some are situational.

## Choosing Reforms

The key to picking reforms is understanding what fits your playstyle:

**Early tiers (1-3).** These shape your government's foundation. For monarchies, you're choosing between reforms that boost legitimacy, prestige, or administrative efficiency. For republics, you're choosing between electoral systems and civic structures. Think about whether you're playing tall (development, trade, economy) or wide (conquest, expansion, military).

**Mid tiers (4-7).** This is where reforms start having a bigger impact. You're choosing between options that affect your economy, your military, or your internal management. If you're playing a conquest-heavy campaign, prioritize reforms that boost your military or administrative efficiency. If you're playing tall, look for reforms that boost development or trade.

**Late tiers (8-12).** These reforms are powerful but come late. They can completely transform your nation, so plan ahead. Some reforms unlock special government mechanics that change how your nation plays.

## Reform Progress Tips

Getting reform progress faster means getting your reforms sooner. Here's how to speed it up:

- **Pick the right government type.** Some governments generate reform progress faster than others. Republics and theocracies generally get more than monarchies.
- **Take ideas that boost reform progress.** The **Administrative** idea group has a reform progress bonus, and some national ideas do too.
- **Watch for events.** Several events give you reform progress as a reward. It's usually worth taking the reform progress over the alternative.
- **Don't reform too early.** This sounds counterintuitive, but some reforms have downsides. Read the tooltip carefully before you pick. A reform that looks good on paper might hurt your playstyle.

## The Absolutism Connection

Government reforms interact with absolutism, which is a late-game mechanic that boosts your administrative efficiency. Some reforms give you absolutism bonuses, and having a high reform tier makes it easier to reach high absolutism. If you're planning a late-game conquest campaign, pay attention to reforms that boost absolutism.

Government reforms are a system you'll interact with throughout the entire game, but you don't need to stress about them. The key is to understand what each reform does and pick the ones that fit your playstyle. Don't just pick the first option. Read the tooltips, think about your campaign goals, and choose accordingly.

The system rewards planning. If you know you're going to play a tall trade empire, pick reforms that boost trade and development. If you're planning a world conquest, pick reforms that boost absolutism and administrative efficiency. The reforms are there to support your strategy, not to dictate it.

title: Why EU4 Still Has a Massive Playerbase After EU5's Launch
metaDescription: EU5 is out, but EU4 still has a massive playerbase. Here's why players are sticking with the decade-old classic and whether it's still worth playing.
content:
Europa Universalis V launched in November 2025, and the natural assumption was that EU4 would start to fade away. That's what usually happens when a sequel comes out. The old game slowly dies as players migrate. But that's not what's happening here. EU4's playerbase has stayed remarkably strong, and there are some very good reasons why.

## A Decade of Content

EU4 has been out since 2013. That's twelve years of DLC, patches, and free updates. The game has accumulated an absolutely enormous amount of content: dozens of DLC packs, hundreds of events, thousands of provinces, and mechanics that have been refined and expanded over a decade.

EU5 is a new game, and it's starting from scratch. It has its own content, but it can't match the sheer depth that EU4 has built up over twelve years. For players who've invested hundreds of hours into EU4, the idea of starting over with a game that has a fraction of the content is a hard sell.

## The Modding Scene

EU4 has one of the most active modding communities in strategy gaming. Total conversions like Extended Timeline and Anbennar, overhaul mods like MEIOU & Taxes, and hundreds of quality-of-life mods have kept the game fresh for years. Some of these mods are essentially entire games built on EU4's foundation.

EU5's modding scene is still in its infancy. It will get there eventually, but it's going to take years to match what EU4's community has built. For players who love modded EU4, there's no reason to switch yet.

## The Learning Curve

Here's the thing about EU4 players: they've spent years learning this game. They know the trade system, the combat mechanics, the diplomatic web, the estate interactions. They've internalized it all.

EU5 is a new game with new mechanics. The pop system, the new trade system, the different approach to estates, it's all different. For a veteran EU4 player, switching to EU5 means going back to being a beginner. That's a hard thing to do when you've spent a decade mastering a game.

## The Price Factor

EU4 has been out for twelve years. It goes on sale constantly. You can pick up the base game for a few dollars, and even the DLC goes on deep discounts regularly. A new player can get the complete EU4 experience for a fraction of what EU5 costs.

EU5 is a new game at full price, with its own DLC roadmap ahead of it. For budget-conscious players, EU4 is simply the better value right now.

## The Community

EU4 has a massive, established community. There are active subreddits, Discord servers, YouTube channels, and Twitch streamers all dedicated to the game. The competitive multiplayer scene is still going strong. When you play EU4, you're part of a huge, active community.

EU5's community is growing, but it's not there yet. For many players, the community is a big part of why they play, and EU4's community isn't going anywhere.

## Is EU4 Still Worth Playing in 2026?

Absolutely. If you've never played EU4, it's still one of the best grand strategy games ever made, and it's cheaper than ever. If you're a returning player, there's a decade of content to explore that you might have missed.

The honest answer is that EU4 and EU5 are different games with different strengths. EU4 has depth, content, and a mature modding scene. EU5 has modern graphics, new mechanics, and the promise of future content. They're not really competing with each other. They're offering different experiences.

EU4's playerbase isn't shrinking because EU5 launched. It's staying strong because EU4 is still a great game in its own right. Twelve years of content, a thriving modding scene, a massive community, and a price point that's hard to beat. That's a combination that's going to keep EU4 alive for years to come.

If you're wondering whether to pick up EU4 in 2026, the answer is yes. It's not going anywhere.

title: How to Create a Custom Nation in EU4
metaDescription: A complete guide to creating custom nations in EU4: from choosing your starting location to spending your points on ideas, traditions, and bonuses.
content:
Custom nations are one of EU4's most underrated features. You can design your own country from scratch. Pick its location, culture, government, ideas, and even its flag. It's a great way to create your own challenge, roleplay a fictional nation, or just mess around with overpowered combinations. Here's everything you need to know.

## Getting Started

When you start a new game, you'll see the option to create a custom nation in the nation selection screen. It's the button that looks like a blank flag. Click it and you're in the editor.

The first thing you'll notice is that everything costs points. You have a budget (the default is 200 points, but you can adjust it in the game settings before you start), and every choice you make costs points: location, ideas, government, ruler. The better the bonus, the more it costs. This is the core balancing mechanic of custom nations.

## Choosing Your Location

Your starting location determines a lot. You can place your nation anywhere on the map, and the game will automatically generate your borders based on the provinces you select.

A few things to think about:

- **Development.** Starting in a high-development region (like Europe or India) gives you a stronger economy but also puts you next to powerful neighbors. Starting in a low-development region (like Siberia or the Americas) is safer but slower.
- **Trade.** If you want to play a trade-focused game, start near a good trade node. The English Channel, Genoa, and Venice are the classic money nodes.
- **Expansion room.** Think about where you can expand. Starting in a crowded region means fighting for every province. Starting in a sparsely populated area gives you room to grow without early wars.

## Spending Your Points

The point system is where custom nations get interesting. Here's what you're spending on:

**Ideas and Traditions.** This is the most important part. You pick a tradition (your first idea bonus) and then a set of ideas. The costs vary based on how powerful the bonus is. For example, +10% discipline is expensive, while +1 tolerance of heretics is cheap. You can pick up to 7 ideas, and the cost increases with each one.

**Government and Religion.** Your government type and religion are free choices, but they affect your gameplay significantly. A republic plays differently from a monarchy, and your religion determines your interactions with neighbors.

**Ruler and Heir.** You can customize your ruler's stats, and better stats cost more points. A 6/6/6 ruler is expensive but gives you a massive early-game advantage. You can also pick traits and decide whether to have an heir.

**Culture and Technology Group.** Your culture determines your national bonuses and who considers you an ally or enemy. Your technology group affects your unit types and tech costs. Western tech is the most expensive but gives the best units.

## The Point Budget

The default 200 points is a good starting point. It forces you to make trade-offs, you can't have everything. Here are some strategies:

If you want a chill, tall playthrough, spend your points on development-boosting ideas and a strong ruler. Play tall, develop your provinces, and don't expand much.

If you'd rather conquer the world, spend your points on military ideas like discipline, morale, and combat ability. Start small but strong, and expand aggressively. Your early armies will be terrifying.

If you want to build a trade empire, spend your points on trade ideas and start in a good trade node. Build a trade empire and let the money roll in.

## The Point Cap

If you want to go wild, you can increase the point cap in the game settings before starting. The maximum is 800 points, which lets you create a truly overpowered nation. This is fun for a single-player power fantasy, but it can make the game boring if you go too far. A 400-point nation is a good sweet spot for a challenging but powerful custom run.

## Tips and Tricks

- **Flag design.** The flag editor is surprisingly deep. You can layer symbols, change colors, and create something that actually looks good. Take a few minutes with it. You'll be looking at that flag for the whole campaign.
- **Name and color.** Your nation's name and map color are also customizable. Pick something you'll enjoy seeing on the map.
- **Achievements.** Custom nations can earn achievements, but there are a few that specifically require custom nations (like "For Odin!" which requires starting as a Norse custom nation). Check the achievement list if you're hunting.
- **Multiplayer.** Custom nations work in multiplayer, which can lead to some very silly games. Just make sure everyone agrees on the point cap first.

Custom nations are a fantastic way to experience EU4 in a completely different way. Whether you want to roleplay a fictional empire, create a challenging start, or just build an overpowered monster for fun, the custom nation editor gives you the tools. Start with the default 200 points to learn the system, then experiment with higher caps once you know what you're doing.

title: Common EU4 Beginner Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
metaDescription: The most common EU4 beginner mistakes that ruin campaigns, and how to avoid them. Learn from other players' failures before you make your own.
content:
Everyone's first EU4 campaign ends in disaster. It's practically a rite of passage. You pick a nation, expand a bit, and then suddenly you're drowning in debt, rebels are everywhere, and your neighbors are carving you up like a Thanksgiving turkey. The good news is that most of these failures come from the same handful of mistakes. Here's what they are and how to avoid them.

## Overextending Too Fast

This is the #1 killer of beginner campaigns. You conquer a bunch of territory, and then the game punishes you with overextension. That causes unrest, which causes rebels, which causes your empire to collapse from within.

The fix is simple: don't take more than you can handle. Watch your overextension percentage. If it's above 100%, you're in dangerous territory. Above 200%, you're basically asking for a disaster. Take territory in chunks, core it, deal with the unrest, and then expand again. The pace matters more than the amount.

## Ignoring Aggressive Expansion

Aggressive expansion (AE) is the diplomatic penalty you get for conquering territory. It makes neighboring nations hate you, and if it gets high enough, they'll form coalitions against you. A coalition of five or six medium nations can easily crush a beginner who's used to fighting one enemy at a time.

The fix: watch the AE icon when you're making peace deals. If it's showing a red skull, you're about to trigger a coalition. Don't take that much territory in one peace deal. Spread your conquests around. Take some land in one region, then switch to another area for a while. AE decays over time, so patience is your friend.

## Not Understanding Mana

Monarch points (admin, diplo, military) are the most important resource in EU4. They're used for everything: coring territory, developing provinces, unlocking ideas, and more. Beginners often waste them on things that don't matter, or don't use them at all.

The fix: never let your monarch points sit at the cap. If you're at 999 admin points, you're wasting potential. Spend them on development, ideas, or coring. Also, don't waste points on harsh treatment of rebels, it's almost never worth it. And be careful with your ruler's stats. A bad ruler (low mana generation) can cripple a campaign, so don't be afraid to disinherit or abdicate if you have a terrible heir.

## Going to War Without a Plan

Beginners often declare war and then just wing it. They march their army around, lose battles, and wonder why they're losing. EU4 is a game of careful planning.

The fix: before you declare war, check your enemy's army size, allies, and military tech. Make sure you have a numbers advantage or a tech advantage. Have a clear goal: take this province, break that alliance, humiliate this rival. And always keep your armies together. Splitting your forces is how you get stack-wiped.

## Forgetting About Army Maintenance

This one's subtle. When you're at peace, you should lower your army maintenance slider. It saves a ton of money. But beginners forget to raise it back up before a war, and then their armies perform terribly because they're under-maintained.

The fix: get in the habit of checking your maintenance slider before and after wars. Lower it at peace, raise it to full before you declare war. It's a small thing, but it makes a huge difference to your economy and your military performance.

## Not Using Your Diplomats

Diplomats are a limited resource, and beginners often let them sit idle. You should be using them constantly. Improving relations with potential allies, fabricating claims on territory you want, and keeping your rivals humiliated all take time, and every month a diplomat sits idle is a month of missed progress.

The fix: always have your diplomats working. Fabricate claims before you need them. Improve relations with nations you want to ally. Send them to improve relations with nations that have high AE against you, it makes the penalty decay faster.

## Ignoring Trade

Trade is one of the most powerful economic systems in EU4, and also one of the most confusing for beginners. Many new players simply ignore it entirely and then they wonder why they're always broke.

The fix: at minimum, send your merchants to the best trade nodes you have access to. If you're playing a European nation, you should be steering trade toward your home node. Don't worry about the full complexity of the trade system at first. Just get your merchants working and collect where you can. As you get more comfortable, you can start optimizing. Want to see how the whole network connects? Check out our [interactive trade node map](/tools/eu4-trade-map).

EU4 is a game where you learn by failing. But you don't have to make every mistake yourself. Avoid these seven and you'll be ahead of where most players are after their first few campaigns. The key themes are: don't overextend, watch your AE, manage your mana, plan your wars, and use your resources (diplomats, merchants, maintenance) actively. Do that, and your first successful campaign is much closer than you think.

title: EU4 Achievement Guide: Easiest Achievements to Unlock First
metaDescription: The easiest EU4 achievements to unlock first, from quick one-session runs to relaxed campaigns. Start your achievement hunting with these.
content:
Achievement hunting in EU4 is a whole hobby in itself. Some achievements are brutal. The kind that take 20 hours of careful planning and a bit of luck. But plenty of them are genuinely easy, and a few you can knock out in a single evening. If you're new to chasing achievements, or just want to pad out your collection without pulling your hair out, this list is for you.

## The One-Session Achievements

These are the ones you can grab in a single sitting, often within the first few decades of a campaign.

**Forever Golden:** Start as Castile, get a golden age. That's it. Castile starts in a strong position with a decent economy, and golden ages trigger naturally once you hit 50 power projection and 50 prestige. You'll get there within the first 20 years just by playing normally. This is probably the easiest achievement in the entire game.

**It's All About the Money:** Accumulate 3000 gold. This sounds harder than it is. As any decent-sized nation, you'll hit this by the mid-1500s just through normal play. Pick a nation with a strong economy like France, Ottomans, or even Portugal, and you'll get there without thinking about it.

**A Fine Goosestep:** Form Prussia. This one takes a bit more effort but is very achievable. Start as Brandenburg, which is the classic path. You need to conquer some territory, convert to Protestantism, and form Prussia. It's a fun campaign that teaches you a lot about the game, and the payoff is getting to play as Prussia, which has arguably the best military ideas in the game.

**The Iron Prince:** Form Prussia as a nation that isn't Brandenburg or the Teutonic Order. This is a step up from A Fine Goosestep but still very doable. Pick a small German state, expand a bit, and form Prussia. It's a good challenge for someone who's played a few campaigns already.

## The Relaxed Campaign Achievements

These take a full campaign but don't require anything stressful or particularly skilled.

**No Trail of Tears:** As a native American nation, own all of your culture group's provinces. Pick a nation like the Cherokee or the Iroquois, and just play tall. You don't need to fight anyone major. Just consolidate your region and survive the Europeans when they show up. The key is to reform your government before the colonizers get too aggressive. It's a chill campaign that's more about survival than conquest.

**The Sun Never Sets on the Indian Empire:** Form the Indian Empire. Start as any Indian nation, Vijayanagar is the easiest pick, and conquer the subcontinent. It's a straightforward conquest campaign with no real threats from outside India until the Europeans arrive late. You can do this at your own pace.

**A Manchurian Candidate:** As a Jurchen tribe, form Qing. Start as Jianzhou, which is the strongest of the Jurchen tribes, and work your way through unifying the tribes, then taking on Ming. The Ming will eventually collapse on their own if you're patient, which makes this easier than it sounds. It's a satisfying campaign that teaches you about the Mandate of Heaven mechanics.

**The Grand Armada:** Have 500 heavy ships. This is a weird one because it's purely an economy check. Play as a rich nation like Great Britain or the Netherlands, build up your economy, and then just spam heavy ships. You'll need a lot of naval force limit, which means you need a lot of development. It's not hard, just takes a while.

## The "Just Play the Game" Achievements

Some achievements you'll get by accident just by playing a normal campaign.

**Viva la Revolución!:** Have a revolution. This happens naturally in the late game if you're playing a large nation. The revolution disaster will fire, you deal with it, and the achievement pops. You don't need to do anything special.

**The Reformer:** Complete a full reform track. Any nation can do this. Just keep playing and spending reform progress, and you'll get it eventually. It's a nice one to pick up in any campaign.

**A Decent Reserve:** Have 100,000 manpower in reserve. As a large nation with a good economy, this happens naturally in the mid-to-late game. Build some manpower buildings if you're short, but honestly, you'll get this just by playing.

## Tips for Achievement Hunting

A few things that make achievement hunting much easier:

- **Use the achievement map mode.** It shows you which provinces you need for each achievement. Invaluable for planning.
- **Check the requirements before you start.** Some achievements have hidden requirements or specific start dates. The wiki is your friend.
- **Don't be afraid to restart.** If your opening goes badly, restart. The first 20 years often determine whether an achievement run is viable.
- **Ironman is required.** All achievements require Ironman mode, so no console commands. Get used to it.

Start with **Forever Golden** and **It's All About the Money**. You'll get both in your first proper campaign without even trying. Then move on to **A Fine Goosestep** for a fun Prussia run, and work your way up from there. Achievement hunting is one of the most rewarding ways to play EU4, and these easy ones are the perfect way to get started.

title: Best EU4 Mods in 2026
metaDescription: The best EU4 mods in 2026, from total conversions to quality-of-life improvements. Here's what's worth installing and what to skip.
content:
Europa Universalis IV has been out for over a decade now, and in that time the modding community has built some genuinely incredible stuff. Some mods completely transform the game, others just fix the little annoyances that Paradox never got around to. With EU5 now out, you might think the mod scene for EU4 would be winding down, but honestly, it's the opposite. The community is still incredibly active, and 2026 has some standout mods worth your time.

Here's my rundown of the best EU4 mods in 2026, broken down by what they do.

## The Total Conversions

If you want a completely different game built on EU4's bones, these are the big ones.

**Extended Timeline** is still the king of total conversions. It lets you play from 58 AD all the way to 9999 AD, with thousands of new nations, historical events, and mechanics that adapt to whatever era you're in. Want to play as the Roman Empire in its prime? Or a futuristic space-faring nation? This mod has you covered. It's been updated consistently for years and remains one of the most impressive mods ever made for any Paradox game.

**Anbennar** is the other major total conversion, and it's a completely different beast. It's a full fantasy world with its own lore, races, magic system, and dozens of unique mission trees. If you've ever wanted to play EU4 but with elves, dwarves, and magic instead of historical nations, this is it. The depth here is staggering. Some mission trees are as detailed as anything Paradox has shipped.

## The Overhaul Mods

These don't replace the game entirely, but they change it significantly.

**MEIOU & Taxes** is the granddaddy of overhaul mods. It adds a population system, a much deeper economy, and a level of simulation detail that makes vanilla EU4 feel almost arcade-like by comparison. The learning curve is steep. This is not a mod for beginners, but if you've played EU4 for hundreds of hours and want something that feels more like a true simulation, this is the one. It's been in development for years and the current version is the most polished it's ever been.

**Voltaire's Nightmare** focuses on the Holy Roman Empire and makes it dramatically more complex and interesting. The HRE in vanilla is a bit of a sideshow, but this mod turns it into a dense, political web of hundreds of tiny states. If you enjoy playing inside the HRE, this is essential.

## Quality of Life Mods

These don't change the game's mechanics, they just make it more pleasant to play.

**Bigger UI** is exactly what it sounds like. It scales up the interface so you don't need a magnifying glass to read tooltips. Simple, essential, and works with most other mods.

**Graphical Map Improvements** is a visual overhaul that makes the map look significantly better without changing gameplay. Better terrain textures, cleaner borders, nicer water. It's subtle but makes a real difference over a long campaign.

**Fast Universalis** is a performance mod that strips out some of the graphical bells and whistles to make the game run much faster on older machines. If your laptop struggles with late-game EU4, this is a lifesaver.

## The Multiplayer Favorites

If you play with friends, a couple of mods are worth mentioning.

**Extended Timeline** works great in multiplayer if everyone's on the same page about the era. **Anbennar** also has a strong multiplayer community. For something lighter, **Better Nation Colors** just makes the map easier to read, which helps when you're trying to figure out who owns what in a chaotic multiplayer game.

## What About the Workshop in 2026?

The Steam Workshop is still the best place to find EU4 mods. The community has been remarkably resilient. Even with EU5 out, the EU4 modding scene is still producing new content and updating existing mods. A few things to keep in mind:

- **Check the last update date.** Some older mods haven't been updated for the latest EU4 patch and may cause crashes or weird behavior. The mods listed above are all actively maintained.
- **Read the comments.** The Workshop comments section is usually the fastest way to find out if a mod is broken after a patch.
- **Use collections.** If you're new to modding, find a well-curated collection and subscribe to it as a bundle. It's much easier than trying to figure out compatibility on your own.

The EU4 modding scene is one of the best in strategy gaming, and it's showing no signs of slowing down. Even with EU5 on the scene, there's a decade of accumulated content here that's absolutely worth exploring.
